findings.impact: Arbitrary, unbounded Cloud SQL spend on the platform's bill from any account, plus exhaustion of the shared GCP project's per-project Cloud SQL instance quota, which denies provisioning to every other tenant.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped the storage route for `tier|limit|storageConfigs.length` — the only hits are the metadata passthroughs at 120/127/417; there is no cap on how many connectors a project or user may hold. Grepped the whole of src/lib and src/app for a tier allowlist (`VALID_TIERS|allowedTiers|db-custom|db-n1`): the only occurrences are the pricing lookup table in src/lib/gcp/monitoring.ts:388-398, which is used for cost *estimation* only and falls back to db-f1-micro for unknown tiers rather than rejecting them. checkUsageLimits (src/lib/billing/caps.ts:43) is not called from any storage route — grep shows its only caller is the deploy route.

findings.title: GitHub webhook deploy path bypasses the usage-limit check enforced on manual deploys
findings.failure_scenario: src/app/api/projects/[id]/deploy/route.ts:54 gates manual deploys with `const { withinLimits, limitType } = await checkUsageLimits(session.user.id); if (!withinLimits) return 403`. Neither webhook deploy path does: `grep -rn checkUsageLimits src/` returns only caps.ts, tiers.ts and the deploy route. handlePushEvent (line 129→194) and handlePullRequestEvent (line 520→590) go straight from createDeployment to submitCloudBuild. A free-tier user (limit 20 deployments / 100 build minutes per month, src/lib/billing/tiers.ts:36-38) exhausts the quota, then simply pushes empty commits to their connected repo — or opens/synchronises PRs — in a loop. Each event fires a full Cloud Build (docker pull, build, push, deploy) and a new always-billed Cloud Run revision, indefinitely.
findings.impact: The monetisation ceiling is trivially bypassed through the platform's primary, most-used deploy trigger: uncapped Cloud Build minutes, Artifact Registry storage and Cloud Run revisions for a $0 account. The push path is also the one that most tenants use exclusively, so the enforced path is the exception, not the rule.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read both webhook handlers end to end. The only gates are the HMAC signature check (line 37), `shouldAutoDeploy(project, branch)` (line 99) and `project.autoDeployPrs === false` (line 515) — all attacker-controlled or attacker-satisfiable, none tied to billing. Confirmed the deployment record is still created, so the usage counter in src/lib/billing/tracker.ts:64 keeps rising; nothing reads it to block.

findings.title: Unbounded project buildTimeout lets a tenant run 24-hour Cloud Builds that escape the build-minutes cap
findings.failure_scenario: Only a `> 0` check — no maximum. The value flows unchanged into the Cloud Build request: src/lib/gcp/cloudbuild.ts:536 `timeout: buildTimeout ? `${buildTimeout}s` : '1800s'`. A tenant PATCHes `{"buildTimeout":86400}` and sets `buildCommand` to something that blocks (the command is inlined into the build step). The buildMinutes quota cannot stop this: src/lib/billing/tracker.ts:98 sums `data.buildDurationMs`, which is only written after a build completes, and checkUsageLimits runs before submission — so all 20 of a free account's monthly deployments can be launched as concurrently-running 24-hour builds before a single minute is ever counted, ~480 build-hours against a 100-minute plan limit. Combined with the webhook bypass above, the deployment count ceiling disappears too.
findings.impact: Cloud Build compute billed to the platform at roughly 300x the tenant's paid allowance, plus occupation of the shared GCP project's concurrent-build quota, which queues and delays every other tenant's deploys.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped every buildTimeout reference in the repo (route.ts:135/153-162, deploy route:194, webhook:187 and :583, cloudbuild.ts:33/70/515/536) — the validation block quoted above is the only check anywhere, and cloudbuild.ts applies no clamp. Confirmed checkUsageLimits (src/lib/billing/caps.ts:14-32) compares against usage computed by getMonthlyUsage, which derives buildMinutes purely from persisted completed-build durations (tracker.ts:96-104), so in-flight builds are invisible to it.

result.coverage_notes:
Swept end-to-end: src/lib/gcp/{auth,iam,cloudrun,cloudsql (createInstance/deleteInstance/updateInstanceSettings),cloudbuild (full build+deploy config),networks,firewall,armor,discovery,labeling,seeding,topology,remediation-utils,security-auditor}.ts; src/app/api/infrastructure/{health,remediate,compliance-report}/route.ts; src/app/api/gcp/discover/route.ts; plus the routes those reach into — src/app/api/projects/[id]/{route,deploy}/route.ts, src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/route.ts (POST+PATCH), src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/[storageId]/remediate/route.ts, src/app/api/webhooks/github/route.ts, src/middleware/rbac.ts, src/lib/db.ts (listProjectsByTeam/getTeamMembership), src/lib/billing/{caps,tiers,tracker}.ts, src/lib/config.ts, src/lib/utils.ts (generateServiceName), src/proxy.ts.

Confirmed architecture facts underpinning several findings: (a) there is a SINGLE shared GCP project — every cloudrun.ts and cloudsql.ts call hardcodes `config.gcp.projectId || process.env.GCP_PROJECT_ID`, and `providerProjectId` from the tenant is only honoured in labeling.ts; (b) there is a SINGLE shared platform SA (`deployify-sa`) plus the default compute SA, with no per-tenant service account anywhere (`grep -c "service-account" src/lib/gcp/cloudbuild.ts` = 0); (c) there is NO platform-admin concept at all — grep for isAdmin/platformAdmin/superadmin across src/lib/auth.ts and src/middleware/rbac.ts returns nothing, and src/proxy.ts's matcher has no rule for /api/infrastructure or /api/gcp, so those routes are reachable by any signed-in customer; (d) the only cost guardrail in the codebase is checkUsageLimits, called from exactly one route.

Deliberately rejected as non-findings: (1) `--allow-unauthenticated` / allUsers run.invoker on tenant Cloud Run services (cloudbuild.ts:377, 420) — this is the intended product behaviour for a public PaaS, not a defect; (2) `gcpProjectId` passthrough to discoverResources GET — the platform SA has no permissions in third-party GCP projects, so cross-org enumeration fails closed (the in-shared-project enumeration it does enable is folded into the DELETE finding, which is the exploitable half); (3) resource-name injection via storage `name` → `resourceName` — the value lands in a JSON body for createInstance, and GCP's own name validation rejects path characters, so I could not construct a concrete bad outcome; (4) armor.ts / firewall.ts — all resource names are server-derived from projectSlug via `dfy-` prefixing, and srcIpRanges come from a fixed table in networks.ts, so no tenant-controlled value reaches a firewall rule.

Not covered (out of assigned scope or not reachable from the GCP surface): storage-validator.ts, monitoring.ts, external-sync.ts, migrations.ts and the ~40 per-storage sub-routes (query, import/export, clone, replica, branch, cutover, migrate-region) — several of these also provision billable GCP resources and likely share the missing-quota pattern of finding 6, but I did not read them closely enough to assert a specific defect. I also did not verify actual deployed IAM policy (no GCP access), so role-blast-radius claims are grounded strictly in the API calls the code makes.

findings.title: CI never runs tests or lint — the only gate is `npm run build`, and the same workflow auto-approves and auto-merges the PR
findings.evidence:
- name: Run build check
        run: npm run build
        continue-on-error: false

      - name: Approve PR
        run: gh pr review --approve "$PR_URL" || echo "..."

      - name: Enable auto-merge
        run: gh pr merge --auto --squash "$PR_URL" || echo "..."

(line 15 gate:)  if: ... || contains(github.event.pull_request.user.login, 'jules') || github.event.pull_request.user.login == 'asangzz'
findings.failure_scenario: There are exactly three workflow files (`auto-merge-jules.yml`, `cron-auto-merge.yml`, `sync-lockfile.yml`). `rg -n 'npm test|npm run test|npm run lint|eslint|playwright' .github/` returns NOTHING. So the 132 `test()`/`it()` cases in the 34 `*.test.ts` files and the `npm run lint` script are never executed by any automation — they only run when a human types them locally. Concretely: a PR from `asangzz` (the repo owner, per `git config user`) or any author matching `jules` that removes the `if (access.role === 'viewer')` guard at `src/app/api/projects/[id]/env/[envId]/reveal/route.ts:29`, or flips `src/lib/billing/payments.ts:74` `if (!webhookSecret) return false` to `return true`, still type-checks and still builds. The workflow therefore succeeds, runs `gh pr review --approve`, then `gh pr merge --auto --squash`, and the change lands on `main` unreviewed within minutes. `cron-auto-merge.yml:38` compounds this: `gh pr merge $pr --squash --admin` bypasses branch protection every 15 minutes for anything marked APPROVED — and the approval it looks for is the one the bot itself just wrote.
findings.impact: The entire test suite and linter are decorative. Any security regression in auth, RBAC, crypto, or billing signature verification reaches production `main` with zero human or automated review. Combined with finding #3 (zero tests on those modules), there is no layer at all that would catch it.
findings.checked_mitigations: Enumerated all of `.github/` (3 files, read end-to-end). Grepped for `npm test`, `npm run test`, `npm run lint`, `eslint`, `playwright` across `.github/` — no matches. Checked `package.json` scripts: `test` and `lint` exist and are runnable, they are simply never invoked by CI. Searched for other CI systems (no `.gitlab-ci.yml`, no `cloudbuild.yaml` at repo root, no `.circleci`).

findings.title: `getSession()` returns a hard-coded enterprise-admin session whenever `MOCK_DB=true`, with no `NODE_ENV` guard — a test hook shipped in the production bundle
findings.failure_scenario: `MOCK_DB` is a plain runtime env var, not a build-time constant, and the `MOCK_DB === 'true'` branch is NOT conjoined with any `NODE_ENV` check — so it is live in a production `NODE_ENV=production` container. Set `MOCK_DB=true` on the Cloud Run service (a plausible operator action: `src/lib/firebase.ts:17` uses the same flag to serve mock data, so an operator debugging a Firestore outage, or a revision cloned from staging, would set it) and every cookie-less request to any of the 84 API routes returns `MOCK_SESSION` — user `audit-test`, tier `enterprise`. `src/proxy.ts:165` does the same for the dashboard: `if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development' || process.env.MOCK_DB === 'true') { return response; }` skips the login redirect entirely. The bypass is also hard-coded into a route handler: `src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/[storageId]/backups/[backupId]/restore/route.ts:22` reads `if (process.env.MOCK_DB === 'true' && id === 'audit-id')` and skips `checkProjectAccess` altogether. Anonymous internet traffic becomes an authenticated enterprise admin.
findings.impact: A single env-var misconfiguration converts the whole platform to unauthenticated enterprise-admin access — project listing, env-var reveal, deploys, storage credential rotation, Cloud SQL restore. There is no test asserting the flag is inert under `NODE_ENV=production`, and per finding #1 no test would run anyway. The codebase already knows the correct pattern — `src/app/api/cron/optimize/route.ts:39` writes `if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production' || process.env.MOCK_DB !== 'true')` — so this is an inconsistency, not a deliberate design.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped every `MOCK_DB` occurrence in `src/` (50+ hits). Confirmed `src/lib/auth.ts:99` and `src/proxy.ts:165` use `NODE_ENV === 'development' || MOCK_DB === 'true'` (OR, so MOCK_DB alone suffices in production), unlike `src/app/api/cron/optimize/route.ts:39` which correctly hard-gates on production. Confirmed `next.config.ts` does not inline or strip `MOCK_DB`. Confirmed `env.example` never mentions `MOCK_DB`, so there is no documented warning. Grepped for any startup assertion rejecting `MOCK_DB` in production — none; `validateConfig()` (src/lib/config.ts:88) only `console.warn`s and does not check this flag.

findings.title: Zero test coverage on every security-critical module: auth, RBAC, crypto, security helpers, edge proxy, and both payment-signature verifiers
findings.failure_scenario: Inventory: 84 `route.ts` handlers under `src/app/api/**`; exactly ONE has a co-located test (`src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/[storageId]/query/route.test.ts`) — 1/84. 39 of 62 non-test files under `src/lib` have no sibling test. `rg -ln 'lib/auth|middleware/rbac|lib/crypto|lib/security|@/proxy|billing/payments' --glob 'src/**/*.test.ts'` returns only the three `*-branching.test.ts` files, and those import `@/lib/db` solely to exercise `getEnvVarsForDeployment` under `MOCK_DB=true` — they do not test auth, RBAC, or crypto. So `src/lib/auth.ts` (JWT mint/verify, session cookie), `src/middleware/rbac.ts` (the single `checkProjectAccess` used by ~40 routes), `src/lib/crypto.ts` (AES-256-GCM secret encryption), `src/lib/security/index.ts` (GitHub webhook HMAC, rate limiter, env-key validation), `src/proxy.ts` (the edge auth/rate-limit layer), and `src/lib/billing/payments.ts` all have literally zero assertions. The quoted line is the concrete cost: `verifyWebhookSignature` compares with `===` (non-constant-time) while the sibling `verifyGitHubWebhookSignature` at `src/lib/security/index.ts:69` correctly uses `crypto.timingSafeEqual` — a live inconsistency in the money path that no test flags. And nothing asserts the fail-closed `if (!webhookSecret) return false`; changing it to `return true` (the exact 'make local dev work without keys' pattern this repo already uses in `auth.ts:99` and `firebase.ts:17`) would let anyone POST `{"event":"payment.captured","payload":{"payment":{"entity":{"notes":{"userId":"<victim>","tierId":"enterprise"}}}}}` to `/api/billing/webhook` and self-provision an enterprise subscription.
findings.impact: The blast-radius modules — session issuance, the sole authorization primitive, secret encryption, and both payment verifiers — are the least tested code in the repo, inverting the risk/coverage relationship. Combined with finding #1 (CI runs no tests), a regression in any of them has no detection mechanism before production.
findings.checked_mitigations: Ran the full test inventory (`find src -name '*.test.ts'`, 34 files) and extracted every import across them — the only production modules imported are gcp/*, github/*, performance/lighthouse, billing/invoices, analytics, dockerfiles, utils, masking, and `@/lib/db` (3 branching tests). Confirmed no `__tests__` directories and no test files outside `src/` (the `.claude/worktrees/` hits are a git worktree copy of the same files, and `npm test`'s `find src ...` does not reach them). Confirmed `src/lib/billing/invoices.test.ts` exists but covers invoice formatting only, not `payments.ts`.

findings.title: Revealing a decrypted secret writes no audit record, while every other env-var mutation does
findings.failure_scenario: The file imports no audit module and calls `logAuditEvent` nowhere — the plaintext secret is returned and the request leaves no trace. By contrast, `src/app/api/projects/[id]/env/route.ts` audits all three mutations (`logAuditEvent` at lines 140, 259, 327), so add/update/delete of a secret is recorded but *reading* it is not. Concretely: a team member with role `developer` (the viewer check at line 29 stops only `viewer`) enumerates the project's env var ids from `GET /api/projects/<id>/env` and then issues `GET /api/projects/<id>/env/<envId>/reveal` for each one, collecting the decrypted DATABASE_URL, Razorpay/Stripe keys, and any GitHub token. `GET /api/teams/<id>/audit` (backed by `listAuditLogs`) shows nothing for these reads. The proxy rate limiter is keyed `${ip}:${pathname}` (src/proxy.ts:124) and each envId is a distinct pathname, so the 100/min budget is per-secret, not per-attacker — enumeration is effectively unthrottled.
findings.impact: Credential exfiltration by an insider or a stolen session cookie is invisible. During incident response there is no way to answer 'which secrets were read, by whom, and when', so the only safe remediation is rotating every secret in every project. This is the single highest-value read in the product and it is the one action with no audit trail.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped every `logAuditEvent` call site in `src/` (30 call sites across 20 route files) — the reveal route is not among them. Confirmed `src/lib/audit.ts` is the only audit sink and `Collections.AUDIT_LOGS` is written nowhere else. Confirmed `trackError` is not called here either (only 2 call sites repo-wide: `src/proxy.ts` and the public proxy route). Confirmed the route is not covered by a broader logging wrapper — there is no `instrumentation.ts` and `src/proxy.ts` logs nothing on the success path.

findings.title: Cloud SQL backup restore is neither audit-logged nor role-gated, and carries a `MOCK_DB` authorization bypass
findings.failure_scenario: Two defects in one destructive handler. (a) `access.role` is never inspected — `rg -c 'access\.role' src/app/api` confirms this file has zero occurrences, while the sibling credential-rotation route `src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/[storageId]/rotate/route.ts:29` correctly does `if (access.role === 'viewer') return 403`. So a user invited as `viewer` can POST to this endpoint and issue a Cloud SQL `restoreBackup`, which overwrites the live production database with an older snapshot — irreversible data loss for every write since that backup. (b) The handler then returns `{success:true}` and calls `logAuditEvent` nowhere (the file imports no audit module), so the destruction leaves no record of who triggered it. (c) The `MOCK_DB && id === 'audit-id'` branch skips `checkProjectAccess` entirely, so with finding #2's flag set, an unauthenticated caller reaches `restoreBackup` for project id `audit-id`.
findings.impact: A read-only collaborator can destroy a team's production database, and the audit log the team would consult afterwards is empty for that action. Backup restore is explicitly one of the security-relevant actions that must be recorded; it is the only destructive storage operation in the tree that is both unaudited and unauthorized.
findings.checked_mitigations: Read the route end-to-end (62 lines) — no `logAuditEvent`, no `access.role` check. Compared against every other storage sub-route: `rotate`, `clone`, `import`, `export`, `cutover`, `ingest`, `apply-index`, `replica`, `replica/promote` all appear in `rg -c 'access\.role'` output; `backups/[backupId]/restore` does not. Confirmed `logAuditEvent` is called by `rotate/route.ts:88`, `clone/route.ts:120`, `import/route.ts:83`, `export/route.ts:78`, `replica/promote/route.ts:64` — but not by the restore route. Confirmed `src/proxy.ts` applies no per-role or per-method gating that would compensate.

findings.title: The edge proxy's in-memory rate-limit Map has no eviction at all, keyed by attacker-controlled pathname
findings.failure_scenario: Expired records are overwritten only if the *same* key is seen again; they are never deleted. The key is `${ip}:${pathname}` and `pathname` is fully attacker-controlled — `src/proxy.ts`'s matcher is `'/((?!favicon.ico|public/).*)'`, so the rate-limit block runs for any request whose path starts with `/api/`, including paths with no matching route. A single client issuing `GET /api/x/1`, `/api/x/2`, ... `/api/x/N` inserts N permanent Map entries (each ~60–80 bytes of key plus a heap object), all of which return 404 from Next's router and none of which are ever reclaimed. A few million such requests — trivially cheap to send, and each individually within the 100/min budget because every key is fresh — grows the Map into the hundreds of megabytes until the Cloud Run container OOMs and is killed mid-request. The identical helper in `src/lib/security/index.ts:42` has `cleanupExpiredEntries()` invoked probabilistically (`if (Math.random() < 0.01)`) at line 20; `src/proxy.ts` was copied from it without that function, so this is an omission rather than a design choice.
findings.impact: Unauthenticated memory-exhaustion of the platform's own Cloud Run service, causing rolling container restarts that drop in-flight deploys and, because the rate-limit state lives only in that memory, reset every client's rate-limit counters on each restart. No metric or alert exists for Map size (see finding #8).
findings.checked_mitigations: Read `src/proxy.ts` end-to-end (214 lines) — there is no cleanup function, no `.delete()` call, no size cap, and no TTL anywhere in the file. Grepped for a Redis-backed limiter (`ioredis` is a dependency but is used only for user-owned storage connectors in `src/lib/redis-branching.ts`, not for platform rate limiting). Confirmed `src/lib/security/index.ts` has the eviction that `src/proxy.ts` lacks, so this is not intentional. Confirmed no external WAF layer is configured for the platform host (`src/lib/gcp/armor.ts` provisions Cloud Armor for user projects, not for Deployify itself).

findings.title: Public proxy failures write an unbounded, awaited Firestore document per request on a path that bypasses the rate limiter
findings.failure_scenario: Requests to a project subdomain never reach the rate limiter. In `src/proxy.ts`, the subdomain branch returns at line 109 — `return NextResponse.rewrite(url, { headers: responseHeaders });` — while the rate-limit block does not begin until line 115 (`if (pathname.startsWith('/api/'))`). The rewrite is internal, so the rewritten `/api/v1/proxy/<slug>/...` request is not re-evaluated by the proxy. Now pick any deployed project whose backing Cloud Run service is scaled to zero, erroring, or whose `productionUrl` is stale: `await fetch(targetUrl, ...)` at line 164 throws, and every single request then `await`s a `db.collection('errors').doc(id).set(event)` write carrying a full stack trace (`src/lib/logging/tracker.ts:51`) before the 502 is returned. There is no sampling, no dedup, no per-project cap, no TTL policy on the collection, and the write is on the critical path so it also inflates 502 latency. An anonymous attacker sending a few hundred requests per second at `https://<slug>.deployify.io/` drives that many writes per second into the platform's shared Firestore. The 502 body additionally echoes `targetUrl`, disclosing the project's internal `*.run.app` origin to the anonymous caller.
findings.impact: Anonymous, unmetered write amplification into the platform's shared Firestore: billing blowup plus contention against the same database that serves sessions, projects, and audit logs for every tenant. Because the write is awaited, a slow Firestore also serializes the error path and holds Cloud Run request slots open.
findings.checked_mitigations: Traced the request path in `src/proxy.ts` line by line and confirmed the subdomain `return` at line 109 precedes the `/api/` rate-limit block at line 115. Confirmed `checkRateLimit` is not called anywhere inside the proxy route handler itself. Grepped `Collections.ERRORS` — one write, no reads, no retention job; grepped `firestore.indexes.json` for a TTL policy on `errors` — none. Confirmed `trackError` has its own try/catch so it cannot itself throw and short-circuit the loop. Confirmed `logEdgeEvent` (line 180) is fire-and-forget, so the awaited write in the catch block is the blocking one.

findings.title: No error-reporting or APM integration anywhere, and the one 'central error tracker' is write-only — nothing ever reads the `errors` collection
findings.failure_scenario: `rg -n 'Collections.ERRORS'` across `src/` returns exactly one hit — this write at line 51. There is no read, no query, no API route, and no component that surfaces the `errors` collection (`rg -n 'ErrorEvent'` matches only the interface declaration and its use inside this same file). So every error that does get tracked is buried in Firestore where no human or alert ever sees it. And almost nothing is tracked: `trackError` has only two call sites repo-wide (`src/proxy.ts:183` and the public proxy route's catch), so 82 of 84 API route handlers report failures solely via `console.error` — 729 `console.*` calls across `src/`, none structured. There is no `@google-cloud/error-reporting`, no Sentry, no OpenTelemetry, and no Datadog in `package.json` (`rg -il 'sentry|@google-cloud/error|opentelemetry|datadog|newrelic' src package.json` returns nothing), and no `src/instrumentation.ts` to register one. No request id or trace field is attached to any log line or to `AuditEvent`/`ErrorEvent`, so the log lines emitted while handling one request cannot be correlated in Cloud Logging. Concretely: rotate `ENCRYPTION_KEY` without re-encrypting stored values and every deploy begins failing at `src/lib/db.ts:241` (`throw new Error('Failed to decrypt secret ...')`) and every secret reveal 500s at `reveal/route.ts:49`. Nothing aggregates, dedups, counts, or alerts on this — the failure is discovered only when a customer opens a support ticket.
findings.impact: No mean-time-to-detection for any production failure: failed deploys, failed Razorpay webhook processing, decrypt failures, and Firestore outages all degrade silently. Post-incident forensics is limited to grepping raw Cloud Run text logs with no request correlation, and the Firestore `errors` collection accumulates cost while providing zero operational value.
findings.checked_mitigations: Grepped `package.json` and all of `src/` for every common error-reporting/APM SDK — zero hits. Confirmed no `src/instrumentation.ts` and no `register()` hook (only `src/app/global-error.tsx` exists, which is a client-side React boundary and does not report anywhere). Grepped for `Collections.ERRORS` reads and for any `/api/**/errors` route — none exist. Grepped `logAuditEvent` and `trackError` signatures in `src/lib/audit.ts` and `src/lib/logging/tracker.ts` for a correlation/trace/request-id field — `AuditEvent` has only `{id, teamId, userId, action, details, createdAt}` and `ErrorEvent` only `{id, projectId, message, stack, path, method, timestamp, metadata}`. Confirmed `src/lib/gcp/monitoring.ts` and `src/lib/gcp/logging.ts` read Cloud Monitoring/Logging for *user* projects, not for the Deployify platform service itself.

result.coverage_notes:
SWEPT — Test inventory: 34 `*.test.ts` files (132 `test()`/`it()` cases), all under `src/`; no `__tests__` dirs, no test files outside `src/` (the `.claude/worktrees/hopeful-ramanujan-1c5e5b/` hits are a git worktree duplicate that `npm test`'s `find src ...` does not reach). Quantified coverage: 1 of 84 API `route.ts` handlers has a co-located test (`src/app/api/projects/[id]/storage/[storageId]/query/route.test.ts`); 39 of 62 non-test files under `src/lib` have no sibling test. Verified by import-extraction across all 34 test files that ZERO tests touch `src/lib/auth.ts`, `src/middleware/rbac.ts`, `src/lib/crypto.ts`, `src/lib/security/index.ts`, `src/proxy.ts`, `src/lib/billing/payments.ts`, the billing webhook/verify routes, or the public proxy route (the three `*-branching.test.ts` files import `@/lib/db` only to exercise `getEnvVarsForDeployment` under `MOCK_DB=true`).

E2E: `@playwright/test` and `playwright` are devDependencies but there is NO `playwright.config.*` anywhere, no file in the repo imports `@playwright/test`, and there is no `test:e2e` script. The only browser automation is three ad-hoc Python scripts (`scripts/verify_ui_177.py`, `scripts/verification/verify_alerts.py`) that hardcode `localhost:3000` and the `audit-id` mock project — not runnable in CI. Playwright is a dead ~200MB dependency.

CI: exactly three workflows, all read end-to-end. `rg 'npm test|npm run lint|eslint|playwright' .github/` → no matches. `auto-merge-jules.yml` runs `npm run build` only, then auto-approves and enables auto-merge; `cron-auto-merge.yml` merges with `--admin` every 15 minutes; `sync-lockfile.yml` pushes lockfile changes to `main`.
